Causal graphs

Directed graphs on Mathlib's Digraph: parents, ancestors, acyclicity, graph surgery; acyclic directed mixed graphs, districts and latent projection.

CausalInference.Graphical.Basic

CausalInference/Graphical/Basic.lean · 86 lines · 9 public theorems · 4 definitions

Parents and children in a directed graph. A causal graph is a Mathlib Digraph V, where G.Adj u v means that there is an edge u → v. This file defines the parents and the children of a vertex, both as sets and, for a finite vertex type with decidable adjacency, as finsets.

Sources: Pearl (2009)

CausalInference.Graphical.Ancestry

CausalInference/Graphical/Ancestry.lean · 391 lines · 55 public theorems · 9 definitions · imports Graphical.Basic

Ancestors and descendants in a directed graph. Directed reachability in a Digraph is Mathlib's Relation.TransGen G.Adj (a directed path with at least one edge) and Relation.ReflTransGen G.Adj (a directed path with zero or more edges). This file names the ancestor relation and the ancestral closures built from them.

Sources: Pearl (2009)

Public declarations (64)

Digraph.IsAncestordefinition

def IsAncestor (G : Digraph V) (u v : V) : Prop

G.IsAncestor u v means that there is a directed path with at least one edge from u to v in G; this is the strict ancestor relation.

Digraph.ancestorsdefinition

def ancestors (G : Digraph V) (v : V) : Set V

The strict ancestors of v: the vertices with a directed path of positive length to v.

Digraph.descendantsdefinition

def descendants (G : Digraph V) (v : V) : Set V

The strict descendants of v: the vertices reached from v by a directed path of positive length.

Digraph.ancestorsOfdefinition

def ancestorsOf (G : Digraph V) (S : Set V) : Set V

The inclusive ancestral closure of S: every vertex with a directed path of length at least zero into S. In particular S ⊆ G.ancestorsOf S.

Digraph.descendantsOfdefinition

def descendantsOf (G : Digraph V) (S : Set V) : Set V

The inclusive descendant closure of S: every vertex reached by a directed path of length at least zero from S. In particular S ⊆ G.descendantsOf S.

Digraph.reachIterdefinition

def reachIter (u : V) : ℕ → Finset V

Saturation from u: stage 0 is {u}, and each stage adds the children of the previous one. Stage n is the set of vertices reachable from u by a directed path of length at most n.

Digraph.reachFinsetdefinition

def reachFinset (u : V) : Finset V

The finset of vertices reachable from u by a directed path of length at least zero, computed as stage Fintype.card V of the saturation reachIter.

CausalInference.Graphical.Acyclic

CausalInference/Graphical/Acyclic.lean · 202 lines · 17 public theorems · 5 definitions · imports Graphical.Ancestry

Directed acyclic graphs. A digraph is acyclic when no vertex is a strict ancestor of itself, that is, when there is no directed cycle (self-loops count as cycles of length one).

Sources: Pearl (2009)

Public declarations (22)

Digraph.IsAcyclicdefinition

def IsAcyclic (G : Digraph V) : Prop

A digraph is acyclic when it has no directed cycle: no vertex reaches itself by a directed path with at least one edge.

theorem IsAcyclic.ne_of_isAncestor (hG : G.IsAcyclic) (huv : G.IsAncestor u v) : u ≠ v

theorem IsAcyclic.isAncestor_asymm (hG : G.IsAcyclic) (huv : G.IsAncestor u v) :
  ¬ G.IsAncestor v u

Digraph.isAcyclic_of_adj_lttheorem

theorem isAcyclic_of_adj_lt {α : Type*} [Preorder α] (f : V → α)
  (hf : ∀ ⦃u v⦄, G.Adj u v → f u < f v) : G.IsAcyclic

A graph that admits a strictly increasing labeling along its edges, into any preorder, is acyclic. No finiteness is needed for this direction.

Digraph.IsAcyclic.ancestors_ssubset_of_adjtheorem

theorem IsAcyclic.ancestors_ssubset_of_adj (hG : G.IsAcyclic) (huv : G.Adj u v) :
  G.ancestors u ⊂ G.ancestors v

In an acyclic graph, an edge u → v makes the strict ancestors of u a proper subset of those of v.

Digraph.IsAcyclic.exists_adj_lttheorem

theorem IsAcyclic.exists_adj_lt (hG : G.IsAcyclic) :
  ∃ f : V → ℕ, ∀ ⦃u v⦄, G.Adj u v → f u < f v

A finite acyclic graph has a topological order: counting strict ancestors gives f : V → ℕ with G.Adj u v → f u < f v.

Digraph.isAcyclic_iff_exists_adj_lttheorem

theorem isAcyclic_iff_exists_adj_lt :
  G.IsAcyclic ↔ ∃ f : V → ℕ, ∀ ⦃u v⦄, G.Adj u v → f u < f v

A graph on a finite vertex type is acyclic if and only if it admits a topological order f : V → ℕ, that is, G.Adj u v → f u < f v.

Digraph.IsAcyclic.exists_parents_eq_emptytheorem

theorem IsAcyclic.exists_parents_eq_empty [Nonempty V] (hG : G.IsAcyclic) :
  ∃ v, G.parents v = ∅

A nonempty finite acyclic graph has a source: a vertex with no parents.

Digraph.IsAcyclic.exists_children_eq_emptytheorem

theorem IsAcyclic.exists_children_eq_empty [Nonempty V] (hG : G.IsAcyclic) :
  ∃ v, G.children v = ∅

A nonempty finite acyclic graph has a sink: a vertex with no children.

CausalInference.Graphical.Mutilation

CausalInference/Graphical/Mutilation.lean · 289 lines · 44 public theorems · 3 definitions · imports Graphical.Acyclic

Graph surgery. The edge deletions used by interventions and by the rules of the do-calculus. All operations keep the vertex type and only remove edges.

Sources: Pearl (2009)

Public declarations (47)

Digraph.deleteIncomingdefinition

def deleteIncoming (G : Digraph V) (X : Set V) : Digraph V

Remove every edge whose head lies in X: u → v survives exactly when v ∉ X. This is Pearl's graph with a bar over X.

Digraph.deleteOutgoingdefinition

def deleteOutgoing (G : Digraph V) (X : Set V) : Digraph V

Remove every edge whose tail lies in X: u → v survives exactly when u ∉ X. This is Pearl's graph with a bar under X.

Digraph.restrictdefinition

def restrict (G : Digraph V) (S : Set V) : Digraph V

Keep only the edges with both endpoints in S; the vertex type is unchanged.

Digraph.deleteIncoming_adjtheorem

theorem deleteIncoming_adj : (G.deleteIncoming X).Adj u v ↔ G.Adj u v ∧ v ∉ X

Digraph.deleteOutgoing_adjtheorem

Digraph.restrict_adjtheorem

theorem restrict_adj : (G.restrict S).Adj u v ↔ G.Adj u v ∧ u ∈ S ∧ v ∈ S

CausalInference.Graphical.ADMG

CausalInference/Graphical/ADMG.lean · 418 lines · 52 public theorems · 18 definitions · imports Graphical.Closure, Graphical.TopologicalOrder

Acyclic directed mixed graphs. A directed mixed graph on a vertex type V has a directed part, a Mathlib Digraph V whose edge u → v is G.directed.Adj u v, and a bidirected part, a Mathlib SimpleGraph V whose edge u ↔ v is G.bidirected.Adj u v. Using SimpleGraph makes the bidirected part symmetric and irreflexive by construction and gives access to Mathlib's connectivity API, which the districts in CausalInference.Graphical.Districts reuse.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Richardson (2003)

Public declarations (70)

CausalInference.ADMGstructure

structure ADMG (V : Type*)

A directed mixed graph on V: a directed part directed : Digraph V (the edge u → v is directed.Adj u v) and a bidirected part bidirected : SimpleGraph V (the edge u ↔ v is bidirected.Adj u v, symmetric and irreflexive). Acyclicity of the directed part is the separate predicate ADMG.IsAcyclic.

CausalInference.ADMG.restrictdefinition

def restrict (G : ADMG V) (S : Set V) : ADMG V

The induced sub-ADMG on S: keep the directed and the bidirected edges with both endpoints in S. The vertex type is unchanged, so vertices outside S become isolated. The directed part is Digraph.restrict.

CausalInference.ADMG.deleteIncomingdefinition

def deleteIncoming (G : ADMG V) (X : Set V) : ADMG V

Pearl's graph with a bar over X, the graph of the intervention do(X): remove every directed edge into X, and remove every bidirected edge with an endpoint in X. A bidirected edge u ↔ v stands for a latent common cause, that is, for arrowheads at both u and v, so cutting all arrows into X removes it as soon as one endpoint is in X.

CausalInference.ADMG.deleteOutgoingdefinition

def deleteOutgoing (G : ADMG V) (X : Set V) : ADMG V

Pearl's graph with a bar under X: remove every directed edge out of X. The bidirected part is unchanged, since a bidirected edge has arrowheads at both endpoints and no tail.

CausalInference.Graphical.Districts

CausalInference/Graphical/Districts.lean · 261 lines · 27 public theorems · 6 definitions · imports Graphical.ADMG

Districts (c-components) of a directed mixed graph. The district of a vertex v is the set of vertices reachable from v by a path of bidirected edges, including v itself. Equivalently, it is the connected component of v in the bidirected part, a Mathlib SimpleGraph, so it is defined through SimpleGraph.Reachable and related to SimpleGraph.ConnectedComponent. Districts are the c-components of Tian and Pearl.

Sources: Richardson (2003); Tian and Pearl (2002)

CausalInference.Graphical.LatentProjection

CausalInference/Graphical/LatentProjection.lean · 1008 lines · 71 public theorems · 9 definitions · imports Graphical.Districts

Latent projection. Given a directed mixed graph G on V and a set L of latent vertices, the latent projection of G onto the observed vertices V \ L keeps the vertex type V and makes every latent vertex isolated. Its edges between observed vertices u and v are:

Sources: Pearl (2009); Richardson (2003); Verma and Pearl (1990)

def LatentPath (D : Digraph V) (L : Set V) (a b : V) : Prop

LatentPath D L a b: there is a directed path in D from a to b with at least one edge, all of whose interior vertices lie in L (the endpoints are unrestricted).

CausalInference.LatentAncdefinition

def LatentAnc (D : Digraph V) (L : Set V) (a b : V) : Prop

LatentAnc D L a b: either a = b, or a is latent and LatentPath D L a b. This is the end segment a → ⋯ → b of a collider-free latent-interior path that arrives at b with an arrowhead, starting from a latent vertex or from the bidirected edge at a = b.

The bidirected adjacency of the latent projection, before symmetrization proofs: u ≠ v, both observed, and either a latent source with latent-interior directed paths to u and v, or a bidirected edge a ↔ b of G followed by LatentAnc segments a ⇝ u, b ⇝ v.

CausalInference.ADMG.projectdefinition

def project (G : ADMG V) (L : Set V) : ADMG V

The latent projection of the directed mixed graph G with latent set L, on the same vertex type, with every latent vertex isolated. Between observed vertices it has * u → v when G has a directed path from u to v with latent interior; * u ↔ v, for u ≠ v, when G has a collider-free latent-interior path between u and v with arrowheads at both ends: either a latent l with latent-interior directed paths to u and to v, or a bidirected edge a ↔ b of G with LatentAnc G.directed L a u and LatentAnc G.directed L b v. projectBiAdj_iff_exists_path and project_directed_adj_iff_exists_path state both edge kinds as path criteria.

CausalInference.ADMG.LatentTrailinductive type

inductive LatentTrail (G : ADMG V) (L : Set V) : Bool → V → V → List V → Prop

G.LatentTrail L a u w l: l is the list of vertices of a walk in G from u to w in which every vertex other than the last lies in L, no vertex is a collider, and the last step enters w through an arrowhead. A step uses a directed edge in either direction or a bidirected edge. The flag a = true records that the walk arrived at u through an arrowhead at u. A collider is a vertex entered and left through arrowheads, so a vertex entered through an arrowhead can only be left along a directed edge out of it. The constructors are: * nil: the one-vertex walk at w, allowed only with flag true (an arrowhead at w); * fwd: a step along u → v from a latent u; it leaves u through a tail and enters v through an arrowhead; * bwd: a step along u ← v from a latent u not entered through an arrowhead; it enters v through a tail; * bi: a step along u ↔ v from a latent u not entered through an arrowhead; it enters v through an arrowhead.

CausalInference.ADMG.ProjectionTraildefinition

def ProjectionTrail (G : ADMG V) (L : Set V) (u w : V) (l : List V) : Prop

G.ProjectionTrail L u w l: l is the list of vertices of a walk from u to w whose interior vertices all lie in L, with no collider, and with an arrowhead at both ends: the first step enters u through an arrowhead (u ← v or u ↔ v), and the rest is a LatentTrail from v. With l.Nodup it is a path.

CausalInference.ADMG.DirectedProjectionTraildefinition

def DirectedProjectionTrail (G : ADMG V) (L : Set V) (u w : V) (l : List V) : Prop

G.DirectedProjectionTrail L u w l: l is the list of vertices of a directed walk u → ⋯ → w with at least one edge whose interior vertices all lie in L. With l.Nodup it is a directed path.

CausalInference.ADMG.LatentTrail.exists_noduptheorem

theorem exists_nodup (p : G.LatentTrail L a u w l) (hw : w ∉ L) :
  ∃ l', l'.Sublist l ∧ G.LatentTrail L a u w l' ∧ l'.Nodup

Shortening to a path: a walk ending at an observed w contains a walk with the same endpoints and flag and no repeated vertex. A repeated vertex is latent, and cutting out the loop between two of its occurrences creates no collider.

CausalInference.ADMG.LatentTrail.shapetheorem

theorem shape (p : G.LatentTrail L a u w l) :
  (a = true → LatentAnc G.directed L u w) ∧

The shape of a LatentTrail. Entered through an arrowhead, it is a LatentAnc segment. Otherwise it runs backward along directed edges to a latent vertex c and then either forward to w, or across a bidirected edge c ↔ d and forward from d to w.

CausalInference.latentProjectiondefinition

def latentProjection (D : Digraph V) (L : Set V) : ADMG V

The latent projection of the directed graph D with latent set L: an ADMG on the same vertex type, with every latent vertex isolated. Between observed vertices it has u → v when D has a directed path from u to v with latent interior, and u ↔ v (for u ≠ v) when some latent l has directed latent-interior paths to both u and v (latentProjection_bidirected_adj).

CausalInference.latentProjection_directed_adjtheorem

theorem latentProjection_directed_adj :
  (latentProjection D L).directed.Adj u v ↔ u ∉ L ∧ v ∉ L ∧ LatentPath D L u v

CausalInference.latentProjection_bidirected_adjtheorem

theorem latentProjection_bidirected_adj :
  (latentProjection D L).bidirected.Adj u v ↔
    u ≠ v ∧ u ∉ L ∧ v ∉ L ∧ ∃ l ∈ L, LatentPath D L l u ∧ LatentPath D L l v

In the latent projection of a DAG, u ↔ v exactly when u and v are distinct observed vertices with a common latent source l reaching each by a directed latent-interior path.

CausalInference.Graphical.DSeparation

CausalInference/Graphical/DSeparation.lean · 517 lines · 48 public theorems · 4 definitions · imports Graphical.Mutilation

d-separation. d-separation in a directed graph G : Digraph V, defined purely graphically through the "Bayes-ball" reachability formulation, together with its basic theory.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Pearl (1988); Verma and Pearl (1988); Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen and Leimer (1990); Shachter (1998)

Public declarations (52)

Digraph.Passesdefinition

def Passes (G : Digraph V) (Z : Set V) (v : V) (b c : Bool) : Prop

G.Passes Z v b c: a trail that arrived at v (through an arrowhead at v if b = true) and leaves v along an edge pointing into v (if c = false) or out of v (if c = true) is not blocked at v given Z. If v is a collider of the trail (b = true and c = false) this means v ∈ G.ancestorsOf Z; otherwise it means v ∉ Z.

Digraph.bayesBalldefinition

def bayesBall (G : Digraph V) (Z : Set V) : Digraph (V × Bool)

The Bayes-ball state graph of G given Z. A state (v, b) records a vertex v reached by a trail, with b = true when the trail arrived at v along an edge pointing into v. There is an edge (v, b) → (w, c) when the trail can continue from v to w: it uses the edge v → w if c = true and the edge w → v if c = false, and v lets the trail pass (Digraph.Passes).

Digraph.DConndefinition

def DConn (G : Digraph V) (X Y Z : Set V) : Prop

G.DConn X Y Z: X and Y are d-connected given Z in G. Some x ∈ X and y ∈ Y, both outside Z, are joined by a trail that is active given Z: every collider of the trail is in G.ancestorsOf Z and every other vertex of the trail is outside Z. The trail is encoded as a path of the Bayes-ball state graph starting at (x, false).

Digraph.DSepdefinition

def DSep (G : Digraph V) (X Y Z : Set V) : Prop

G.DSep X Y Z: X and Y are d-separated by Z in G, that is, not d-connected: every trail between a vertex of X \ Z and a vertex of Y \ Z has a collider outside G.ancestorsOf Z or a non-collider in Z.

  (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (v, a) (w, true) ↔ G.Adj v w ∧ v ∉ Z

theorem bayesBall_adj_false_false :
  (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (v, false) (w, false) ↔ G.Adj w v ∧ v ∉ Z

theorem passes_comm : G.Passes Z v b c ↔ G.Passes Z v (!c) (!b)

Passing is invariant under reversing the trail: the arrival and departure flags swap and are negated.

  v ∉ Z

A trail leaving a state that was not entered through an arrowhead starts outside Z.

Digraph.mem_ancestorsOf_of_reflTransGen_bayesBalltheorem

theorem mem_ancestorsOf_of_reflTransGen_bayesBall {s : V × Bool}
  (h : ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj s (w, false)) (hs : s.2 = true) :
  s.1 ∈ G.ancestorsOf Z

A trail that is entered through an arrowhead and later arrives somewhere through a tail must turn at a collider, which is a descendant of its first vertex; so the first vertex is in G.ancestorsOf Z.

  ∃ c, ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (u, b) (w, c)

A directed path out of a vertex that is not an ancestor of Z is an active trail given Z, whatever the arrival flag at its first vertex.

Digraph.reflTransGen_bayesBall_reversetheorem

theorem reflTransGen_bayesBall_reverse {s t : V × Bool}
  (h : ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj s t) (e : Bool) (he : G.Passes Z t.1 t.2 e) :
  ∃ c, ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (t.1, !e) (s.1, c) ∧ G.Passes Z s.1 c (!s.2)

Reversal of an active trail, generalized over the flags at both ends: a trail from s to t that may continue past t with departure flag e can be reversed into a trail from (t.1, !e) to some (s.1, c) that may continue past s.1 with departure flag !s.2.

  (hm : m ∈ G.ancestorsOf Z) (hv : v ∉ Z) : G.DConn {u} {v} Z

Digraph.dSep_of_blocktheorem

theorem dSep_of_block (hu : ∀ w, G.Adj u w ∨ G.Adj w u → w = m)
  (hpar : ∀ w, G.Adj w m → w = u) (hm : m ∈ Z) (huY : u ∉ Y) : G.DSep {u} Y Z

Blocking at a conditioned vertex with no other connection. Suppose the only neighbor of u (in either direction) is m, the only possible parent of m is u, and m ∈ Z. Then u is d-separated given Z from every set not containing u. This covers the chain u → m → v and the fork u ← m → v when no other edge touches u or enters m: conditioning on the middle vertex blocks.

Digraph.dSep_of_collidertheorem

theorem dSep_of_collider (hu : ∀ w, G.Adj u w ∨ G.Adj w u → w = m) (hch : ∀ w, ¬ G.Adj m w)
  (hm : m ∉ Z) (huY : u ∉ Y) (hmY : m ∉ Y) : G.DSep {u} Y Z

An unconditioned collider with no descendants blocks. Suppose the only neighbor of u (in either direction) is m, the vertex m has no children and m ∉ Z. Then u is d-separated given Z from every set containing neither u nor m. This covers the collider u → m ← v with no other edge touching u or leaving m: without conditioning on m (or a descendant), u and v are d-separated.

  G.DSep {v} (G.descendantsOf {v})ᶜ (G.parents v)

In an acyclic graph, a vertex is d-separated from its non-descendants given its parents. Since parents are in the conditioning set and endpoints in the conditioning set are blocked, this is equivalent to the textbook form with the non-descendants that are not parents.

CausalInference.Graphical.DSeparationDecide

CausalInference/Graphical/DSeparationDecide.lean · 258 lines · 10 public theorems · 3 definitions · imports Graphical.DSeparation

Deciding d-separation, and the textbook path definition. The definition Digraph.DConn of CausalInference.Graphical.DSeparation is reachability in the Bayes-ball state graph. This file states the textbook definitions by active trails and by active simple paths, proves that both agree with Digraph.DConn, and derives decidability of d-separation on finite graphs.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Shachter (1998)

Public declarations (13)

Digraph.ActiveTrailinductive type

inductive ActiveTrail (G : Digraph V) (Z : Set V) : Bool → V → V → List V → Prop

G.ActiveTrail Z a u w l: l is the list of vertices of a trail from u to w in G that is active given Z. A trail is a walk in the underlying undirected graph whose steps each use an edge of G in either direction. The flag a = true records that the trail was entered at u through an arrowhead at u. The constructors are: * nil: the one-vertex trail at v; its vertex is an endpoint, hence a non-collider, so v ∉ Z; * fwd: a step along u → v; the trail leaves u through a tail, so u is a non-collider and u ∉ Z; * bwd: a step along u ← v from a vertex u not entered through an arrowhead; u is a non-collider and u ∉ Z; * collider: a step along u ← v from a vertex u entered through an arrowhead; u is a collider and must lie in G.ancestorsOf Z (it or a descendant is in Z).

Digraph.DConnTraildefinition

def DConnTrail (G : Digraph V) (X Y Z : Set V) : Prop

G.DConnTrail X Y Z: a vertex of X and a vertex of Y are joined by a trail that is active given Z (vertices may repeat).

Digraph.DConnPathdefinition

def DConnPath (G : Digraph V) (X Y Z : Set V) : Prop

G.DConnPath X Y Z: a vertex of X and a vertex of Y are joined by a simple path (no repeated vertex) that is active given Z: every collider of the path is in G.ancestorsOf Z and every other vertex of the path, endpoints included, is outside Z. This is the textbook definition of d-connection.

  w ∉ Z ∧ ∃ e, ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (u, a) (w, e)

An active trail is a path of the Bayes-ball state graph ending outside Z.

Prepending one step of the state graph to an active trail.

A path of the Bayes-ball state graph ending outside Z gives an active trail.

theorem dConn_iff_dConnTrail : G.DConn X Y Z ↔ G.DConnTrail X Y Z

The Bayes-ball definition of d-connection agrees with the definition by active trails.

theorem ActiveTrail.exists_suffix {x : V} (p : G.ActiveTrail Z a u w l) (hx : x ∈ l) :
  ∃ b l', l' <:+ l ∧ G.ActiveTrail Z b x w l' ∧
    ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (u, a) (x, b)

The suffix of an active trail from a later occurrence of a vertex x is an active trail from x, for the arrival flag b of that occurrence, and the state graph reaches (x, b) from the start.

Digraph.ActiveTrail.of_reflTransGen_looptheorem

theorem ActiveTrail.of_reflTransGen_loop (p : G.ActiveTrail Z b u w l)

Cutting out a loop: if the state graph leads from (u, a) back to (u, b), then an active trail from u entered with flag b is also active when entered with flag a.

The Bayes-ball definition of d-connection agrees with the textbook definition by active simple paths.

CausalInference.Graphical.Induce

CausalInference/Graphical/Induce.lean · 166 lines · 15 public theorems · 2 definitions · imports Graphical.TopologicalOrder

Induced subgraphs on a subtype. Digraph.restrict G S keeps the vertex type, so every vertex outside S survives as an isolated vertex. The induced subgraph Digraph.induce G S : Digraph S instead has exactly the vertices of S, with the edges of G between them. The pinned Mathlib has no Digraph.induce or Digraph.comap, so it is defined here.

CausalInference.Graphical.Factorization

CausalInference/Graphical/Factorization.lean · 360 lines · 19 public theorems · 5 definitions · imports Basic.FiniteCondIndep, Graphical.Mutilation

Markov factorization along a directed graph. Finite variables indexed by the vertices of a Digraph V, with a Markov kernel for each vertex given its parents, and distributions that factorize as the product of these kernels.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Lauritzen (1996); Pearl (1988)

CausalInference.FiniteDist.margAt_insert_of_margAt_inserttheorem

theorem margAt_insert_of_margAt_insert (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) {A B : Finset V} {v : V}
  (hAB : A ⊆ B) (hvB : v ∉ B) (f : (∀ v, α v) → ℝ)
  (hf : ∀ y y', (∀ u ∈ insert v A, y u = y' u) → f y = f y')
  (h : ∀ y, p.margAt (insert v B) y = f y * p.margAt B y) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.margAt (insert v A) x = f x * p.margAt A x

Lifting a product decomposition of a marginal to smaller sets. Suppose A ⊆ B, v ∉ B, and p(x_{B ∪ {v}}) = f x * p(x_B) for all x, where f depends only on the coordinates in A ∪ {v}. Then p(x_{A ∪ {v}}) = f x * p(x_A).

CausalInference.FiniteDist.sum_agreeOn_compl_eq_sum_updatetheorem

theorem sum_agreeOn_compl_eq_sum_update {M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M] (F : (∀ v, α v) → M)
  {T : Finset V} {s : V} (hs : s ∈ T) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  ∑ y ∈ FiniteDist.agreeOn Tᶜ x, F y =
    ∑ y ∈ FiniteDist.agreeOn (T.erase s)ᶜ x, ∑ a : α s, F (Function.update y s a)

Splitting off one coordinate s ∈ T from a sum over the configurations that agree with x outside T.

structure MarkovKernels (G : Digraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (α : V → Type*)

Markov kernels for the vertices of G: for each vertex v and each configuration of its parents, a probability mass function on the values of v.

The factor of v at the full configuration x: the kernel of v evaluated at the parent configuration of x and the value x v.

The product of the factors of the vertices in S at the configuration x.

theorem factor_nonneg (v : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) : 0 ≤ k.factor v x

Digraph.MarkovKernels.prodOn_nonnegtheorem

theorem prodOn_nonneg (S : Finset V) (x : ∀ v, α v) : 0 ≤ k.prodOn S x

Digraph.MarkovKernels.prodOn_emptytheorem

theorem prodOn_empty (x : ∀ v, α v) : k.prodOn ∅ x = 1

theorem factor_congr {v : V} {x y : ∀ v, α v} (h : ∀ u, u = v ∨ G.Adj u v → x u = y u) :
  k.factor v x = k.factor v y

The factor of v depends only on the coordinates of v and of its parents.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.factor_update_of_not_adjtheorem

theorem factor_update_of_not_adj [DecidableEq V] {s v : V} (hsv : s ≠ v) (hadj : ¬ G.Adj s v)
  (x : ∀ v, α v) (a : α s) : k.factor v (Function.update x s a) = k.factor v x

Changing the value of a vertex s that is neither v nor a parent of v does not change the factor of v.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.sum_factor_updatetheorem

theorem sum_factor_update [DecidableEq V] {s : V} (hs : ¬ G.Adj s s) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  ∑ a : α s, k.factor s (Function.update x s a) = ∑ a : α s, k.kernel s
    ((G.parentsFinset s).restrict x) a

Summing the factor of a vertex without a self-loop over its own values gives one.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.sum_update_prodOntheorem

theorem sum_update_prodOn [DecidableEq V] {S : Finset V} {s : V} (hs : s ∈ S)
  (hsink : ∀ v ∈ S, ¬ G.Adj s v) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  ∑ a : α s, k.prodOn S (Function.update x s a) = k.prodOn (S.erase s) x

Summing out a sink. If s ∈ S has no child in S (in particular no self-loop), then summing the product of the factors over S over the values of x s gives the product over S.erase s.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.sum_agreeOn_prodOntheorem

theorem sum_agreeOn_prodOn [DecidableEq V] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)] (hG : G.IsAcyclic)
  {S T : Finset V} (hTS : T ⊆ S)
  (hT : ∀ u ∈ T, ∀ v ∈ S, G.Adj u v → v ∈ T) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  ∑ y ∈ FiniteDist.agreeOn Tᶜ x, k.prodOn S y = k.prodOn (S \ T) x

Summing out a child-closed set of vertices. For an acyclic graph, if T ⊆ S and every child inside S of a vertex of T lies in T, then summing the product of the factors over S over the coordinates in T (with the other coordinates fixed to those of x) gives the product over S \ T.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.nonempty_valuetheorem

theorem nonempty_value (hG : G.IsAcyclic) (v : V) : Nonempty (α v)

For an acyclic graph with Markov kernels, every value type is nonempty: by induction along a topological order, a vertex whose parents have values has a parent configuration, and the kernel there sums to one, so the vertex has a value.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.nonempty_configtheorem

theorem nonempty_config (hG : G.IsAcyclic) : Nonempty (∀ v, α v)

For an acyclic graph with Markov kernels, there is a configuration.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.sum_prodOn_univtheorem

theorem sum_prodOn_univ [DecidableEq V] (hG : G.IsAcyclic) :
  ∑ x, k.prodOn univ x = 1

Normalization. For an acyclic graph, the product of any family of Markov kernels sums to one over all configurations.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.jointDistdefinition

def jointDist [DecidableEq V] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)] (hG : G.IsAcyclic) :
  FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)

For an acyclic graph, the product of a family of Markov kernels as a finite distribution on configurations.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.jointDist_applytheorem

theorem jointDist_apply [DecidableEq V] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)] (hG : G.IsAcyclic)
  (x : ∀ v, α v) : k.jointDist hG x = ∏ v, k.factor v x

Digraph.MarkovKernels.margAt_of_ancestraltheorem

theorem margAt_of_ancestral [DecidableEq V] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)] (hG : G.IsAcyclic)
  {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)} (hp : ∀ x, p x = ∏ v, k.factor v x) {A : Finset V}
  (hA : ∀ v ∈ A, ∀ u, G.Adj u v → u ∈ A) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.margAt A x = k.prodOn A x

Marginal on an ancestral set. If p is the product of the kernels of an acyclic graph and A is closed under taking parents, then the marginal mass of p on A at x is the product of the factors of the vertices of A.

Digraph.mem_of_adj_of_ancestorsOf_eqtheorem

theorem _root_.Digraph.mem_of_adj_of_ancestorsOf_eq {A : Finset V}
  (hA : G.ancestorsOf (A : Set V) = A) {u v : V} (hv : v ∈ A) (huv : G.Adj u v) : u ∈ A

A finset whose ancestral closure (in the sense of Digraph.ancestorsOf) is itself is closed under taking parents.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.margAt_of_ancestorsOf_eqtheorem

theorem margAt_of_ancestorsOf_eq [DecidableEq V] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)] (hG : G.IsAcyclic)
  {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)} (hp : ∀ x, p x = ∏ v, k.factor v x) {A : Finset V}
  (hA : G.ancestorsOf (A : Set V) = A) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.margAt A x = ∏ v ∈ A, k.factor v x

The marginal on an ancestral set A (with G.ancestorsOf A = A) of a distribution that factorizes according to an acyclic G is the product of the kernels of the vertices of A.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.margAt_insert_parentstheorem

theorem margAt_insert_parents [DecidableEq V] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)] (hG : G.IsAcyclic)
  {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)} (hp : ∀ x, p x = ∏ v, k.factor v x) (v : V)
  (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.margAt (insert v (G.parentsFinset v)) x =
    k.kernel v ((G.parentsFinset v).restrict x) (x v) * p.margAt (G.parentsFinset v) x

The kernel is the conditional distribution given the parents, in product form: p(x_v, x_pa(v)) = kernel v x_pa(v) x_v * p(x_pa(v)).

Digraph.Factorizesdefinition

def Factorizes [DecidableEq V] (G : Digraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
  (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) : Prop

A distribution p on configurations factorizes according to G when there are Markov kernels with p x = ∏ v, kernel v (x restricted to the parents of v) (x v) for all x.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.factorizes_jointDisttheorem

theorem MarkovKernels.factorizes_jointDist [DecidableEq V] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)]

  G.Factorizes (k.jointDist hG)

The product of the kernels of an acyclic graph factorizes according to the graph.

The nondescendants of v: the vertices other than v that are not reached from v by a directed path.

Digraph.LocalMarkovdefinition

def LocalMarkov (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) : Prop

The local directed Markov property of p with respect to G: every vertex is conditionally independent of its nondescendants other than its parents, given its parents.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.localMarkovtheorem

  {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)} (hp : ∀ x, p x = ∏ v, k.factor v x) : G.LocalMarkov p

Factorization implies the local Markov property. If p is the product of the Markov kernels k of an acyclic graph G, then every vertex is conditionally independent of its nondescendants given its parents.

  (h : G.Factorizes p) : G.LocalMarkov p

Factorization implies the local Markov property, for a distribution that factorizes according to an acyclic graph.

Digraph.mem_of_reflTransGen_of_closedtheorem

  {c w : V} (hcw : Relation.ReflTransGen G.Adj c w) (hw : w ∈ A) : c ∈ A

A set closed under taking parents is closed under taking ancestors.

Digraph.condKernelsdefinition

def condKernels (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) : G.MarkovKernels α

The conditional distribution of each vertex given its parents under p, as Markov kernels: P(x_v = a, x_pa = z) / P(x_pa = z) when P(x_pa = z) > 0, and the uniform distribution on α v for parent configurations of probability zero (a convention that does not affect the factorization, since those configurations carry no mass).

Digraph.condKernels_factortheorem

theorem condKernels_factor (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) (v : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  (condKernels G p).factor v x =
    if p.margAt (G.parentsFinset v) x = 0 then (1 / Fintype.card (α v) : ℝ)
    else p.margAt (insert v (G.parentsFinset v)) x / p.margAt (G.parentsFinset v) x

The factor of v for condKernels at x, in terms of marginal masses.

Digraph.LocalMarkov.margAt_eq_prodOntheorem

theorem LocalMarkov.margAt_eq_prodOn (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)}
  (hL : G.LocalMarkov p) {A : Finset V} (hA : ∀ w ∈ A, ∀ u, G.Adj u w → u ∈ A)
  (x : ∀ v, α v) : p.margAt A x = (condKernels G p).prodOn A x

Local Markov implies factorization, on ancestral sets: if p satisfies the local Markov property for an acyclic G, then on every set A closed under taking parents the marginal of p is the product of the conditional kernels condKernels G p of the vertices of A.

Digraph.LocalMarkov.factorizestheorem

theorem LocalMarkov.factorizes (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)}
  (hL : G.LocalMarkov p) : G.Factorizes p

Local Markov implies factorization: for an acyclic graph, a distribution satisfying the local Markov property is the product of its conditional kernels condKernels G p.

theorem factorizes_iff_localMarkov (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)} :
  G.Factorizes p ↔ G.LocalMarkov p

For an acyclic graph, factorization and the local Markov property are equivalent.

CausalInference.Graphical.GlobalMarkov

CausalInference/Graphical/GlobalMarkov.lean · 429 lines · 24 public theorems · 4 definitions · imports Graphical.LocalMarkov, Graphical.DSeparationDecide

The global Markov property. Soundness of d-separation: a finite distribution that factorizes according to an acyclic graph satisfies every conditional independence read off the graph by d-separation. Consequently factorization, the local Markov property and the global Markov property are equivalent.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Lauritzen (1996); Verma and Pearl (1988); Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen and Leimer (1990)

Public declarations (28)

CausalInference.FiniteDist.CondIndepFun.of_left_condtheorem

theorem CondIndepFun.of_left_cond (h : p.CondIndepFun X Y Z) {X' : Ω → β'}
  (φ : β → δ → β') (hX : ∀ ω, X' ω = φ (X ω) (Z ω)) : p.CondIndepFun X' Y Z

Conditional independence passes to any function of the first variable and the conditioning variable: X ⫫ Y | Z implies φ(X, Z) ⫫ Y | Z.

  (hY : ∀ ω, Y' ω = ψ (Y ω) (Z ω)) : p.CondIndepFun X Y' Z

Conditional independence passes to any function of the second variable and the conditioning variable: X ⫫ Y | Z implies X ⫫ ψ(Y, Z) | Z.

theorem CondIndep.union_cond_left (h : p.CondIndep X Y Z) : p.CondIndep (X ∪ Z) Y Z

Adding the conditioning coordinates to the first set preserves conditional independence.

Adding the conditioning coordinates to the second set preserves conditional independence.

theorem condIndep_sdiff_iff : p.CondIndep (X \ Z) (Y \ Z) Z ↔ p.CondIndep X Y Z

Coordinates in the conditioning set are irrelevant on either side: X ⫫ Y | Z holds exactly when X \ Z ⫫ Y \ Z | Z does.

Digraph.reflTransGen_bayesBall_of_reflTransGen_revtheorem

theorem reflTransGen_bayesBall_of_reflTransGen_rev {v t : V} (h : ReflTransGen G.Adj v t)
  (hv : v ∉ G.ancestorsOf Z) : ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (t, false) (v, false)

A directed path v → ⋯ → t whose first vertex is not an ancestor of Z, read backwards from t, is an active trail given Z that always moves against the edges (arrival flag false).

Digraph.DSep.reach_familytheorem

theorem DSep.reach_family (hsep : G.DSep X Y Z) (hXZ : ∀ x ∈ X, x ∉ Z) {v u w : V}
  (hvA : v ∈ G.ancestorsOf (X ∪ Y ∪ Z)) (hu : u = v ∨ G.Adj u v) (hw : w = v ∨ G.Adj w v)
  (huZ : u ∉ Z) {x : V} (hx : x ∈ X) {b : Bool}
  (hxu : ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (x, false) (u, b)) :
  ∃ x ∈ X, ∃ c, ReflTransGen (G.bayesBall Z).Adj (x, false) (w, c)

Families are not split by d-separation. Suppose X is disjoint from Z, X and Y are d-separated by Z, the vertex v lies in the ancestral closure of X ∪ Y ∪ Z, and u and w are members of the family {v} ∪ parents v with u ∉ Z. If an active trail given Z leads from a vertex of X to u, then an active trail given Z leads from a vertex of X to w.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.condIndep_of_dSep_of_disjointtheorem

theorem MarkovKernels.condIndep_of_dSep_of_disjoint (k : G.MarkovKernels α) (hG : G.IsAcyclic)
  {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)} (hp : ∀ x, p x = ∏ v, k.factor v x) {X Y Z : Finset V}
  (hXZ : Disjoint X Z) (hYZ : Disjoint Y Z) (hsep : G.DSep ↑X ↑Y ↑Z) :
  p.CondIndep X Y Z

d-separation implies conditional independence, for sets disjoint from the conditioning set. Let A be the ancestral closure of X ∪ Y ∪ Z, let S be the vertices of A \ Z reached from X by an active trail given Z, and T = (A \ Z) \ S. By DSep.reach_family, the family of each vertex of A meets at most one of S and T, so the product of the kernels over A (the marginal on A) splits into a factor depending on S ∪ Z and one depending on T ∪ Z.

Digraph.Factorizes.condIndep_of_dSeptheorem

theorem Factorizes.condIndep_of_dSep (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)}
  (h : G.Factorizes p) {X Y Z : Finset V} (hsep : G.DSep ↑X ↑Y ↑Z) : p.CondIndep X Y Z

Soundness of d-separation (the directed global Markov property). If p factorizes according to an acyclic graph G and X and Y are d-separated by Z in G, then the coordinates in X and those in Y are conditionally independent given those in Z. The sets are arbitrary finsets: coordinates in Z are irrelevant on both sides (Digraph.dSep_diff_iff, FiniteDist.condIndep_sdiff_iff). No positivity is assumed.

Digraph.GlobalMarkovdefinition

def GlobalMarkov (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) : Prop

The directed global Markov property of p with respect to G: whenever X and Y are d-separated by Z in G, the coordinates in X and Y are conditionally independent given those in Z.

Digraph.Factorizes.globalMarkovtheorem

theorem Factorizes.globalMarkov (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)}
  (h : G.Factorizes p) : G.GlobalMarkov p

Factorization implies the global Markov property.

Digraph.GlobalMarkov.localMarkovtheorem

theorem GlobalMarkov.localMarkov (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)}
  (h : G.GlobalMarkov p) : G.LocalMarkov p

The global Markov property implies the local one: the local statements are the instances given by Digraph.IsAcyclic.dSep_nondescendants_parents.

  ↑({2} : Finset (Fin 3)) ↑(∅ : Finset (Fin 3))

CausalInference.GraphExamples.exists_factorizes_condIndep_not_dSeptheorem

theorem exists_factorizes_condIndep_not_dSep :
  ∃ (p : FiniteDist (Fin 3 → Bool)) (X Y Z : Finset (Fin 3)), collider.Factorizes p ∧
    p.CondIndep X Y Z ∧ ¬ collider.DSep ↑X ↑Y ↑Z

The converse of soundness fails. There is a distribution factorizing according to an acyclic graph with a conditional independence that is not a d-separation: the exclusive-or distribution over the collider 0 → 2 ← 1 (an unfaithful distribution; Pearl 2009, section 2.4). So for a fixed distribution, conditional independence does not imply d-separation.

CausalInference.Graphical.GlobalMarkovCompleteness

CausalInference/Graphical/GlobalMarkovCompleteness.lean · 119 lines · 3 public theorems · 1 definition · imports Graphical.GlobalMarkov

Completeness of d-separation: the single-edge case. The second half of Pearl (2009), Theorem 1.2.4 (Geiger and Pearl): if X and Y are d-connected given Z in an acyclic graph G, some distribution factorizing according to G violates X ⫫ Y | Z. This file proves only the special case in which the d-connecting trail is a single edge.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Geiger and Pearl (1990)

  G.MarkovKernels (fun _ : V => Bool)

theorem exists_factorizes_not_condIndep_of_adj (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {u v : V} (huv : G.Adj u v)
  {Z : Finset V} (hu : u ∉ Z) (hv : v ∉ Z) :
  ∃ p : FiniteDist (V → Bool), G.Factorizes p ∧ ¬ p.CondIndep {u} {v} Z

Completeness of d-separation for a single edge. If u → v is an edge of an acyclic graph and neither u nor v is in Z (so {u} and {v} are d-connected given Z, Digraph.dConn_of_adj), then some distribution over binary variables factorizes according to G and violates {u} ⫫ {v} | Z: the one in which v copies u and all other vertices are independent fair bits.

Conditional independence of the random variables X and Y given Z, in product form: P(X = a, Y = b, Z = c) * P(Z = c) = P(X = a, Z = c) * P(Y = b, Z = c) for all values.

theorem CondIndepFun.contraction (h1 : p.CondIndepFun X Y Z)
  (h2 : p.CondIndepFun X W (fun ω => (Y ω, Z ω))) :
  p.CondIndepFun X (fun ω => (Y ω, W ω)) Z

CausalInference.FiniteDist.CondIndepFun.intersectiontheorem

theorem CondIndepFun.intersection [Finite ε]
  (hpos : ∀ b c d, 0 < p.probOf (fun ω => Y ω = b ∧ Z ω = c ∧ W ω = d))
  (h1 : p.CondIndepFun X Y (fun ω => (Z ω, W ω)))
  (h2 : p.CondIndepFun X W (fun ω => (Z ω, Y ω))) :
  p.CondIndepFun X (fun ω => (Y ω, W ω)) Z

Intersection: if the joint law of (Y, Z, W) is strictly positive, then X ⫫ Y | (Z, W) and X ⫫ W | (Z, Y) imply X ⫫ (Y, W) | Z. Positivity of the masses p ω alone does not suffice (FiniteDist.not_condIndepFun_intersection).

theorem condIndepFun_iff_exists_mul [Finite β] [Finite γ] :

    ∀ a b c, p.probOf (fun ω => X ω = a ∧ Y ω = b ∧ Z ω = c) = f a c * g b c

The factorization criterion: X ⫫ Y | Z iff the joint mass of (X, Y, Z) factors as f a c * g b c.

CausalInference.FiniteDist.CondIndepdefinition

def CondIndep (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) (X Y Z : Finset V) : Prop

Conditional independence of the coordinates in X and those in Y given those in Z: p(x_X, x_Y, x_Z) * p(x_Z) = p(x_X, x_Z) * p(x_Y, x_Z) for all configurations of X, Y, Z, where p(·) are marginal masses.

CausalInference.FiniteDist.CondIndep.intersectiontheorem

theorem CondIndep.intersection (hp : ∀ x, 0 < p x) (hYZ : Disjoint Y Z) (hYW : Disjoint Y W)
  (hZW : Disjoint Z W) (h1 : p.CondIndep X Y (Z ∪ W)) (h2 : p.CondIndep X W (Z ∪ Y)) :
  p.CondIndep X (Y ∪ W) Z

Intersection: for a strictly positive distribution and pairwise disjoint Y, Z, W, X ⫫ Y | Z ∪ W and X ⫫ W | Z ∪ Y imply X ⫫ Y ∪ W | Z. Positivity cannot be dropped (FiniteDist.not_condIndep_intersection), and neither can disjointness: with Y = W the two hypotheses hold trivially.

CausalInference.FiniteDist.probOf_restrict_eq_margAttheorem

theorem probOf_restrict_eq_margAt (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.probOf (fun y => X.restrict y = X.restrict x ∧ Y.restrict y = Y.restrict x ∧
    Z.restrict y = Z.restrict x) = p.margAt (X ∪ Y ∪ Z) x

The joint probability that a configuration agrees with x on X, Y and Z is the marginal mass at x on X ∪ Y ∪ Z.

    p.margAt (X ∪ Z) x

theorem probOf_restrict_eq_margAt₁ (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.probOf (fun y => Z.restrict y = Z.restrict x) = p.margAt Z x

CausalInference.FiniteDist.CondIndep.margAt_multheorem

theorem CondIndep.margAt_mul (h : p.CondIndep X Y Z) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.margAt (X ∪ Y ∪ Z) x * p.margAt Z x = p.margAt (X ∪ Z) x * p.margAt (Y ∪ Z) x

Conditional independence in cylinder form, with full configurations: p(x_{X ∪ Y ∪ Z}) * p(x_Z) = p(x_{X ∪ Z}) * p(x_{Y ∪ Z}).

CausalInference.FiniteDist.condIndep_iff_margAt_multheorem

theorem condIndep_iff_margAt_mul (hXY : Disjoint X Y) (hXZ : Disjoint X Z)
  (hYZ : Disjoint Y Z) :
  p.CondIndep X Y Z ↔ ∀ x, p.margAt (X ∪ Y ∪ Z) x * p.margAt Z x =
    p.margAt (X ∪ Z) x * p.margAt (Y ∪ Z) x

For pairwise disjoint sets, the cylinder form characterizes conditional independence.

CausalInference.FiniteDist.condIndep_of_margAt_eq_multheorem

theorem condIndep_of_margAt_eq_mul (hXY : Disjoint X Y) (hXZ : Disjoint X Z)
  (hYZ : Disjoint Y Z) (f g : (∀ v, α v) → ℝ)
  (hf : ∀ x x', (∀ v ∈ X ∪ Z, x v = x' v) → f x = f x')
  (hg : ∀ x x', (∀ v ∈ Y ∪ Z, x v = x' v) → g x = g x')
  (h : ∀ x, p.margAt (X ∪ Y ∪ Z) x = f x * g x) : p.CondIndep X Y Z

The factorization criterion in cylinder form, for pairwise disjoint sets: if the marginal mass on X ∪ Y ∪ Z is f x * g x with f depending only on the coordinates in X ∪ Z and g only on those in Y ∪ Z, then X ⫫ Y | Z.

CausalInference.FiniteDist.not_condIndepFun_intersectiontheorem

theorem not_condIndepFun_intersection :
  ∃ (p : FiniteDist Bool) (X Y W : Bool → Bool) (Z : Bool → Unit), (∀ ω, 0 < p ω) ∧
    p.CondIndepFun X Y (fun ω => (Z ω, W ω)) ∧ p.CondIndepFun X W (fun ω => (Z ω, Y ω)) ∧
    ¬ p.CondIndepFun X (fun ω => (Y ω, W ω)) Z

Intersection fails for random variables when only the masses are positive: under the uniform distribution on Bool, with X = Y = W the identity and Z constant, X ⫫ Y | (Z, W) and X ⫫ W | (Z, Y) hold but X ⫫ (Y, W) | Z fails. Here the joint law of (Y, Z, W) is not positive.

def copies3 : FiniteDist (Fin 3 → Bool)

theorem copies3_apply (x : Fin 3 → Bool) :

CausalInference.FiniteDist.not_condIndep_intersectiontheorem

theorem not_condIndep_intersection :
  copies3.CondIndep {0} {1} (∅ ∪ {2}) ∧ copies3.CondIndep {0} {2} (∅ ∪ {1}) ∧
    ¬ copies3.CondIndep {0} ({1} ∪ {2}) ∅

Intersection fails for coordinate sets without positivity: for three perfectly correlated fair bits, {0} ⫫ {1} | {2} and {0} ⫫ {2} | {1} hold but {0} ⫫ {1, 2} fails.

CausalInference.Basic.FiniteDistribution

CausalInference/Basic/FiniteDistribution.lean · 438 lines · 48 public theorems · 13 definitions

Finite probability distributions. A finite probability distribution on a finite type Ω is a real-valued mass function that is nonnegative and sums to one. Real values (rather than ENNReal, as in Mathlib's PMF) keep the arithmetic of the finite theory easy; the bridge FiniteDist.toPMF and FiniteDist.toMeasure connects it to Mathlib's measure theory.

Sources: Lauritzen (1996)

  p.margAt T x ≤ p.margAt S x

CausalInference.FiniteDist.marginal_marginaltheorem

theorem marginal_marginal (p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)) {S T : Finset V} (hST : S ⊆ T) :
  (p.marginal T).map (Finset.restrict₂ hST) = p.marginal S

Marginalizing twice: the marginal on S of the marginal on T ⊇ S is the marginal on S.

  (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  p.margAt A x = ∑ y ∈ agreeOn (B \ A)ᶜ x, p.margAt B y

Marginalizing a marginal, in cylinder form: for A ⊆ B, the marginal mass on A at x is the sum of the marginal masses on B over the configurations that agree with x outside B \ A.

theorem sum_agreeOn_compl_singleton {M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M] (f : (∀ v, α v) → M)
  (s : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  ∑ y ∈ agreeOn ({s} : Finset V)ᶜ x, f y = ∑ a : α s, f (Function.update x s a)

Summing over the configurations that agree with x except at one coordinate s is summing over the values at s.

Partial identification

Identified sets and point identification for a generic model class; Manski bounds with sharpness.

CausalInference.PartialIdentification.IdentifiedSet

CausalInference/PartialIdentification/IdentifiedSet.lean · 186 lines · 14 public theorems · 2 definitions

Identified sets and point identification. A generic, probability-free framework for partial identification in the sense of Manski. A type M of models carries an observation map obs : M → O (the observed data law, or any observable summary of it) and a parameter θ : M → Θ. A set S : Set M collects the models satisfying the maintained assumptions.

Sources: Manski (2003)

Public declarations (16)

CausalInference.identifiedSetdefinition

def identifiedSet (S : Set M) (obs : M → O) (θ : M → Θ) (o : O) : Set Θ

The identified set of the parameter θ at the observed value o under the maintained assumptions S: all values θ m for models m ∈ S whose observation obs m equals o.

CausalInference.PointIdentifieddefinition

def PointIdentified (S : Set M) (obs : M → O) (θ : M → Θ) : Prop

The parameter θ is point identified on the model class S from the observation obs: any two models of S that produce the same observation have the same parameter value.

CausalInference.mem_identifiedSettheorem

theorem mem_identifiedSet {o : O} {t : Θ} :
  t ∈ identifiedSet S obs θ o ↔ ∃ m ∈ S, obs m = o ∧ θ m = t

CausalInference.mem_identifiedSet_selftheorem

theorem mem_identifiedSet_self {m : M} (hm : m ∈ S) : θ m ∈ identifiedSet S obs θ (obs m)

A model in S contributes its parameter value to the identified set at its own observation.

CausalInference.pointIdentified_iff_subsingletontheorem

theorem pointIdentified_iff_subsingleton :
  PointIdentified S obs θ ↔ ∀ o, (identifiedSet S obs θ o).Subsingleton

Point identification holds if and only if every identified set has at most one element.

CausalInference.identifiedSet_eq_singletontheorem

theorem identifiedSet_eq_singleton (h : PointIdentified S obs θ) {m : M} (hm : m ∈ S) :
  identifiedSet S obs θ (obs m) = {θ m}

Under point identification, the identified set at the observation of a model m ∈ S is exactly the singleton {θ m}.

CausalInference.pointIdentified_iff_exists_factortheorem

theorem pointIdentified_iff_exists_factor [Nonempty Θ] :
  PointIdentified S obs θ ↔ ∃ f : O → Θ, ∀ m ∈ S, θ m = f (obs m)

Point identification holds if and only if the parameter factors through the observation on the model class: there is f : O → Θ with θ m = f (obs m) for every m ∈ S. The parameter type is assumed nonempty; without this the factor f may fail to exist when S is empty and O is not.

CausalInference.identifiedSet_monotheorem

theorem identifiedSet_mono (h : S' ⊆ S) (o : O) :
  identifiedSet S' obs θ o ⊆ identifiedSet S obs θ o

Stronger maintained assumptions (a smaller model class) give a smaller identified set.

CausalInference.PointIdentified.monotheorem

theorem PointIdentified.mono (h : PointIdentified S obs θ) (hS : S' ⊆ S) :
  PointIdentified S' obs θ

Point identification is inherited by any smaller model class.

CausalInference.identifiedSet_inter_subsettheorem

theorem identifiedSet_inter_subset (o : O) :
  identifiedSet (S ∩ S') obs θ o ⊆ identifiedSet S obs θ o ∩ identifiedSet S' obs θ o

The identified set under the conjunction of two assumptions is contained in the intersection of the two identified sets.

CausalInference.not_pointIdentified_ifftheorem

theorem not_pointIdentified_iff :
  ¬ PointIdentified S obs θ ↔ ∃ m ∈ S, ∃ m' ∈ S, obs m = obs m' ∧ θ m ≠ θ m'

The parameter fails to be point identified if and only if two models of S produce the same observation but different parameter values.

CausalInference.not_pointIdentified_of_memtheorem

theorem not_pointIdentified_of_mem {o : O} {t t' : Θ} (ht : t ∈ identifiedSet S obs θ o)
  (ht' : t' ∈ identifiedSet S obs θ o) (hne : t ≠ t') : ¬ PointIdentified S obs θ

Two distinct parameter values in the same identified set witness non-identification.

CausalInference.identifiedSet_comp_obstheorem

theorem identifiedSet_comp_obs {O' : Type*} (g : O → O') (p : O') :
  identifiedSet S (g ∘ obs) θ p = ⋃ o ∈ g ⁻¹' {p}, identifiedSet S obs θ o

Coarsening the observation through a map g : O → O': the identified set at a coarse value p is the union of the identified sets at all fine observations o with g o = p.

CausalInference.identifiedSet_comp_paramtheorem

theorem identifiedSet_comp_param {Θ' : Type*} (h : Θ → Θ') (o : O) :
  identifiedSet S obs (h ∘ θ) o = h '' identifiedSet S obs θ o

Transforming the parameter through a map h : Θ → Θ': the identified set of h ∘ θ is the image under h of the identified set of θ.

CausalInference.PointIdentified.of_comp_obstheorem

theorem PointIdentified.of_comp_obs {O' : Type*} (g : O → O')
  (h : PointIdentified S (g ∘ obs) θ) : PointIdentified S obs θ

Point identification from a coarser observation g ∘ obs implies point identification from the finer observation obs.

CausalInference.identifiedSet_comp_obs_eqtheorem

theorem identifiedSet_comp_obs_eq {O' : Type*} (g : O → O') (T : O' → Set Θ)
  (h : ∀ m ∈ S, identifiedSet S obs θ (obs m) = T (g (obs m))) {m₀ : M} (hm₀ : m₀ ∈ S) :
  identifiedSet S (g ∘ obs) θ (g (obs m₀)) = T (g (obs m₀))

Identified sets under a coarser observation. Suppose that at every attainable fine observation obs m (with m ∈ S) the identified set depends on obs m only through the coarse value g (obs m), being equal to T (g (obs m)). Then the identified set from the coarse observation g ∘ obs at every attainable coarse value g (obs m₀) is T (g (obs m₀)).

CausalInference.PartialIdentification.Manski

CausalInference/PartialIdentification/Manski.lean · 849 lines · 52 public theorems · 14 definitions · imports PartialIdentification.IdentifiedSet

Manski bounds for a binary treatment with bounded outcomes. Worst-case (no-assumption) bounds on the integrated potential outcomes and on the integrated treatment effect, their sharpness by explicit construction, and their tightening under monotone treatment response.

Sources: Manski (1990); Manski (1997); Manski (2003)

Public declarations (66)

CausalInference.Manski.integral_mem_Icc_of_eqOntheorem

theorem integral_mem_Icc_of_eqOn [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {lo hi : ℝ} {s : Set Ω}
  (hs : MeasurableSet s) {f y : Ω → ℝ} (hf : Measurable f) (hfb : ∀ ω, f ω ∈ Icc lo hi)
  (hfy : EqOn f y s) :
  ∫ ω, f ω ∂μ ∈ Icc (∫ ω in s, y ω ∂μ + lo * μ.real sᶜ) (∫ ω in s, y ω ∂μ + hi * μ.real sᶜ)

Core estimate: if f is measurable with values in [lo, hi] and agrees with y on a measurable set s, then ∫ f lies between ∫_s y + lo μ(sᶜ) and ∫_s y + hi μ(sᶜ).

CausalInference.Manski.integrable_of_mem_Icctheorem

theorem integrable_of_mem_Icc [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {lo hi : ℝ} {f : Ω → ℝ} (hf : Measurable f)
  (hfb : ∀ ω, f ω ∈ Icc lo hi) : Integrable f μ

A bounded measurable real function on a finite measure space is integrable.

CausalInference.Manski.POModelstructure

structure POModel (Ω : Type*)

A potential outcome model on the sample space Ω: the treated potential outcome Y1 and the control potential outcome Y0, both real-valued.

CausalInference.Manski.treateddefinition

def treated (A : Ω → Bool) : Set Ω

The treated event {A = 1} of a binary treatment A : Ω → Bool.

CausalInference.Manski.measurableSet_treatedtheorem

theorem measurableSet_treated {A : Ω → Bool} (hA : Measurable A) : MeasurableSet (treated A)

CausalInference.Manski.observeddefinition

def observed (A : Ω → Bool) (m : POModel Ω) : Ω → ℝ

The observed outcome Y = Y1 on {A = 1} and Y = Y0 on {A = 0} (consistency).

CausalInference.Manski.boundedModelsdefinition

def boundedModels (lo hi : ℝ) : Set (POModel Ω)

The model class with no assumption beyond bounded outcomes: both potential outcomes are measurable with values in [lo, hi].

CausalInference.Manski.mtrModelsdefinition

def mtrModels (lo hi : ℝ) : Set (POModel Ω)

Bounded models satisfying monotone treatment response: Y0 ≤ Y1 pointwise.

CausalInference.Manski.meanY1definition

def meanY1 (μ : Measure Ω) (m : POModel Ω) : ℝ

The integral ∫ Y1 dμ of the treated potential outcome; the mean E[Y1] when μ is a probability measure.

CausalInference.Manski.meanY0definition

def meanY0 (μ : Measure Ω) (m : POModel Ω) : ℝ

The integral ∫ Y0 dμ of the control potential outcome; the mean E[Y0] when μ is a probability measure.

CausalInference.Manski.atedefinition

def ate (μ : Measure Ω) (m : POModel Ω) : ℝ

The integrated treatment effect ∫ Y1 dμ - ∫ Y0 dμ; the average treatment effect E[Y1] - E[Y0] when μ is a probability measure.

CausalInference.Manski.boundY1definition

def boundY1 (μ : Measure Ω) (A : Ω → Bool) (c : ℝ) (y : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ

The Manski bound for ∫ Y1 dμ with fill value c: ∫_{A = 1} y dμ + c μ(A = 0). With c = lo it is the lower bound, with c = hi the upper bound. It depends only on observed data.

CausalInference.Manski.boundY0definition

def boundY0 (μ : Measure Ω) (A : Ω → Bool) (c : ℝ) (y : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ

The Manski bound for ∫ Y0 dμ with fill value c: ∫_{A = 0} y dμ + c μ(A = 1).

CausalInference.Manski.setIntegral_eq_measureReal_mul_condtheorem

theorem setIntegral_eq_measureReal_mul_cond [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (s : Set Ω) (y : Ω → ℝ) :
  ∫ ω in s, y ω ∂μ = μ.real s * ∫ ω, y ω ∂(ProbabilityTheory.cond μ s)

The integral of y over a set s is the mass of s times the integral of y against the conditional measure μ[|s] = μ(s)⁻¹ • μ.restrict s. When 0 < μ(s) the second factor is the conditional mean of y given s; when μ(s) = 0 both sides are zero. The identity holds for every y; for a y that is not integrable on s both integrals take Lean's default value zero, so the statement carries content only for integrable y, as for the bounded outcomes used in this file.

CausalInference.Manski.boundY1_eq_condtheorem

theorem boundY1_eq_cond [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (c : ℝ) (y : Ω → ℝ) :
  boundY1 μ A c y = μ.real (treated A) * ∫ ω, y ω ∂(ProbabilityTheory.cond μ (treated A)) +
    c * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ

The textbook form of the Manski bound for ∫ Y1 dμ: the treated mass times the conditional mean of y among the treated, plus c times the control mass. For a probability measure with 0 < P(A = 1) this reads E[Y | A = 1] P(A = 1) + c P(A = 0).

CausalInference.Manski.boundY0_eq_condtheorem

theorem boundY0_eq_cond [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (c : ℝ) (y : Ω → ℝ) :
  boundY0 μ A c y = μ.real (treated A)ᶜ * ∫ ω, y ω ∂(ProbabilityTheory.cond μ (treated A)ᶜ) +
    c * μ.real (treated A)

The textbook form of the Manski bound for ∫ Y0 dμ: for a probability measure with 0 < P(A = 0) it reads E[Y | A = 0] P(A = 0) + c P(A = 1).

CausalInference.Manski.meanY1_mem_Icctheorem

theorem meanY1_mem_Icc [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {m : POModel Ω}
  (hm : m ∈ boundedModels lo hi) :
  meanY1 μ m ∈ Icc (boundY1 μ A lo (observed A m)) (boundY1 μ A hi (observed A m))

No-assumption bounds on ∫ Y1 dμ (Manski 1990): for every bounded model, ∫_{A = 1} Y dμ + lo μ(A = 0) ≤ ∫ Y1 dμ ≤ ∫_{A = 1} Y dμ + hi μ(A = 0), where Y is the observed outcome.

CausalInference.Manski.meanY0_mem_Icctheorem

theorem meanY0_mem_Icc [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {m : POModel Ω}
  (hm : m ∈ boundedModels lo hi) :
  meanY0 μ m ∈ Icc (boundY0 μ A lo (observed A m)) (boundY0 μ A hi (observed A m))

No-assumption bounds on ∫ Y0 dμ: ∫_{A = 0} Y dμ + lo μ(A = 1) ≤ ∫ Y0 dμ ≤ ∫_{A = 0} Y dμ + hi μ(A = 1).

CausalInference.Manski.ate_mem_Icctheorem

theorem ate_mem_Icc [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {m : POModel Ω}
  (hm : m ∈ boundedModels lo hi) :
  ate μ m ∈ Icc (boundY1 μ A lo (observed A m) - boundY0 μ A hi (observed A m))
    (boundY1 μ A hi (observed A m) - boundY0 μ A lo (observed A m))

No-assumption bounds on the integrated treatment effect: boundY1 lo - boundY0 hi ≤ ∫ Y1 dμ - ∫ Y0 dμ ≤ boundY1 hi - boundY0 lo.

CausalInference.Manski.ate_bounds_width_finitetheorem

theorem ate_bounds_width_finite [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) (y : Ω → ℝ) :
  (boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y) - (boundY1 μ A lo y - boundY0 μ A hi y) =
    (hi - lo) * μ.real univ

For a finite measure, the upper endpoint minus the lower endpoint of the no-assumption bounds on the integrated treatment effect is exactly (hi - lo) * μ(Ω), whatever the observed data. This is an algebraic identity: it holds for every y and also when hi < lo, in which case the difference is negative and there is no interval to speak of.

CausalInference.Manski.ate_bounds_widththeorem

theorem ate_bounds_width [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) (y : Ω → ℝ) :
  (boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y) - (boundY1 μ A lo y - boundY0 μ A hi y) = hi - lo

For a probability measure, the upper endpoint minus the lower endpoint of the no-assumption bounds on the average treatment effect is exactly hi - lo, whatever the observed data. As in ate_bounds_width_finite, the identity also holds when hi < lo; it is the width of a genuine interval only when lo ≤ hi.

CausalInference.Manski.filldefinition

def fill (A : Ω → Bool) (y g1 g0 : Ω → ℝ) : POModel Ω

The model that agrees with the observed outcome y where it is observed and is filled with g1 (for Y1 on {A = 0}) and g0 (for Y0 on {A = 1}) where it is not.

CausalInference.Manski.observed_filltheorem

theorem observed_fill (y g1 g0 : Ω → ℝ) : observed A (fill A y g1 g0) = y

CausalInference.Manski.fill_mem_boundedModelstheorem

theorem fill_mem_boundedModels (hA : Measurable A) {y g1 g0 : Ω → ℝ} (hy : Measurable y)
  (hg1 : Measurable g1) (hg0 : Measurable g0) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi)
  (hg1b : ∀ ω, g1 ω ∈ Icc lo hi) (hg0b : ∀ ω, g0 ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  fill A y g1 g0 ∈ boundedModels lo hi

CausalInference.Manski.meanY1_filltheorem

theorem meanY1_fill [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y g1 g0 : Ω → ℝ}
  (hm : fill A y g1 g0 ∈ boundedModels lo hi) :
  meanY1 μ (fill A y g1 g0) = ∫ ω in treated A, y ω ∂μ + ∫ ω in (treated A)ᶜ, g1 ω ∂μ

CausalInference.Manski.meanY0_filltheorem

theorem meanY0_fill [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y g1 g0 : Ω → ℝ}
  (hm : fill A y g1 g0 ∈ boundedModels lo hi) :
  meanY0 μ (fill A y g1 g0) = ∫ ω in treated A, g0 ω ∂μ + ∫ ω in (treated A)ᶜ, y ω ∂μ

CausalInference.Manski.exists_combo_of_mem_Icctheorem

theorem exists_combo_of_mem_Icc {u v t : ℝ} (ht : t ∈ Icc u v) :
  ∃ a b : ℝ, 0 ≤ a ∧ 0 ≤ b ∧ a + b = 1 ∧ a * u + b * v = t

Every point of Icc u v is a convex combination of u and v; no order between u and v is needed.

CausalInference.Manski.combo_mem_Icctheorem

theorem combo_mem_Icc {a b lo hi : ℝ} (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hb : 0 ≤ b) (hab : a + b = 1)
  (hlh : lo ≤ hi) : a * lo + b * hi ∈ Icc lo hi

A convex combination of lo ≤ hi lies in [lo, hi].

CausalInference.Manski.exists_model_meanY1_eqtheorem

theorem exists_model_meanY1_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) {t : ℝ}
  (ht : t ∈ Icc (boundY1 μ A lo y) (boundY1 μ A hi y)) :
  ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, observed A m = y ∧ meanY1 μ m = t

Sharpness of the bounds on ∫ Y1 dμ, by explicit construction: for observed data y (measurable with values in [lo, hi]) and every t between the lower and the upper bound, there is a bounded model with the same observed outcome y and ∫ Y1 dμ = t. Its Y1 equals y on {A = 1} and a suitable constant in [lo, hi] on {A = 0}.

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_meanY1theorem

theorem identifiedSet_meanY1 [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (meanY1 μ) y =
    Icc (boundY1 μ A lo y) (boundY1 μ A hi y)

The identified set for ∫ Y1 dμ under bounded outcomes alone is exactly the Manski interval. The observation is the realized outcome function ω ↦ Y ω on the fixed finite measure space (Ω, μ) with the fixed treatment A; models differ only in their potential outcomes.

CausalInference.Manski.exists_model_meanY0_eqtheorem

theorem exists_model_meanY0_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) {t : ℝ}
  (ht : t ∈ Icc (boundY0 μ A lo y) (boundY0 μ A hi y)) :
  ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, observed A m = y ∧ meanY0 μ m = t

Sharpness of the bounds on ∫ Y0 dμ, by explicit construction: every t between the lower and the upper bound is ∫ Y0 dμ of a bounded model with observed outcome y. Its Y0 equals y on {A = 0} and a suitable constant in [lo, hi] on {A = 1}.

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_meanY0theorem

theorem identifiedSet_meanY0 [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (meanY0 μ) y =
    Icc (boundY0 μ A lo y) (boundY0 μ A hi y)

The identified set for ∫ Y0 dμ under bounded outcomes alone is exactly the Manski interval, with the same observation as in identifiedSet_meanY1.

CausalInference.Manski.exists_model_ate_eqtheorem

theorem exists_model_ate_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) {t : ℝ}
  (ht : t ∈ Icc (boundY1 μ A lo y - boundY0 μ A hi y) (boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y)) :
  ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, observed A m = y ∧ ate μ m = t

Sharpness of the bounds on the integrated treatment effect, by explicit construction: every value between boundY1 lo - boundY0 hi and boundY1 hi - boundY0 lo is the integrated treatment effect of a bounded model with observed outcome y.

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_atetheorem

theorem identifiedSet_ate [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (ate μ) y =
    Icc (boundY1 μ A lo y - boundY0 μ A hi y) (boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y)

The identified set for the integrated treatment effect under bounded outcomes alone is exactly the Manski interval. For the finite measure μ its endpoints differ by (hi - lo) * μ(Ω) (see ate_bounds_width_finite); this is hi - lo only when μ is a probability measure (see ate_bounds_width). The observation is the realized outcome function on the fixed (Ω, μ) with the fixed treatment A.

CausalInference.Manski.not_subsingleton_identifiedSet_meanY1theorem

theorem not_subsingleton_identifiedSet_meanY1 [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {y : Ω → ℝ} (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) (hlh : lo < hi)
  (hpos : 0 < μ.real (treated A)ᶜ) :
  ¬ (identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (meanY1 μ) y).Subsingleton

Non-identification of ∫ Y1 dμ at every admissible observation: if the control group has positive mass and lo < hi, the identified set at the observed outcome y contains at least two points (both endpoints of the Manski interval).

CausalInference.Manski.not_pointIdentified_meanY1theorem

theorem not_pointIdentified_meanY1 [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) (hlh : lo < hi)
  (hpos : 0 < μ.real (treated A)ᶜ) :
  ¬ PointIdentified (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (meanY1 μ)

Non-identification of ∫ Y1 dμ under bounded outcomes alone: if the control group has positive mass and lo < hi, two bounded models with the same observed outcome have different values of ∫ Y1 dμ. The witness observation is the constant outcome lo.

CausalInference.Manski.zero_mem_ate_boundstheorem

theorem zero_mem_ate_bounds [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  (0 : ℝ) ∈ Icc (boundY1 μ A lo y - boundY0 μ A hi y) (boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y)

Zero lies in the no-assumption bounds on the integrated treatment effect, for any admissible observed outcome: the model with Y1 = Y0 = y has effect zero.

CausalInference.Manski.boundY1_lo_sub_boundY0_hi_nonpostheorem

  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  boundY1 μ A lo y - boundY0 μ A hi y ≤ 0

The no-assumption lower bound on the integrated treatment effect is never positive, for any admissible observed outcome.

CausalInference.Manski.zero_le_boundY1_hi_sub_boundY0_lotheorem

theorem zero_le_boundY1_hi_sub_boundY0_lo [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  0 ≤ boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y

The no-assumption upper bound on the integrated treatment effect is never negative, for any admissible observed outcome.

CausalInference.Manski.not_subsingleton_identifiedSet_atetheorem

theorem not_subsingleton_identifiedSet_ate [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) (hlh : lo < hi) (hpos : 0 < μ.real univ) :
  ¬ (identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (ate μ) y).Subsingleton

Non-identification of the integrated treatment effect at every admissible observation: if lo < hi and μ has positive total mass, the identified set at y contains at least two points, because its endpoints differ by (hi - lo) * μ(Ω) > 0.

CausalInference.Manski.not_pointIdentified_atetheorem

theorem not_pointIdentified_ate [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) (hlh : lo < hi) :
  ¬ PointIdentified (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (ate μ)

The average treatment effect is not point identified under bounded outcomes alone, for a probability measure and lo < hi: the bounds have width hi - lo > 0. The witness observation is the constant outcome lo.

CausalInference.Manski.not_subsingleton_identifiedSet_sign_atetheorem

theorem not_subsingleton_identifiedSet_sign_ate [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {y : Ω → ℝ} (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) (hlh : lo < hi)
  (hpos : 0 < μ.real univ) :
  ¬ (identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (observed A) (fun m => SignType.sign (ate μ m))
    y).Subsingleton

The sign of the integrated treatment effect is not identified at any admissible observation without assumptions beyond bounded outcomes: if lo < hi and μ has positive total mass, the identified set of sign (ate) at y contains 0 and a nonzero sign. Whether both a positive and a negative sign occur depends on y; for example, y = hi on the treated and y = lo on the controls gives lower endpoint 0.

The sign of the average treatment effect is not point identified under bounded outcomes alone, for a probability measure and lo < hi.

CausalInference.Manski.ate_mem_Icc_of_mem_mtrModelstheorem

Bounds on the integrated treatment effect under monotone treatment response and bounded outcomes (Manski 1997): the lower bound improves to 0; the upper bound is the no-assumption upper bound boundY1 hi - boundY0 lo.

CausalInference.Manski.exists_mtr_model_ate_eqtheorem

theorem exists_mtr_model_ate_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) {t : ℝ}
  (ht : t ∈ Icc 0 (boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y)) :
  ∃ m ∈ mtrModels lo hi, observed A m = y ∧ ate μ m = t

Sharpness of the monotone treatment response bounds, by explicit construction: every value between 0 and boundY1 hi - boundY0 lo is the integrated treatment effect of a bounded model satisfying monotone treatment response with observed outcome y. The model fills Y1 on {A = 0} with a y + b hi and Y0 on {A = 1} with b lo + a y.

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_ate_mtrtheorem

theorem identifiedSet_ate_mtr [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ}
  (hy : Measurable y) (hyb : ∀ ω, y ω ∈ Icc lo hi) :
  identifiedSet (mtrModels lo hi) (observed A) (ate μ) y =
    Icc 0 (boundY1 μ A hi y - boundY0 μ A lo y)

The identified set for the integrated treatment effect under monotone treatment response and bounded outcomes is exactly [0, boundY1 hi - boundY0 lo]. Compared with identifiedSet_ate, the lower endpoint moves up from boundY1 lo - boundY0 hi ≤ 0 to 0 and the upper endpoint is unchanged. The observation is the realized outcome function on the fixed (Ω, μ) with the fixed treatment A.

CausalInference.Manski.meanY1_mem_Icc_of_mem_mtrModelstheorem

theorem meanY1_mem_Icc_of_mem_mtrModels [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {m : POModel Ω} (hm : m ∈ mtrModels lo hi) :
  meanY1 μ m ∈ Icc (∫ ω, observed A m ω ∂μ) (boundY1 μ A hi (observed A m))

Bounds on ∫ Y1 dμ under monotone treatment response and bounded outcomes (Manski 1997): ∫ Y dμ ≤ ∫ Y1 dμ ≤ boundY1 hi. The lower bound improves from boundY1 lo to the integral of the observed outcome, since Y1 ≥ Y0 = Y on the controls.

CausalInference.Manski.meanY0_mem_Icc_of_mem_mtrModelstheorem

theorem meanY0_mem_Icc_of_mem_mtrModels [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {m : POModel Ω} (hm : m ∈ mtrModels lo hi) :
  meanY0 μ m ∈ Icc (boundY0 μ A lo (observed A m)) (∫ ω, observed A m ω ∂μ)

Bounds on ∫ Y0 dμ under monotone treatment response and bounded outcomes (Manski 1997): boundY0 lo ≤ ∫ Y0 dμ ≤ ∫ Y dμ. The upper bound improves from boundY0 hi to the integral of the observed outcome, since Y0 ≤ Y1 = Y on the treated.

The model fills Y1 on {A = 0} with a y + b hi and Y0 on {A = 1} with y.

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_meanY0_mtrtheorem

The observed arm integrals (∫_{A = 1} y dμ, ∫_{A = 0} y dμ) of an outcome function y.

CausalInference.Manski.lawArmIntegraldefinition

def lawArmIntegral (L : Measure (Bool × ℝ)) (b : Bool) : ℝ

The arm integral of a measure L on Bool × ℝ: the integral of the second coordinate over the slice {(a, v) | a = b}.

CausalInference.Manski.lawArmIntegral_jointLawtheorem

theorem lawArmIntegral_jointLaw (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ} (hy : Measurable y)
  (b : Bool) :
  lawArmIntegral (jointLaw μ A y) b = ∫ ω in {ω | A ω = b}, y ω ∂μ

The arm integral of the joint law of (A, y) on the slice a = b is the integral of y over {A = b}.

CausalInference.Manski.lawArmIntegral_jointLaw_truetheorem

theorem lawArmIntegral_jointLaw_true (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ} (hy : Measurable y) :
  lawArmIntegral (jointLaw μ A y) true = ∫ ω in treated A, y ω ∂μ

The arm integral over {A = 1} is a functional of the joint law of (A, y).

CausalInference.Manski.lawArmIntegral_jointLaw_falsetheorem

theorem lawArmIntegral_jointLaw_false (hA : Measurable A) {y : Ω → ℝ} (hy : Measurable y) :
  lawArmIntegral (jointLaw μ A y) false = ∫ ω in (treated A)ᶜ, y ω ∂μ

The arm integral over {A = 0} is a functional of the joint law of (A, y).

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_meanY1_armIntegralstheorem

theorem identifiedSet_meanY1_armIntegrals [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {p : ℝ × ℝ} (hp : ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, armIntegrals μ A (observed A m) = p) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (fun m => armIntegrals μ A (observed A m)) (meanY1 μ) p =
    Icc (p.1 + lo * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ) (p.1 + hi * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ)

The identified set for ∫ Y1 dμ under bounded outcomes alone, when the observation is the pair of observed arm integrals: at every attainable value p it is [p.1 + lo μ(A = 0), p.1 + hi μ(A = 0)].

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_meanY0_armIntegralstheorem

theorem identifiedSet_meanY0_armIntegrals [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {p : ℝ × ℝ} (hp : ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, armIntegrals μ A (observed A m) = p) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (fun m => armIntegrals μ A (observed A m)) (meanY0 μ) p =
    Icc (p.2 + lo * μ.real (treated A)) (p.2 + hi * μ.real (treated A))

The identified set for ∫ Y0 dμ under bounded outcomes alone, when the observation is the pair of observed arm integrals: at every attainable value p it is [p.2 + lo μ(A = 1), p.2 + hi μ(A = 1)].

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_ate_armIntegralstheorem

theorem identifiedSet_ate_armIntegrals [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {p : ℝ × ℝ} (hp : ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, armIntegrals μ A (observed A m) = p) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (fun m => armIntegrals μ A (observed A m)) (ate μ) p =
    Icc (p.1 + lo * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ - (p.2 + hi * μ.real (treated A)))
      (p.1 + hi * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ - (p.2 + lo * μ.real (treated A)))

The identified set for the integrated treatment effect under bounded outcomes alone, when the observation is the pair of observed arm integrals: at every attainable value p it is [p.1 + lo μ(A = 0) - (p.2 + hi μ(A = 1)), p.1 + hi μ(A = 0) - (p.2 + lo μ(A = 1))].

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_meanY1_jointLawtheorem

theorem identifiedSet_meanY1_jointLaw [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {L : Measure (Bool × ℝ)} (hL : ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, jointLaw μ A (observed A m) = L) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (fun m => jointLaw μ A (observed A m)) (meanY1 μ) L =
    Icc (lawArmIntegral L true + lo * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ)
      (lawArmIntegral L true + hi * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ)

The identified set for ∫ Y1 dμ under bounded outcomes alone, when the observation is the joint law L of (A, Y): at every attainable law it is [∫_{a = 1} v dL + lo μ(A = 0), ∫_{a = 1} v dL + hi μ(A = 0)].

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_meanY0_jointLawtheorem

theorem identifiedSet_meanY0_jointLaw [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {L : Measure (Bool × ℝ)} (hL : ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, jointLaw μ A (observed A m) = L) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (fun m => jointLaw μ A (observed A m)) (meanY0 μ) L =
    Icc (lawArmIntegral L false + lo * μ.real (treated A))
      (lawArmIntegral L false + hi * μ.real (treated A))

The identified set for ∫ Y0 dμ under bounded outcomes alone, when the observation is the joint law L of (A, Y): at every attainable law it is [∫_{a = 0} v dL + lo μ(A = 1), ∫_{a = 0} v dL + hi μ(A = 1)].

CausalInference.Manski.identifiedSet_ate_jointLawtheorem

theorem identifiedSet_ate_jointLaw [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hA : Measurable A)
  {L : Measure (Bool × ℝ)} (hL : ∃ m ∈ boundedModels lo hi, jointLaw μ A (observed A m) = L) :
  identifiedSet (boundedModels lo hi) (fun m => jointLaw μ A (observed A m)) (ate μ) L =
    Icc (lawArmIntegral L true + lo * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ -
        (lawArmIntegral L false + hi * μ.real (treated A)))
      (lawArmIntegral L true + hi * μ.real (treated A)ᶜ -
        (lawArmIntegral L false + lo * μ.real (treated A)))

The identified set for the integrated treatment effect under bounded outcomes alone, when the observation is the joint law L of (A, Y): at every attainable law it is the Manski interval with the arm integrals read off L.

Randomized experiments

Design-based inference in a finite population: Bernoulli and complete randomization, Neyman's variance, Fisher's randomization test.

CausalInference.Designs.Randomized.Bernoulli

CausalInference/Designs/Randomized/Bernoulli.lean · 155 lines · 5 public theorems · 2 definitions · imports Designs.Randomized.FinitePopulation

The Bernoulli design. Each unit is treated by an independent coin flip with probability p. The probability of an assignment a is ∏_i (p if a i else 1 - p). We prove the finite-pattern product law (independence of the flips), so that each unit is treated with probability p and two distinct units with probability p * p; the Horvitz-Thompson estimator is unbiased for the finite-population average treatment effect when 0 < p < 1, and we compute its variance. Source: Imbens and Rubin (2015), Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences.

Sources: Imbens and Rubin (2015)
