CausalInference.IVModel.InstrumentIndependencedefinition

def InstrumentIndependence (μ : Measure Ω) : Prop

Instrument independence: the instrument Z is independent of the vector of all potential treatments and potential outcomes (joint independence). This is stronger than the definition of an instrument in Pearl (2009, Causality), which asks only for the graphical or counterfactual independence of Z from the outcome's other causes, and stronger than the marginal exchangeability Y^{z,d} independent of Z for each (z, d) used by Hernan and Robins (Causal Inference: What If). It is unconditional: no covariate version is formalized.

CausalInference.IVModel.Relevancedefinition

def Relevance (μ : Measure Ω) : Prop

Relevance: both instrument arms have positive mass, P(Z = true) ≠ 0 and P(Z = false) ≠ 0, and the first stage E[Dobs | Z = true] - E[Dobs | Z = false] is nonzero. The positivity conjuncts matter: without them a constant instrument Z = true with D ≡ true would have first stage 1 - 0 = 1, because the conditional mean given the null event {Z = false} is 0 by Lean's conventions.

Monotonicity: almost surely, a unit that takes the treatment when the instrument is false also takes it when the instrument is true (D false ≤ D true with false < true).

  (hz : μ (M.instrumentEq z) ≠ 0) :
  (μ[|M.instrumentEq z]).map M.potentials = μ.map M.potentials

Under instrument independence, the law of the vector of potential variables given Z = z equals its unconditional law, provided P(Z = z) ≠ 0.

CausalInference.IVModel.condMean_potentialstheorem

theorem condMean_potentials [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hI : M.InstrumentIndependence μ) {z : Bool}
  (hz : μ (M.instrumentEq z) ≠ 0) {φ : Potentials → ℝ} (hφ : Measurable φ)
  (_hint : Integrable (fun ω ↦ φ (M.potentials ω)) μ) :
  M.condMean μ (fun ω ↦ φ (M.potentials ω)) z = ∫ ω, φ (M.potentials ω) ∂μ

Under instrument independence and P(Z = z) ≠ 0, the conditional mean given Z = z of a measurable function of the potential variables, integrable under μ, equals its unconditional mean. The integrability hypothesis _hint is not used by the proof: the conditional and unconditional laws of the potential variables coincide, so the two Bochner integrals agree even when both are Lean's totalized value 0. It is required so that the statement is about two finite means.

CausalInference.InstrumentalVariables.PrincipalStrata

CausalInference/InstrumentalVariables/PrincipalStrata.lean · 181 lines · 15 public theorems · 8 definitions · imports InstrumentalVariables.Basic

Principal strata of a binary instrumental variable model. Each unit belongs to exactly one principal stratum, determined by its pair of potential treatments (D false, D true) (Angrist, Imbens and Rubin, 1996): always-takers (true, true), never-takers (false, false), compliers (false, true) and defiers (true, false).

Sources: Angrist, Imbens and Rubin (1996)

The local average treatment effect theorem. Identification of the complier average causal effect by the Wald ratio, for a binary instrument and a binary treatment: Imbens and Angrist (1994, Identification and estimation of local average treatment effects) and Angrist, Imbens and Rubin (1996, Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables).

Sources: Imbens and Angrist (1994); Angrist, Imbens and Rubin (1996)

The complier average causal effect E[Y z true - Y z false | compliers] at instrument value z: the mean unit-level effect under the conditional measure μ[|compliers].

  ∫ ω, f ω ∂μ[|s] = (μ.real s)⁻¹ * ∫ ω in s, f ω ∂μ

A conditional mean given s is μ(s)⁻¹ ∫_s f (both sides vanish when μ(s) = 0).

  M.firstStage μ = μ.real M.compliers - μ.real M.defiers

First-stage decomposition: under instrument independence and 0 < P(Z = z) for both values z, E[Dobs | Z = true] - E[Dobs | Z = false] = P(compliers) - P(defiers).

CausalInference.IVModel.reducedForm_eqtheorem

theorem reducedForm_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hE : M.Exclusion μ)
  (hI : M.InstrumentIndependence μ) (hY : ∀ z, Integrable (M.YD z) μ)
  (h₁ : μ (M.instrumentEq true) ≠ 0) (h₀ : μ (M.instrumentEq false) ≠ 0) (z : Bool) :
  M.reducedForm μ =
    ∫ ω in M.compliers, M.effect z ω ∂μ - ∫ ω in M.defiers, M.effect z ω ∂μ

Reduced-form decomposition: under the exclusion restriction, instrument independence, integrable responses Y z (D z) for both z, and P(Z = z) ≠ 0 for both values z, E[Yobs | Z = true] - E[Yobs | Z = false] = E[(Y 1 - Y 0) 1_compliers] - E[(Y 1 - Y 0) 1_defiers], where Y d is Y z d for any fixed instrument value z.

theorem reducedForm_eq_of_integrable [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hE : M.Exclusion μ)
  (hI : M.InstrumentIndependence μ) (hY : ∀ z d, Integrable (M.Y z d) μ)
  (h₁ : μ (M.instrumentEq true) ≠ 0) (h₀ : μ (M.instrumentEq false) ≠ 0) (z : Bool) :
  M.reducedForm μ =
    ∫ ω in M.compliers, M.effect z ω ∂μ - ∫ ω in M.defiers, M.effect z ω ∂μ

The reduced-form decomposition assuming every potential outcome Y z d integrable.

CausalInference.IVModel.wald_eq_complierEffecttheorem

theorem wald_eq_complierEffect [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hE : M.Exclusion μ)
  (hI : M.InstrumentIndependence μ) (hM : M.Monotonicity μ) (hR : M.Relevance μ)
  (hY : ∀ z, Integrable (M.YD z) μ) (z : Bool) :
  M.wald μ = M.complierEffect μ z

The LATE theorem (Imbens and Angrist, 1994). Assume the exclusion restriction, instrument independence, monotonicity, relevance (P(Z = true) ≠ 0, P(Z = false) ≠ 0 and a nonzero first stage; under the other assumptions the last is 0 < P(compliers), see IVModel.relevance_iff), and integrable responses Y z (D z) for both instrument values. Then the Wald ratio (E[Yobs | Z = true] - E[Yobs | Z = false]) / (E[Dobs | Z = true] - E[Dobs | Z = false]) equals the complier average causal effect E[Y z true - Y z false | compliers], for either instrument value z. Without relevance the compliers would be null and the equation would hold only as 0 = 0, by Lean's conventions for x / 0 and for conditioning on a null set. Relevance excludes that degenerate case and makes both sides genuine: the Wald ratio is then a quotient by a nonzero first stage of differences of conditional means given events of positive mass, and μ[|compliers] is a probability measure.

CausalInference.IVModel.wald_eq_complierEffect_of_integrabletheorem

theorem wald_eq_complierEffect_of_integrable [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hE : M.Exclusion μ)
  (hI : M.InstrumentIndependence μ) (hM : M.Monotonicity μ) (hR : M.Relevance μ)
  (hY : ∀ z d, Integrable (M.Y z d) μ) (z : Bool) :
  M.wald μ = M.complierEffect μ z

The LATE theorem assuming every potential outcome Y z d integrable (a stronger integrability hypothesis than in IVModel.wald_eq_complierEffect).

CausalInference.IVModel.complierMean_true_eqtheorem

theorem complierMean_true_eq [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hE : M.Exclusion μ)
  (hI : M.InstrumentIndependence μ) (hM : M.Monotonicity μ) (hR : M.Relevance μ)
  (hY : ∀ z, Integrable (M.YD z) μ) (z : Bool) :
  ∫ ω, M.Y z true ω ∂μ[|M.compliers] =
    (M.condMean μ (fun ω ↦ M.Yobs ω * M.DobsReal ω) true -
      M.condMean μ (fun ω ↦ M.Yobs ω * M.DobsReal ω) false) / M.firstStage μ

Complier mean of the treated potential outcome (Imbens and Rubin, 1997, Estimating outcome distributions for compliers in instrumental variables models). Under exclusion, instrument independence, monotonicity, relevance and integrable responses Y z (D z): E[Y z true | compliers] = (E[Yobs Dobs | Z = 1] - E[Yobs Dobs | Z = 0]) / firstStage.

CausalInference.IVModel.complierMean_false_eqtheorem

  ∫ ω, M.Y z false ω ∂μ[|M.compliers] =
    (M.condMean μ (fun ω ↦ M.Yobs ω * (1 - M.DobsReal ω)) false -
      M.condMean μ (fun ω ↦ M.Yobs ω * (1 - M.DobsReal ω)) true) / M.firstStage μ

Complier mean of the untreated potential outcome. Under the same assumptions, E[Y z false | compliers] = (E[Yobs (1 - Dobs) | Z = 0] - E[Yobs (1 - Dobs) | Z = 1]) / firstStage.

CausalInference.IVModel.wald_eq_effectTreatedtheorem

theorem wald_eq_effectTreated [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hE : M.Exclusion μ)
  (hI : M.InstrumentIndependence μ) (hR : M.Relevance μ) (hY : ∀ z, Integrable (M.YD z) μ)
  (hOne : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, M.D false ω = false) (z : Bool) :
  M.wald μ = ∫ ω, M.effect z ω ∂μ[|{ω | M.Dobs ω = true}]

One-sided noncompliance. Assume the exclusion restriction, instrument independence, relevance, integrable responses Y z (D z), and that no unit takes the treatment when the instrument is false (D false = false almost surely; this implies monotonicity). Then the Wald ratio equals the average treatment effect on the treated E[Y z true - Y z false | Dobs = true]. Under these assumptions P(Dobs = true) = P(Z = true) P(compliers) > 0, so the right side is a genuine conditional mean.

CausalInference.InstrumentalVariables.Counterexamples

CausalInference/InstrumentalVariables/Counterexamples.lean · 253 lines · 26 public theorems · 4 definitions · imports InstrumentalVariables.LATE

Counterexamples for binary instrumental variables. Concrete finite models showing that the hypotheses of the LATE theorem (CausalInference.IVModel.wald_eq_complierEffect) cannot simply be dropped, and that the IV assumptions identify only the complier effect, in line with Imbens and Angrist (1994, Identification and estimation of local average treatment effects).

Sources: Imbens and Angrist (1994)

CausalInference.IVCounterexample.Spacedefinition

abbrev Space (n : ℕ) : Type

The sample space Bool × Fin n: the first coordinate is the instrument, the second is a unit type that carries all potential variables.

CausalInference.IVCounterexample.Pdefinition

def P (n : ℕ) : Measure (Space n)

The product of the uniform distributions on Bool and on Fin n: the instrument is a fair coin, drawn independently of a unit type that is uniform on Fin n. This reading requires n ≠ 0: for n = 0 the sample space is empty and P 0 is the zero measure. Accordingly the probability-measure instance and every lemma below that uses it assume [NeZero n].

def modelA : IVModel (Space 3)

Counterexample (a), on Bool × Fin 3: units 0 and 1 are compliers with unit-level effect 1; unit 2 is a defier with unit-level effect 4. The outcome is the effect if treated and 0 otherwise, whatever the instrument value.

theorem modelA_not_reversed_monotonicity :
  ¬ ∀ᵐ ω ∂P 3, modelA.D true ω ≤ modelA.D false ω

Monotonicity fails in modelA in the reversed direction as well: the compliers (units 0 and 1) violate D true ≤ D false.

CausalInference.IVCounterexample.wald_ne_of_not_monotonicitytheorem

theorem wald_ne_of_not_monotonicity :
  modelA.Exclusion (P 3) ∧ modelA.InstrumentIndependence (P 3) ∧ modelA.Relevance (P 3) ∧
    0 < P 3 (modelA.instrumentEq true) ∧ P 3 (modelA.instrumentEq true) < 1 ∧
    (∀ z d, Integrable (modelA.Y z d) (P 3)) ∧ ¬ modelA.Monotonicity (P 3) ∧
    (¬ ∀ᵐ ω ∂P 3, modelA.D true ω ≤ modelA.D false ω) ∧
    ∀ z, modelA.wald (P 3) ≠ modelA.complierEffect (P 3) z ∧
      modelA.wald (P 3) ≠ modelA.ate (P 3) z

Counterexample (a): without monotonicity the Wald ratio need not be the complier effect or the average treatment effect. In modelA the exclusion restriction, instrument independence, relevance, 0 < P(Z = true) < 1 and integrability hold, and monotonicity fails in both directions (D false ≤ D true fails because of the defier, D true ≤ D false because of the compliers), so the failure is not an artifact of the labeling of the instrument; the Wald ratio is -2, while the complier average causal effect is 1 and the average treatment effect is 2.

Counterexample (b), on Bool × Fin 2, indexed by c : ℝ: unit 0 is a complier whose outcome is 1 if treated and 0 otherwise; unit 1 is a never-taker whose outcome is 0 if untreated and c if treated. The treated outcome of a never-taker is never observed.

CausalInference.IVCounterexample.ate_not_identifiedtheorem

theorem ate_not_identified :
  (modelB 0).LATEAssumptions (P 2) ∧ (modelB 1).LATEAssumptions (P 2) ∧
    (P 2).map (modelB 0).observed = (P 2).map (modelB 1).observed ∧
    ∀ z, (modelB 0).ate (P 2) z ≠ (modelB 1).ate (P 2) z

Counterexample (b): the IV assumptions do not identify the average treatment effect. The models modelB 0 and modelB 1 share the sample space, the probability measure and the observed-data law (the law of (Z, Dobs, Yobs)), both satisfy exclusion, instrument independence, monotonicity, relevance (with 0 < P(Z = true) < 1) and integrability, and their average treatment effects are 1 / 2 and 1.

CausalInference.InstrumentalVariables.Bounds

CausalInference/InstrumentalVariables/Bounds.lean · 985 lines · 60 public theorems · 16 definitions · imports InstrumentalVariables.Counterexamples, PartialIdentification.Manski

Bounds on the average treatment effect with a binary instrument. Partial identification of the average treatment effect in the binary instrumental variable model CausalInference.IVModel with outcomes in [lo, hi], following Robins (1989), Manski (1990, Nonparametric bounds on treatment effects) and Balke and Pearl (1997, Bounds on treatment effects from studies with imperfect compliance), and the testable implications of the IV assumptions.

Sources: Manski (1990); Robins (1989); Balke and Pearl (1997)

CausalInference.measureReal_mul_integral_condtheorem

theorem measureReal_mul_integral_cond {Ω : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω] {μ : Measure Ω}
  [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (s : Set Ω) (f : Ω → ℝ) :
  μ.real s * ∫ ω, f ω ∂μ[|s] = ∫ ω in s, f ω ∂μ

For a finite measure, μ(s) E[f | s] = ∫_s f, where E[f | s] is the integral against the conditional measure μ[|s]. If μ(s) = 0 both sides vanish; the identity carries no information then, and every use below either has μ(s) > 0 or does not divide by μ(s).

The lower IV bound on the average treatment effect, a function of the observation o alone: E[Y 1{D=1} | Z=1] - E[Y 1{D=0} | Z=0] + lo P(D=0 | Z=1) - hi P(D=1 | Z=0).

CausalInference.IVBounds.upperBounddefinition

def upperBound (μ : Measure Ω) (lo hi : ℝ) (o : Ω → Bool × Bool × ℝ) : ℝ

The upper IV bound on the average treatment effect, a function of the observation o alone: E[Y 1{D=1} | Z=1] - E[Y 1{D=0} | Z=0] + hi P(D=0 | Z=1) - lo P(D=1 | Z=0).

CausalInference.IVBounds.lowerBoundSwapdefinition

def lowerBoundSwap (μ : Measure Ω) (lo hi : ℝ) (o : Ω → Bool × Bool × ℝ) : ℝ

The IV lower bound with the instrument arms swapped, a function of the observation o alone: E[Y 1{D=1} | Z=0] - E[Y 1{D=0} | Z=1] + lo P(D=0 | Z=0) - hi P(D=1 | Z=1). For a binary outcome (lo = 0, hi = 1) it is P(Y=1, D=1 | Z=0) + P(Y=0, D=0 | Z=1) - 1.

CausalInference.IVBounds.upperBoundSwapdefinition

def upperBoundSwap (μ : Measure Ω) (lo hi : ℝ) (o : Ω → Bool × Bool × ℝ) : ℝ

The IV upper bound with the instrument arms swapped: E[Y 1{D=1} | Z=0] - E[Y 1{D=0} | Z=1] + hi P(D=0 | Z=0) - lo P(D=1 | Z=1). For a binary outcome it is 1 - P(Y=0, D=1 | Z=0) - P(Y=1, D=0 | Z=1).

CausalInference.IVBounds.upperBound_sub_lowerBoundtheorem

theorem upperBound_sub_lowerBound (μ : Measure Ω) (lo hi : ℝ) (o : Ω → Bool × Bool × ℝ) :
  upperBound μ lo hi o - lowerBound μ lo hi o =
    (hi - lo) * (obsMean μ o untreatedInd true + obsMean μ o treatedInd false)

Width of the IV bounds, without assumptions. For any measure and any observation map, upperBound - lowerBound = (hi - lo) (P(D=0 | Z=1) + P(D=1 | Z=0)): the width is hi - lo times the sum of the two noncompliance rates. This follows from the definitions alone.
