CausalInference.MissingData.Mechanisms

CausalInference/MissingData/Mechanisms.lean · 380 lines · 12 public theorems · 4 definitions · imports MissingData.Basic

Missingness mechanisms: MCAR, MAR, MNAR. Missingness mechanisms after Rubin (1976), stated with Mathlib independence and conditional independence, together with a mean-independence form of MAR that is what the weighting identities use.

Sources: Rubin (1976); Little and Rubin

Public declarations (16)

CausalInference.MissingData.MCARdefinition

def MCAR (μ : Measure Ω) (X : Ω → 𝒳) (Y : Ω → ℝ) (R : Ω → Bool) : Prop

Missing completely at random: the response indicator R is independent of the pair (X, Y) of covariate and full-data outcome.

CausalInference.MissingData.MARdefinition

def MAR [StandardBorelSpace Ω] (μ : Measure Ω) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {X : Ω → 𝒳}
  (hX : Measurable X) (R : Ω → Bool) (Y : Ω → ℝ) : Prop

Missing at random (full form): the response indicator R and the outcome Y are conditionally independent given the σ-algebra generated by the covariate X. This is the everywhere form of MAR for a single outcome with an always observed covariate; Rubin's (1976) original definition is a weaker condition on the realized data.

CausalInference.MissingData.MNARdefinition

def MNAR [StandardBorelSpace Ω] (μ : Measure Ω) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {X : Ω → 𝒳}
  (hX : Measurable X) (R : Ω → Bool) (Y : Ω → ℝ) : Prop

Missing not at random: the negation of the full conditional independence form MAR.

CausalInference.MissingData.MARMeandefinition

def MARMean (μ : Measure Ω) (X : Ω → 𝒳) (Y : Ω → ℝ) (R : Ω → Bool) : Prop

Missing at random, mean-independence form: the conditional expectation of the response indicator given (X, Y) agrees almost everywhere with its conditional expectation given X alone, E[1{R} | X, Y] = E[1{R} | X]. For measurable X, Y, R on a finite measure it is equivalent to the conditional independence form MAR (marMean_iff_mar). The predicate is meaningful only for measurable X, Y and R on a finite measure, and the weighting and identification theorems that use it assume these. Otherwise condExp is 0 by convention: if X is not measurable both sides are 0 and the predicate holds for every R; if the trimmed measures are not σ-finite (for instance for counting measure on ℕ with constant X) both sides can again be 0 whatever the mechanism.

CausalInference.MissingData.comap_le_comap_prodtheorem

theorem comap_le_comap_prod :
  MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance ≤
    MeasurableSpace.comap (fun ω => (X ω, Y ω)) inferInstance

The σ-algebra generated by X is contained in the one generated by (X, Y).

CausalInference.MissingData.condExp_indicator_preimage_of_indeptheorem

theorem condExp_indicator_preimage_of_indep [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {m : MeasurableSpace Ω}
  (hm : m ≤ mΩ) (hR : Measurable[mΩ] R)
  (hind : Indep (MeasurableSpace.comap R inferInstance) m μ) {s : Set Bool}
  (hs : MeasurableSet s) :
  μ⟦R ⁻¹' s | m⟧ =ᵐ[μ] fun _ => μ.real (R ⁻¹' s)

If R is independent of a σ-algebra m contained in the ambient one, then the conditional expectation given m of the indicator of R ∈ s is almost everywhere the constant μ (R ∈ s).

CausalInference.MissingData.MCAR.marMeantheorem

theorem MCAR.marMean [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : MCAR μ X Y R) (hX : Measurable X)
  (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) : MARMean μ X Y R

MCAR implies the mean-independence form of MAR: both conditional expectations of the response indicator equal the constant μ {R = true} almost everywhere.

CausalInference.MissingData.MCAR.condExp_intertheorem

theorem MCAR.condExp_inter [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : MCAR μ X Y R) (hX : Measurable X)
  (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) {s : Set Bool} {t : Set ℝ} (hs : MeasurableSet s)
  (ht : MeasurableSet t) :
  μ⟦R ⁻¹' s ∩ Y ⁻¹' t | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance⟧ =ᵐ[μ]
    fun ω => μ.real (R ⁻¹' s) * (μ⟦Y ⁻¹' t | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance⟧) ω

If R ∈ s is independent of the σ-algebra of (X, Y), then given X the indicator of R ∈ s and that of Y ∈ t factorize: E[1{R ∈ s, Y ∈ t} | X] = μ (R ∈ s) E[1{Y ∈ t} | X].

CausalInference.MissingData.MCAR.martheorem

theorem MCAR.mar [StandardBorelSpace Ω] [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : MCAR μ X Y R)
  (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) : MAR μ hX R Y

MCAR implies the full conditional independence form of MAR.

CausalInference.MissingData.MAR.marMeantheorem

theorem MAR.marMean [StandardBorelSpace Ω] [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X)
  (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) (h : MAR μ hX R Y) : MARMean μ X Y R

The full conditional independence form of MAR implies its mean-independence form: if R ⫫ Y | X then E[1{R} | X, Y] = E[1{R} | X] almost everywhere.

CausalInference.MissingData.MARMean.condExp_indicator_preimage_eqtheorem

theorem MARMean.condExp_indicator_preimage_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : MARMean μ X Y R)
  (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) (s : Set Bool) :
  μ⟦R ⁻¹' s | MeasurableSpace.comap (fun ω => (X ω, Y ω)) inferInstance⟧ =ᵐ[μ]
    μ⟦R ⁻¹' s | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance⟧

Under the mean form of MAR, the conditional expectation of the indicator of any response event R ∈ s is the same given (X, Y) as given X: a function of a Boolean R is affine in the response indicator.

CausalInference.MissingData.MARMean.martheorem

theorem MARMean.mar [StandardBorelSpace Ω] [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : MARMean μ X Y R)
  (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) : MAR μ hX R Y

The mean-independence form of MAR implies the full conditional independence form: for a Boolean response indicator, E[1{R} | X, Y] = E[1{R} | X] gives R ⫫ Y | X.

CausalInference.MissingData.marMean_iff_martheorem

theorem marMean_iff_mar [StandardBorelSpace Ω] [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X)
  (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) : MARMean μ X Y R ↔ MAR μ hX R Y

For a Boolean response indicator and measurable variables on a finite measure, the mean-independence form of MAR is equivalent to the conditional independence form R ⫫ Y | X.

CausalInference.MissingData.MARMean.comptheorem

theorem MARMean.comp [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : MARMean μ X Y R) (hX : Measurable X)
  (hY : Measurable Y) {g : ℝ → ℝ} (hg : Measurable g) : MARMean μ X (g ∘ Y) R

The mean-independence form of MAR is stable under measurable transformations of the outcome: if E[1{R} | X, Y] = E[1{R} | X] then E[1{R} | X, g(Y)] = E[1{R} | X], because the σ-algebra of (X, g(Y)) lies between those of X and of (X, Y).

CausalInference.MissingData.MNAR.not_mcartheorem

theorem MNAR.not_mcar [StandardBorelSpace Ω] [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X)
  (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) (h : MNAR μ hX R Y) : ¬ MCAR μ X Y R

An MNAR mechanism is not MCAR.

CausalInference.MissingData.MCAR.completeCaseMean_eqtheorem

theorem MCAR.completeCaseMean_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : MCAR μ X Y R) (hR : Measurable R)
  (hY : Integrable Y μ) (hpos : μ (R ⁻¹' {true}) ≠ 0) :
  completeCaseMean μ R Y = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Under MCAR the complete-case mean identifies the full-data mean: E[Y | R = true] = E[Y], provided the response event has positive probability and Y is integrable.

CausalInference.MissingData.Weighting

CausalInference/MissingData/Weighting.lean · 531 lines · 18 public theorems · 0 definitions · imports MissingData.Mechanisms

Identification under MAR: inverse probability weighting and outcome regression. Identification of the full-data mean E[Y] from the observed data when the outcome is missing at random given an always observed covariate X, in the mean-independence form MARMean. All statements use conditional expectations (MeasureTheory.condExp), so no conditioning on events of probability zero occurs.

Sources: Little and Rubin; Robins, Rotnitzky and Zhao (1994)

Public declarations (18)

CausalInference.MissingData.integral_mul_eq_of_condExp_eqtheorem

theorem integral_mul_eq_of_condExp_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {m : MeasurableSpace Ω} (hm : m ≤ mΩ)
  {r g p : Ω → ℝ} (hr : Integrable r μ) (hg : StronglyMeasurable[m] g)
  (hrg : Integrable (fun ω => r ω * g ω) μ) (hp : μ[r | m] =ᵐ[μ] p) :
  Integrable (fun ω => p ω * g ω) μ ∧ ∫ ω, r ω * g ω ∂μ = ∫ ω, p ω * g ω ∂μ

The weighting lemma. If the conditional expectation of r given a sub-σ-algebra m is almost everywhere p, and g is m-measurable with r g integrable, then the product p g is integrable and E[r g] = E[p g].

CausalInference.MissingData.lintegral_ofReal_mul_eq_of_condExp_eqtheorem

theorem lintegral_ofReal_mul_eq_of_condExp_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {m : MeasurableSpace Ω}
  (hm : m ≤ mΩ) {r p : Ω → ℝ} (hr : Integrable r μ) (hr0 : 0 ≤ᵐ[μ] r)
  (hp : μ[r | m] =ᵐ[μ] p) {G : Ω → ℝ≥0∞} (hG : Measurable[m] G) :
  ∫⁻ ω, ENNReal.ofReal (r ω) * G ω ∂μ = ∫⁻ ω, ENNReal.ofReal (p ω) * G ω ∂μ

The weighting lemma for nonnegative weights and Lebesgue integrals. If r ≥ 0 is integrable with E[r | m] = p almost everywhere, then ∫⁻ r G = ∫⁻ p G for every m-measurable G : Ω → [0, ∞]. No integrability of the products is needed.

CausalInference.MissingData.integrable_mul_of_condExp_eqtheorem

theorem integrable_mul_of_condExp_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {m : MeasurableSpace Ω} (hm : m ≤ mΩ)
  {r g p : Ω → ℝ} (hr : Integrable r μ) (hr0 : 0 ≤ᵐ[μ] r) (hg : StronglyMeasurable[m] g)
  (hp : μ[r | m] =ᵐ[μ] p) (hpg : Integrable (fun ω => p ω * g ω) μ) :
  Integrable (fun ω => r ω * g ω) μ

The converse integrability half of the weighting lemma for nonnegative weights. If r ≥ 0 is integrable with E[r | m] = p almost everywhere, g is m-measurable, and p g is integrable, then r g is integrable.

CausalInference.MissingData.measurable_comap_prodtheorem

theorem measurable_comap_prod {β : Type*} [MeasurableSpace β] {h : 𝒳 × ℝ → β}
  (hh : Measurable h) :
  Measurable[MeasurableSpace.comap (fun ω => (X ω, Y ω)) inferInstance]
    (fun ω => h (X ω, Y ω))

A function of (X, Y) is measurable for the σ-algebra generated by (X, Y).

CausalInference.MissingData.integrable_ipw_of_condExp_eqtheorem

theorem integrable_ipw_of_condExp_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {p : Ω → ℝ}
  (hpm : StronglyMeasurable[MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] p)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] p)
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < p ω) (hYi : Integrable Y μ) :
  Integrable (fun ω => respInd R ω * Y ω / p ω) μ

Integrability of the inverse probability weighted outcome. Let p be a σ(X)-measurable version of the response propensity E[1{R} | X], assume the mean-independence form of MAR and p > 0 almost surely. If Y is integrable then so is 1{R} Y / p; indeed E[1{R} |Y| / p] = E[|Y|].

CausalInference.MissingData.ipw_identity_of_condExp_eqtheorem

theorem ipw_identity_of_condExp_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {p : Ω → ℝ}
  (hpm : StronglyMeasurable[MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] p)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] p)
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < p ω) (hYi : Integrable Y μ) :
  ∫ ω, respInd R ω * Y ω / p ω ∂μ = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Inverse probability weighting under MAR with a σ(X)-measurable version p of the response propensity E[1{R} | X] (for instance the conditional expectation itself). Under the mean-independence form of MAR, p > 0 almost surely and integrability of Y, E[1{R} Y / p] = E[Y].

CausalInference.MissingData.integrable_ipwtheorem

theorem integrable_ipw [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω)) (hYi : Integrable Y μ) :
  Integrable (fun ω => respInd R ω * Y ω / π (X ω)) μ

Integrability of the inverse probability weighted outcome: if π ∘ X is a version of the response propensity E[1{R} | X], MAR holds in the mean-independence form, π(X) > 0 almost surely and Y is integrable, then 1{R} Y / π(X) is integrable.

CausalInference.MissingData.ipw_identitytheorem

theorem ipw_identity [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω)) (hYi : Integrable Y μ) :
  ∫ ω, respInd R ω * Y ω / π (X ω) ∂μ = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Inverse probability weighting under MAR. Let π ∘ X be a version of the response propensity E[1{R} | X], assume the mean-independence form of MAR, almost sure positivity of π(X), and integrability of Y. Then the weighted outcome is integrable (integrable_ipw) and E[1{R} Y / π(X)] = E[Y].

CausalInference.MissingData.ipw_identity_of_integrable_weightedtheorem

theorem ipw_identity_of_integrable_weighted [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X)
  (hY : Measurable Y) (hR : Measurable R) {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω))
  (hint : Integrable (fun ω => respInd R ω * Y ω / π (X ω)) μ) :
  ∫ ω, respInd R ω * Y ω / π (X ω) ∂μ = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Inverse probability weighting under MAR, assuming integrability of the weighted outcome instead of that of Y. Let π ∘ X be a version of the response propensity E[1{R} | X], assume the mean-independence form of MAR, almost sure positivity of π(X), and integrability of 1{R} Y / π(X). Then E[1{R} Y / π(X)] = E[Y].

CausalInference.MissingData.ipw_identity_of_letheorem

theorem ipw_identity_of_le [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) {c : ℝ} (hc : 0 < c) (hbd : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, c ≤ π (X ω))
  (hYi : Integrable Y μ) :
  ∫ ω, respInd R ω * Y ω / π (X ω) ∂μ = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Inverse probability weighting with the propensity bounded away from zero: if Y is integrable and π(X) ≥ c > 0 almost surely, then under MAR E[1{R} Y / π(X)] = E[Y].

CausalInference.MissingData.ipw_weight_integraltheorem

theorem ipw_weight_integral [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hR : Measurable R)
  {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω)) :
  Integrable (fun ω => respInd R ω / π (X ω)) μ ∧ ∫ ω, respInd R ω / π (X ω) ∂μ = 1

Normalization of the inverse probability weights: if π ∘ X is a version of the response propensity E[1{R} | X] on a probability space and π(X) > 0 almost surely, then the weight 1{R} / π(X) is integrable and E[1{R} / π(X)] = 1. No missingness assumption is needed. This is the normalization behind the Hajek form of the IPW estimator.

CausalInference.MissingData.ipw_identity_covariatetheorem

theorem ipw_identity_covariate [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hR : Measurable R)
  {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω)) {h : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hh : Measurable h)
  (hhi : Integrable (fun ω => h (X ω)) μ) :
  Integrable (fun ω => respInd R ω * h (X ω) / π (X ω)) μ ∧
    ∫ ω, respInd R ω * h (X ω) / π (X ω) ∂μ = ∫ ω, h (X ω) ∂μ

Inverse probability weighting of a function of the covariate: if π ∘ X is a version of the response propensity E[1{R} | X], π(X) > 0 almost surely and h(X) is integrable, then 1{R} h(X) / π(X) is integrable and E[1{R} h(X) / π(X)] = E[h(X)].

CausalInference.MissingData.aipw_identity_of_propensitytheorem

theorem aipw_identity_of_propensity [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω)) (hYi : Integrable Y μ)
  {h : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hh : Measurable h) (hhi : Integrable (fun ω => h (X ω)) μ) :
  ∫ ω, (respInd R ω * Y ω / π (X ω) - (respInd R ω - π (X ω)) / π (X ω) * h (X ω)) ∂μ =
    ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

The augmented inverse probability weighted identity of Robins, Rotnitzky and Zhao (1994), first robustness case: the propensity is correct. If π ∘ X is a version of E[1{R} | X], MAR holds in the mean-independence form, π(X) > 0 almost surely, Y is integrable and h(X) is any integrable function of the covariate, then E[1{R} Y / π(X) - (1{R} - π(X)) / π(X) h(X)] = E[Y].

CausalInference.MissingData.aipw_identity_of_regressiontheorem

theorem aipw_identity_of_regression [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {π : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hYi : Integrable Y μ) {h : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hh : Measurable h)
  (hreg : μ[Y | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => h (X ω))
  (hint : Integrable (fun ω => respInd R ω * (Y ω - h (X ω)) / π (X ω)) μ) :
  ∫ ω, (respInd R ω * Y ω / π (X ω) - (respInd R ω - π (X ω)) / π (X ω) * h (X ω)) ∂μ =
    ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

The augmented inverse probability weighted identity, second robustness case: the outcome regression is correct. If h(X) is a version of E[Y | X], MAR holds in the mean-independence form and π is any measurable function with π(X) > 0 almost surely (not necessarily the response propensity), then E[1{R} Y / π(X) - (1{R} - π(X)) / π(X) h(X)] = E[Y], provided the weighted residual 1{R} (Y - h(X)) / π(X) is integrable. Together with aipw_identity_of_propensity this is the double robustness of the augmented estimator.

CausalInference.MissingData.regression_ae_eqtheorem

theorem regression_ae_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {π μ₁ : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω)) (hYi : Integrable Y μ)
  (hreg : μ[respInd R * Y | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ]
    fun ω => π (X ω) * μ₁ (X ω)) :
  (fun ω => μ₁ (X ω)) =ᵐ[μ] μ[Y | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance]

Outcome regression (standardization) under MAR, almost everywhere form. Let π ∘ X be a version of E[1{R} | X] and let μ₁ : 𝒳 → ℝ satisfy E[1{R} Y | X] = π(X) μ₁(X) almost everywhere; on {π(X) > 0} this makes μ₁(X) a version of the complete-case regression E[Y | X, R = true], and it involves only observed quantities. Under the mean-independence form of MAR, almost sure positivity of π(X) and integrability of Y, μ₁(X) is a version of E[Y | X].

CausalInference.MissingData.regression_identitytheorem

theorem regression_identity [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hR : Measurable R) {π μ₁ : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hπ : Measurable π)
  (hprop : μ[respInd R | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π (X ω))
  (hmar : MARMean μ X Y R) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π (X ω)) (hYi : Integrable Y μ)
  (hreg : μ[respInd R * Y | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ]
    fun ω => π (X ω) * μ₁ (X ω)) :
  ∫ ω, μ₁ (X ω) ∂μ = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Outcome regression (standardization) under MAR. Under the hypotheses of regression_ae_eq, μ₁(X) is a version of E[Y | X], hence E[μ₁(X)] = E[Y].

CausalInference.MissingData.ipcw_identitytheorem

theorem ipcw_identity [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {Δ : Ω → Bool} (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)
  (hΔ : Measurable Δ) {K : 𝒳 → ℝ} (hK : Measurable K)
  (hprop : μ[respInd Δ | MeasurableSpace.comap X inferInstance] =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => K (X ω))
  (hnoninf : MARMean μ X Y Δ) (hpos : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < K (X ω))
  (hint : Integrable (fun ω => respInd Δ ω * Y ω / K (X ω)) μ) :
  ∫ ω, respInd Δ ω * Y ω / K (X ω) ∂μ = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Inverse probability of censoring weighting. An outcome Y is observed only for the uncensored units, Δ ω = true. If K ∘ X is a version of the probability E[1{Δ} | X] of remaining uncensored given the baseline covariate X, censoring is noninformative in the mean-independence sense E[1{Δ} | X, Y] = E[1{Δ} | X], K(X) > 0 almost surely, and the weighted outcome is integrable, then E[1{Δ} Y / K(X)] = E[Y]. This is ipw_identity with the uncensored indicator in the role of the response indicator.

CausalInference.MissingData.ipcw_identity_two_periodtheorem

theorem ipcw_identity_two_period [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {𝒴 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝒴]
  {L₀ : Ω → 𝒳} {L₁ : Ω → 𝒴} {R₁ R₂ : Ω → Bool} (hL₀ : Measurable L₀) (hL₁ : Measurable L₁)
  (hY : Measurable Y) (hR₁ : Measurable R₁) (hR₂ : Measurable R₂) {π₁ : 𝒳 → ℝ}
  {π₂ : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → ℝ} (hπ₁ : Measurable π₁) (hπ₂ : Measurable π₂)
  (h₁ : μ[respInd R₁ | MeasurableSpace.comap (fun ω => (L₀ ω, L₁ ω, Y ω)) inferInstance]
    =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => π₁ (L₀ ω))
  (h₂ : μ[respInd R₂ |
      MeasurableSpace.comap (fun ω => (L₀ ω, L₁ ω, Y ω, R₁ ω)) inferInstance]
    =ᵐ[μ] fun ω => respInd R₁ ω * π₂ (L₀ ω, L₁ ω))
  (hpos₁ : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π₁ (L₀ ω)) (hpos₂ : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, 0 < π₂ (L₀ ω, L₁ ω))
  (hint : Integrable (fun ω => respInd R₂ ω * Y ω / (π₁ (L₀ ω) * π₂ (L₀ ω, L₁ ω))) μ) :
  ∫ ω, respInd R₂ ω * Y ω / (π₁ (L₀ ω) * π₂ (L₀ ω, L₁ ω)) ∂μ = ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ

Inverse probability of censoring weighting over two periods with a time-varying covariate. A unit has baseline covariate L₀, a covariate L₁ measured at time one, and outcome Y; R₁ ω = true means the unit is uncensored at time one and R₂ ω = true that it is uncensored at time two (so Y is observed). Assume: * h₁: given (L₀, L₁, Y), the probability of remaining uncensored at time one is π₁(L₀), that is E[1{R₁} | L₀, L₁, Y] = π₁(L₀) (censoring at time one is noninformative given L₀, and π₁(L₀) is that probability); * h₂: given (L₀, L₁, Y, R₁), the probability of being uncensored at time two is 1{R₁} π₂(L₀, L₁), that is E[1{R₂} | L₀, L₁, Y, R₁] = 1{R₁} π₂(L₀, L₁) (units censored at time one stay censored, and among the others censoring at time two is noninformative given (L₀, L₁) with probability π₂(L₀, L₁) of remaining uncensored); * positivity: π₁(L₀) > 0 and π₂(L₀, L₁) > 0 almost surely; * the weighted outcome 1{R₂} Y / (π₁(L₀) π₂(L₀, L₁)) is integrable. Then E[1{R₂} Y / (π₁(L₀) π₂(L₀, L₁))] = E[Y].

CausalInference.MissingData.Identification

CausalInference/MissingData/Identification.lean · 151 lines · 4 public theorems · 2 definitions · imports MissingData.Weighting

Law-level identification of the full-data mean. The weighting identities of CausalInference.MissingData.Weighting are equalities of integrals on the sample space with a supplied version of the response propensity. This file turns them into identification statements: on suitable classes of admissible models the full-data mean E[Y] is a function of the observed-data law, in the sense of IsObservedDataFunctional.

Public declarations (6)

CausalInference.MissingData.condExp_comp_ae_eqtheorem

theorem condExp_comp_ae_eq {Ω β : Type*} {m : MeasurableSpace β} {mΩ : MeasurableSpace Ω}
  {mβ : MeasurableSpace β} {μ : Measure Ω} [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {T : Ω → β} (hT : Measurable T)
  (hm : m ≤ mβ) {f : β → ℝ} (hf : Integrable f (μ.map T)) :
  (fun ω => (μ.map T)[f | m] (T ω)) =ᵐ[μ] μ[f ∘ T | m.comap T]

Conditional expectations pull back along a measurable map. If T : Ω → β is measurable, m is a sub-σ-algebra of β and f is integrable under the push forward μ.map T, then E_{μ.map T}[f | m] ∘ T is almost everywhere E_μ[f ∘ T | T⁻¹ m].

CausalInference.MissingData.ipwFunctionaldefinition

def ipwFunctional (ν : Measure (𝒳 × Bool × ℝ)) : ℝ

The inverse probability weighting functional of a law ν of the observed data (x, r, w): ∫ w / p_ν(x) dν, where p_ν = E_ν[1{r = true} | x] is the response propensity computed from ν itself (the conditional expectation given the σ-algebra generated by the first coordinate).

CausalInference.MissingData.marPositiveModelsdefinition

def marPositiveModels : Set (MissingDataModel Ω 𝒳)

The class of admissible missing-data models with integrable outcome, satisfying the mean-independence form of MAR, whose response propensity E[1{R} | X] is almost surely positive.

CausalInference.MissingData.fullMean_eq_ipwFunctionaltheorem

theorem fullMean_eq_ipwFunctional {M : MissingDataModel Ω 𝒳} (hM : M ∈ marPositiveModels) :
  M.fullMean = ipwFunctional M.observedLaw

Identification of the full-data mean under MAR and positivity: on marPositiveModels, E[Y] equals the inverse probability weighting functional of the observed-data law.

CausalInference.MissingData.isObservedDataFunctional_fullMean_of_martheorem

theorem isObservedDataFunctional_fullMean_of_mar :
  IsObservedDataFunctional (marPositiveModels : Set (MissingDataModel Ω 𝒳))
    MissingDataModel.fullMean

Under MAR and positivity the full-data mean is a function of the observed-data law on marPositiveModels, through ipwFunctional.

CausalInference.MissingData.isObservedDataFunctional_fullMean_of_mcartheorem

theorem isObservedDataFunctional_fullMean_of_mcar {S : Set (MissingDataModel Ω 𝒳)}
  (hS : ∀ M ∈ S, M.IsAdmissible ∧ Integrable M.Y M.μ ∧ MCAR M.μ M.X M.Y M.R ∧
    M.μ (M.R ⁻¹' {true}) ≠ 0) :
  IsObservedDataFunctional S MissingDataModel.fullMean

Under MCAR the full-data mean is a function of the observed-data law on every class of admissible models with integrable outcome and a response event of positive probability: it equals the complete-case mean, which is computed from the observed-data law.

Selection bias and measurement error

Selection on a common effect, misclassification, and the built-in selection bias of hazard ratios, in finite settings.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio

CausalInference/Bias/HazardRatio.lean · 272 lines · 13 public theorems · 11 definitions

The built-in selection bias of hazard ratios. A finite two-period survival model with a binary treatment A, a binary unmeasured frailty U independent of A, death at time 1 Y1 and death at time 2 Y2.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020)

Public declarations (24)

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.dead1Massdefinition

def dead1Mass (a : Bool) : ℝ

The mass P(A = a, Y1 = 1) = ∑ u, pA a pU u r1 a u.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.armMassdefinition

def armMass (a : Bool) : ℝ

The mass P(A = a) of the treatment arm a.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.surv1Massdefinition

def surv1Mass (a : Bool) : ℝ

The mass P(A = a, Y1 = 0) = ∑ u, pA a pU u (1 - r1 a u) of the time 1 survivors in arm a.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.dead2Massdefinition

def dead2Mass (a : Bool) : ℝ

The mass P(A = a, Y1 = 0, Y2 = 1) = ∑ u, pA a pU u (1 - r1 a u) r2 a u.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.hazard1definition

def hazard1 (a : Bool) : ℝ

The time 1 hazard P(Y1 = 1 | A = a), equal to the time 1 risk.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.hazard2definition

def hazard2 (a : Bool) : ℝ

The time 2 hazard P(Y2 = 1 | A = a, Y1 = 0): the risk at time 2 among the time 1 survivors.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.stratumHazard2definition

def stratumHazard2 (a u : Bool) : ℝ

The time 2 hazard within the frailty stratum U = u: P(Y2 = 1 | A = a, U = u, Y1 = 0).

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.frailtyWeightdefinition

def frailtyWeight (a u : Bool) : ℝ

The frailty distribution among the time 1 survivors of arm a: P(U = u | A = a, Y1 = 0) = pA a pU u (1 - r1 a u) / P(A = a, Y1 = 0).

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.hazard2_eq_weightedtheorem

theorem hazard2_eq_weighted (a : Bool) :
  hazard2 pA pU r1 r2 a = ∑ u, frailtyWeight pA pU r1 a u * r2 a u

The time 2 hazard conditions on survival: it is the average of the stratum risks r2 a u over the frailty distribution P(U = u | A = a, Y1 = 0) of the survivors, which depends on the arm a through r1 a u even though U is independent of A. The weights sum to one when the survivor mass is nonzero (frailtyWeight_add).

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.stratumHazard2_eqtheorem

theorem stratumHazard2_eq (a u : Bool) (h : pA a * pU u * (1 - r1 a u) ≠ 0) :
  stratumHazard2 pA pU r1 r2 a u = r2 a u

Within a frailty stratum with positive survivor mass, the time 2 hazard is r2 a u.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.stratum_hazardRatio2_eq_onetheorem

theorem stratum_hazardRatio2_eq_one (u : Bool)
  (hnull : ∀ u, r2 true u = r2 false u)
  (h1 : pA true * pU u * (1 - r1 true u) ≠ 0) (h0 : pA false * pU u * (1 - r1 false u) ≠ 0)
  (hr : r2 false u ≠ 0) :
  stratumHazard2 pA pU r1 r2 true u / stratumHazard2 pA pU r1 r2 false u = 1

Under no effect of treatment at time 2, the stratum-specific time 2 hazard ratio is one: the conditional hazard ratio correctly shows the absence of an effect.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.frailtyWeight_lt_ifftheorem

theorem frailtyWeight_lt_iff (hA : ∀ a, 0 < pA a) (hU : ∀ u, 0 < pU u)
  (hs : ∀ a u, 0 < 1 - r1 a u) :
  frailtyWeight pA pU r1 true true < frailtyWeight pA pU r1 false true ↔
    (1 - r1 true true) * (1 - r1 false false) < (1 - r1 true false) * (1 - r1 false true)

Selection by survival. With 0 < pU u, positive arm probabilities and positive survival probabilities s a u = 1 - r1 a u, the treated survivors are less likely than the untreated survivors to have U = 1 if and only if s 1 1 * s 0 0 < s 1 0 * s 0 1, that is, if and only if treatment improves survival relatively more in the stratum U = 0.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.frailtyWeight_addtheorem

theorem frailtyWeight_add (a : Bool) (ha : surv1Mass pA pU r1 a ≠ 0) :
  frailtyWeight pA pU r1 a true + frailtyWeight pA pU r1 a false = 1

When the survivor mass of arm a is nonzero, the survivors' frailty distribution is a probability distribution: P(U = 1 | A = a, Y1 = 0) + P(U = 0 | A = a, Y1 = 0) = 1.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.hazard2_sub_of_noEffecttheorem

theorem hazard2_sub_of_noEffect (hnull : ∀ u, r2 true u = r2 false u)
  (h1 : surv1Mass pA pU r1 true ≠ 0) (h0 : surv1Mass pA pU r1 false ≠ 0) :
  hazard2 pA pU r1 r2 true - hazard2 pA pU r1 r2 false =
    (r2 false true - r2 false false) *
      (frailtyWeight pA pU r1 true true - frailtyWeight pA pU r1 false true)

Under no effect of treatment at time 2 (r2 a u = r2 0 u for both arms), the difference of the time 2 hazards is (r2 · 1 - r2 · 0) (w 1 1 - w 0 1), where w a 1 = P(U = 1 | A = a, Y1 = 0). It is nonzero as soon as the frailty affects time 2 risk and the survivors' frailty distributions differ between the arms.

CausalInference.Bias.HazardRatio.hazard2_lt_of_noEffecttheorem

theorem hazard2_lt_of_noEffect (hA : ∀ a, 0 < pA a) (hU : ∀ u, 0 < pU u)
  (hs : ∀ a u, 0 < 1 - r1 a u) (hnull : ∀ u, r2 true u = r2 false u)
  (hprot : r2 false true < r2 false false)
  (hsel : (1 - r1 true true) * (1 - r1 false false) < (1 - r1 true false) * (1 - r1 false true)) :
  hazard2 pA pU r1 r2 false < hazard2 pA pU r1 r2 true

The built-in selection bias of the time 2 hazard ratio. Under no effect of treatment at time 2, if U = 1 is protective at time 2 (r2 · 1 < r2 · 0) and treatment improves time 1 survival relatively more in the stratum U = 0, then the time 2 hazard is larger in the treated than in the untreated.

Fair laws for treatment and frailty.

  (∀ u, exR1 true u < exR1 false u) ∧ (∀ a, exR1 a true < exR1 a false) ∧
    exR2 false true < exR2 false false ∧ ∀ a u, 0 < 1 - exR1 a u

In the example, treatment lowers the time 1 risk in each frailty stratum, the haplotype U = 1 lowers the risk at both times, and all time 1 survival probabilities are positive.

CausalInference.Bias.Misclassification

CausalInference/Bias/Misclassification.lean · 485 lines · 29 public theorems · 19 definitions · imports Bias.Selection

Measurement error and misclassification. Finite results on measurement bias for a treatment A and an outcome Y measured as A* and Y*.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Dosemeci, Wacholder and Lubin (1990)

Public declarations (48)

CausalInference.Bias.observedTabledefinition

def observedTable [Fintype α] [Fintype β] (p : α → β → ℝ) (K : α → β → α' → β' → ℝ)
  (a' : α') (y' : β') : ℝ

The observed table of (A*, Y*): the true table p a y pushed through the measurement kernel K a y a' y' = P(A* = a', Y* = y' | A = a, Y = y).

CausalInference.Bias.observed_indep_of_indeptheorem

theorem observed_indep_of_indep [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [Fintype α'] [Fintype β']
  (p : α → β → ℝ) (hp : TableIndep p) (hT : ∑ a, ∑ y, p a y ≠ 0)
  (kA : α → α' → ℝ) (kY : β → β' → ℝ) :
  TableIndep (observedTable p fun a y a' y' ↦ kA a a' * kY y y')

Independent nondifferential error preserves the null (What If, Fine Point 9.1). If the true table is independent (A ⫫ Y) with nonzero total mass and the measurement kernel is a product kA a a' * kY y y' (the error of A* depends only on A, that of Y* only on Y, and the two are independent), then the observed table is independent (A* ⫫ Y*).

CausalInference.Bias.exactKerneldefinition

def exactKernel [DecidableEq α] (b b' : α) : ℝ

The kernel of a variable measured without error: P(B* = b' | B = b) = [b = b'].

CausalInference.Bias.riskdefinition

def risk (q : α → Bool → ℝ) (a : α) : ℝ

The risk P(Y = 1 | A = a) = q a 1 / (q a 1 + q a 0) of a table q of (A, Y) with binary Y. Every use carries the hypothesis that the row mass is nonzero.

CausalInference.Bias.binaryKerneldefinition

def binaryKernel (se sp : ℝ) (b b' : Bool) : ℝ

The classification kernel of a binary variable with sensitivity se and specificity sp: P(B* = 1 | B = 1) = se, P(B* = 0 | B = 1) = 1 - se, P(B* = 1 | B = 0) = 1 - sp, P(B* = 0 | B = 0) = sp.

CausalInference.Bias.binaryKernel_sumtheorem

theorem binaryKernel_sum (se sp : ℝ) (b : Bool) : ∑ b', binaryKernel se sp b b' = 1

Each row of the binary classification kernel sums to one.

CausalInference.Bias.riskDiffdefinition

def riskDiff (q : Bool → Bool → ℝ) : ℝ

The risk difference P(Y = 1 | A = 1) - P(Y = 1 | A = 0) of a table of (A, Y).

CausalInference.Bias.outcomeMisclassifieddefinition

def outcomeMisclassified (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) : Bool → Bool → ℝ

The observed table of (A, Y*) when treatment is measured exactly and the outcome is misclassified with sensitivity se and specificity sp that do not depend on treatment (nondifferential outcome misclassification).

CausalInference.Bias.outcomeMisclassified_applytheorem

theorem outcomeMisclassified_apply (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) (a y' : Bool) :
  outcomeMisclassified p se sp a y' = ∑ y, p a y * binaryKernel se sp y y'

CausalInference.Bias.outcome_risk_eqtheorem

theorem outcome_risk_eq (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) (a : Bool)
  (hrow : p a true + p a false ≠ 0) :
  risk (outcomeMisclassified p se sp) a = (1 - sp) + (se + sp - 1) * risk p a

Under nondifferential outcome misclassification, the observed risk in each treatment arm is P(Y* = 1 | A = a) = (1 - sp) + (se + sp - 1) P(Y = 1 | A = a).

CausalInference.Bias.outcome_riskDiff_eqtheorem

theorem outcome_riskDiff_eq (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ)
  (h1 : p true true + p true false ≠ 0) (h0 : p false true + p false false ≠ 0) :
  riskDiff (outcomeMisclassified p se sp) = (se + sp - 1) * riskDiff p

Under nondifferential outcome misclassification, the observed risk difference is the true risk difference times se + sp - 1.

CausalInference.Bias.outcome_riskDiff_toward_nulltheorem

theorem outcome_riskDiff_toward_null (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) (hse : se ≤ 1)
  (hsp : sp ≤ 1) (h : 1 < se + sp)
  (h1 : p true true + p true false ≠ 0) (h0 : p false true + p false false ≠ 0) :
  (0 < riskDiff (outcomeMisclassified p se sp) ↔ 0 < riskDiff p) ∧
    (riskDiff (outcomeMisclassified p se sp) = 0 ↔ riskDiff p = 0) ∧

Bias toward the null without reversal. Under nondifferential outcome misclassification with se ≤ 1, sp ≤ 1 and se + sp > 1, the observed risk difference has the same sign as the true one and no larger absolute value.

CausalInference.Bias.outcome_riskDiff_reversedtheorem

theorem outcome_riskDiff_reversed (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) (h : se + sp < 1)
  (h1 : p true true + p true false ≠ 0) (h0 : p false true + p false false ≠ 0)
  (hrd : 0 < riskDiff p) :
  riskDiff (outcomeMisclassified p se sp) < 0

When se + sp < 1 the classification is worse than chance and the observed risk difference has the opposite sign of the true one: the hypothesis se + sp > 1 cannot be dropped.

CausalInference.Bias.exposureMisclassifieddefinition

def exposureMisclassified (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) : Bool → Bool → ℝ

The observed table of (A*, Y) when the outcome is measured exactly and treatment is misclassified with sensitivity se and specificity sp that do not depend on the outcome (nondifferential treatment misclassification).

CausalInference.Bias.exposureMisclassified_applytheorem

theorem exposureMisclassified_apply (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) (a' y : Bool) :
  exposureMisclassified p se sp a' y = ∑ a, p a y * binaryKernel se sp a a'

CausalInference.Bias.exposureWeightdefinition

def exposureWeight (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) (a' : Bool) : ℝ

The positive predictive weight P(A = 1 | A* = a') under treatment misclassification, where n a = p a 1 + p a 0 is the mass of A = a.

CausalInference.Bias.exposure_risk_eqtheorem

theorem exposure_risk_eq (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ) (a' : Bool)
  (h1 : p true true + p true false ≠ 0) (h0 : p false true + p false false ≠ 0)
  (hobs : ∑ a, (p a true + p a false) * binaryKernel se sp a a' ≠ 0) :
  risk (exposureMisclassified p se sp) a' =
    exposureWeight p se sp a' * risk p true +
      (1 - exposureWeight p se sp a') * risk p false

Under nondifferential treatment misclassification the observed risk in the stratum A* = a' is the mixture w P(Y = 1 | A = 1) + (1 - w) P(Y = 1 | A = 0) with w = P(A = 1 | A* = a').

CausalInference.Bias.exposureWeight_subtheorem

theorem exposureWeight_sub (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ)
  (hobs1 : ∑ a, (p a true + p a false) * binaryKernel se sp a true ≠ 0)
  (hobs0 : ∑ a, (p a true + p a false) * binaryKernel se sp a false ≠ 0) :
  exposureWeight p se sp true - exposureWeight p se sp false =
    (p true true + p true false) * (p false true + p false false) * (se + sp - 1) /
      ((∑ a, (p a true + p a false) * binaryKernel se sp a true) *
        ∑ a, (p a true + p a false) * binaryKernel se sp a false)

The difference of the predictive weights between the observed strata: P(A = 1 | A* = 1) - P(A = 1 | A* = 0) = n1 n0 (se + sp - 1) / (D1 D0), where n a is the mass of A = a and D a' the mass of A* = a'.

CausalInference.Bias.exposure_riskDiff_toward_nulltheorem

theorem exposure_riskDiff_toward_null (p : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (se sp : ℝ)
  (hp : ∀ a y, 0 ≤ p a y) (hse : se ≤ 1) (hsp : sp ≤ 1)
  (h : 1 < se + sp) (h1 : 0 < p true true + p true false)
  (h0 : 0 < p false true + p false false)
  (hobs1 : 0 < ∑ a, (p a true + p a false) * binaryKernel se sp a true)
  (hobs0 : 0 < ∑ a, (p a true + p a false) * binaryKernel se sp a false) :
  ∃ c, 0 < c ∧ c ≤ 1 ∧
    riskDiff (exposureMisclassified p se sp) = c * riskDiff p

Nondifferential treatment misclassification of a binary treatment biases the risk difference toward the null without reversing it. If both treatment levels and both observed levels have positive mass, se ≤ 1, sp ≤ 1 and se + sp > 1, then the observed risk difference P(Y = 1 | A* = 1) - P(Y = 1 | A* = 0) equals c times the true one for some 0 < c ≤ 1.

CausalInference.Bias.uniformTabledefinition

def uniformTable (_ _ : Bool) : ℝ

The joint table of independent fair binary A and Y: every cell has mass 1/4.

CausalInference.Bias.uniformTable_indeptheorem

theorem uniformTable_indep : TableIndep uniformTable

The fair table satisfies the null A ⫫ Y.

CausalInference.Bias.IsMeasurementKerneldefinition

def IsMeasurementKernel (K : Bool → Bool → Bool → Bool → ℝ) : Prop

A kernel K a y a' y' is a measurement kernel: nonnegative with every row summing to one.

CausalInference.Bias.differentialKerneldefinition

def differentialKernel (a y a' y' : Bool) : ℝ

Differential treatment error (recall bias, What If section 9.2, Figure 9.4): the outcome is measured exactly, individuals with Y = 1 always report A* = 1, and individuals with Y = 0 report their true treatment. The error of A* depends on the true outcome. The errors are independent, since Y has no error.

CausalInference.Bias.differentialKernel_isMeasurementKerneltheorem

theorem differentialKernel_isMeasurementKernel : IsMeasurementKernel differentialKernel

CausalInference.Bias.differentialExample_not_indeptheorem

theorem differentialExample_not_indep :
  ¬ TableIndep (observedTable uniformTable differentialKernel)

Differential error creates an association under the null: with A ⫫ Y, the observed A* and Y are dependent (P(A* = 1, Y = 1) = 1/2 while P(A* = 1) P(Y = 1) = 3/8).

CausalInference.Bias.differentialExample_valuestheorem

theorem differentialExample_values :
  observedTable uniformTable differentialKernel true true = 1 / 2 ∧
    (observedTable uniformTable differentialKernel true true +
        observedTable uniformTable differentialKernel true false) *
      (observedTable uniformTable differentialKernel true true +
        observedTable uniformTable differentialKernel false true) = 3 / 8

The numbers of the differential example (the observed table has total mass one): P(A* = 1, Y = 1) = 1/2 while P(A* = 1) P(Y = 1) = 3/4 * 1/2 = 3/8.

CausalInference.Bias.dependentKerneldefinition

def dependentKernel (a y a' y' : Bool) : ℝ

Dependent nondifferential errors (What If section 9.2, Figure 9.3): with probability 1/2 both variables are recorded correctly, and with probability 1/2 a common error (for example poor recall) records both as 1. The error source is independent of (A, Y), so the errors are nondifferential, but the errors of A* and Y* are dependent.

CausalInference.Bias.dependentKernel_isMeasurementKerneltheorem

theorem dependentKernel_isMeasurementKernel : IsMeasurementKernel dependentKernel

CausalInference.Bias.dependentKernel_nondifferentialtheorem

theorem dependentKernel_nondifferential :
  (∀ a y₁ y₂ a', ∑ y', dependentKernel a y₁ a' y' = ∑ y', dependentKernel a y₂ a' y') ∧
    ∀ a₁ a₂ y y', ∑ a', dependentKernel a₁ y a' y' = ∑ a', dependentKernel a₂ y a' y'

The dependent kernel is nondifferential: the law of A* given (A, Y) does not depend on Y, and the law of Y* given (A, Y) does not depend on A.

CausalInference.Bias.dependentExample_not_indeptheorem

theorem dependentExample_not_indep :
  ¬ TableIndep (observedTable uniformTable dependentKernel)

Dependent errors create an association under the null: with A ⫫ Y, the observed A* and Y* are dependent (P(A* = 1, Y* = 1) = 5/8 while P(A* = 1) P(Y* = 1) = 9/16).

CausalInference.Bias.dependentExample_valuestheorem

theorem dependentExample_values :
  observedTable uniformTable dependentKernel true true = 5 / 8 ∧
    (observedTable uniformTable dependentKernel true true +
        observedTable uniformTable dependentKernel true false) *
      (observedTable uniformTable dependentKernel true true +
        observedTable uniformTable dependentKernel false true) = 9 / 16

The numbers of the dependent example (the observed table has total mass one): P(A* = 1, Y* = 1) = 5/8 while P(A* = 1) P(Y* = 1) = 3/4 * 3/4 = 9/16.

CausalInference.Bias.trendRiskdefinition

def trendRisk (a : Fin 3) : ℝ

True risk P(Y = 1 | A = a) = (a + 1) / 10 for a three-level treatment A ∈ {0, 1, 2}.

CausalInference.Bias.trendTabledefinition

def trendTable (a : Fin 3) (y : Bool) : ℝ

The true joint table of (A, Y): A uniform on three levels and P(Y = 1 | A) = trendRisk.

CausalInference.Bias.trendKerneldefinition

def trendKernel : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℝ

A nondifferential classification of the three-level treatment, with rows P(A* = · | A = 0) = (1/4, 3/4, 0), P(A* = · | A = 1) = (0, 1/4, 3/4) and P(A* = · | A = 2) = (3/4, 0, 1/4).

CausalInference.Bias.trendObserveddefinition

def trendObserved : Fin 3 → Bool → ℝ

The observed table of (A*, Y): the outcome is measured exactly and the treatment error does not depend on the outcome (independent nondifferential error).

CausalInference.Bias.trendKernel_stochastictheorem

theorem trendKernel_stochastic :
  (∀ a a', 0 ≤ trendKernel a a') ∧ ∀ a, ∑ a', trendKernel a a' = 1

CausalInference.Bias.trendKernel_meantheorem

theorem trendKernel_mean :
  ∑ a' : Fin 3, ((a' : ℕ) : ℝ) * trendKernel 0 a' = 3 / 4 ∧
    ∑ a' : Fin 3, ((a' : ℕ) : ℝ) * trendKernel 1 a' = 7 / 4 ∧
    ∑ a' : Fin 3, ((a' : ℕ) : ℝ) * trendKernel 2 a' = 1 / 2

The conditional mean E[A* | A = a] is 3/4, 7/4, 1/2 for a = 0, 1, 2: it is not monotone in a.

CausalInference.Bias.tableCovdefinition

def tableCov (q : Fin 3 → Bool → ℝ) : ℝ

The covariance E[X Y] - E[X] E[Y] of the treatment level X ∈ {0, 1, 2} and the binary outcome Y under a table q of total mass one.

CausalInference.Bias.trend_totaltheorem

theorem trend_total :
  ∑ a, ∑ y, trendTable a y = 1 ∧ ∑ a, ∑ y, trendObserved a y = 1

Both the true and the observed tables have total mass one.

CausalInference.Bias.trendExample_reversaltheorem

theorem trendExample_reversal :
  risk trendTable 0 < risk trendTable 1 ∧ risk trendTable 1 < risk trendTable 2 ∧
    tableCov trendTable = 1 / 15 ∧ tableCov trendObserved = -1 / 120 ∧
    risk trendObserved 0 = 1 / 4 ∧ risk trendObserved 1 = 1 / 8 ∧
    risk trendObserved 2 = 9 / 40

Trend reversal under independent nondifferential error (What If, Fine Point 9.1). The true risks increase in the treatment level (1/10 < 1/5 < 3/10) and the true covariance of treatment level and outcome is 1/15 > 0. The observed covariance of A* and Y is -1/120 < 0: the observed trend has the opposite direction. The observed category risks P(Y = 1 | A* = a') are 1/4, 1/8, 9/40.

CausalInference.Bias.observedPrevalencedefinition

def observedPrevalence (se sp π : ℝ) : ℝ

The observed prevalence P(B* = 1) of a binary variable with true prevalence π, sensitivity se and specificity sp, by the law of total probability.

CausalInference.Bias.observedPrevalence_eqtheorem

theorem observedPrevalence_eq (se sp π : ℝ) :
  observedPrevalence se sp π = (1 - sp) + (se + sp - 1) * π

CausalInference.Bias.prevalence_correctiontheorem

theorem prevalence_correction (se sp π : ℝ) (h : se + sp ≠ 1) :
  π = (observedPrevalence se sp π - (1 - sp)) / (se + sp - 1)

Correction for misclassification: with known se and sp and se + sp ≠ 1, the true prevalence is recovered from the observed one as π = (P(B* = 1) - (1 - sp)) / (se + sp - 1).

CausalInference.Bias.prevalence_not_identifiedtheorem

theorem prevalence_not_identified (se sp π π' : ℝ) (h : se + sp = 1) :
  observedPrevalence se sp π = observedPrevalence se sp π'

When se + sp = 1 the observed prevalence is 1 - sp whatever the true prevalence, so the true prevalence is not identified and the condition se + sp ≠ 1 cannot be dropped.

CausalInference.Bias.misclassMatrixdefinition

def misclassMatrix (se sp : ℝ) : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℝ

The misclassification matrix: rows are the true value (index 0 negative, 1 positive), columns the observed value, entries P(B* = j | B = i).

CausalInference.Bias.vecMul_misclassMatrixtheorem

theorem vecMul_misclassMatrix (se sp π : ℝ) :
  (![1 - π, π] ᵥ* misclassMatrix se sp) 1 = observedPrevalence se sp π

The observed distribution is the true distribution times the misclassification matrix; its positive entry is the observed prevalence.

CausalInference.Bias.misclassMatrix_dettheorem

theorem misclassMatrix_det (se sp : ℝ) : (misclassMatrix se sp).det = se + sp - 1

The determinant of the misclassification matrix is se + sp - 1.

CausalInference.Bias.misclassMatrix_correctiontheorem

theorem misclassMatrix_correction (se sp : ℝ) (h : se + sp ≠ 1) (v : Fin 2 → ℝ) :
  (v ᵥ* misclassMatrix se sp) ᵥ* (misclassMatrix se sp)⁻¹ = v

Matrix correction: when se + sp ≠ 1 the misclassification matrix is invertible and every true distribution v is recovered from the observed one, v = (v M) M⁻¹.

CausalInference.Bias.Selection

CausalInference/Bias/Selection.lean · 290 lines · 15 public theorems · 7 definitions

Selection on a common effect. Finite results on selection bias for two marginally independent causes A and E of a selection or survival indicator.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020)

Public declarations (22)

CausalInference.Bias.TableIndepdefinition

def TableIndep {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β] (q : α → β → ℝ) : Prop

Scale-free independence of a two-way table q of masses (a joint law, or its restriction to a stratum): for every cell, q a b times the total mass equals the row total of a times the column total of b. For a stratum with positive mass this is conditional independence of the row and column variables given the stratum.

CausalInference.Bias.tableIndep_multheorem

theorem tableIndep_mul {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β] (f : α → ℝ) (g : β → ℝ) :
  TableIndep fun a b ↦ f a * g b

A product table f a * g b is independent, with no normalization needed.

CausalInference.Bias.tableIndep_bool_ifftheorem

theorem tableIndep_bool_iff (q : Bool → Bool → ℝ) :
  TableIndep q ↔ q true true * q false false = q true false * q false true

For a two-by-two table, independence is equivalent to equality of the cross products: q 1 1 * q 0 0 = q 1 0 * q 0 1, that is, an odds ratio of one.

CausalInference.Bias.stratumdefinition

def stratum (pA : α → ℝ) (pE : β → ℝ) (s : α → β → ℝ) (a : α) (e : β) : ℝ

The restriction of the joint law of (A, E, S) to the stratum S = 1, when A and E are independent with marginal laws pA and pE and P(S = 1 | A = a, E = e) = s a e: the mass P(A = a, E = e, S = 1) = pA a * pE e * s a e. With s = fun _ _ ↦ 1 it is the joint law of (A, E) itself.

CausalInference.Bias.stratum_indep_of_multiplicativetheorem

theorem stratum_indep_of_multiplicative [Fintype α] [Fintype β] (pA : α → ℝ) (pE : β → ℝ)
  (s : α → β → ℝ) (g : β → ℝ) (h : α → ℝ) (hs : ∀ a e, s a e = g e * h a) :
  TableIndep (stratum pA pE s)

Selection without bias, the multiplicative survival model (What If, Technical Point 8.2). If A ⫫ E and the selection (survival) probability factorizes as P(S = 1 | A = a, E = e) = g(e) h(a), then A and E remain independent in the selected stratum.

CausalInference.Bias.stratum_one_indeptheorem

theorem stratum_one_indep [Fintype α] [Fintype β] (pA : α → ℝ) (pE : β → ℝ) :
  TableIndep (stratum pA pE fun _ _ ↦ 1)

Before selection, A and E are independent: the table pA a * pE e is independent.

CausalInference.Bias.multiplicative_of_stratum_indeptheorem

theorem multiplicative_of_stratum_indep [Fintype α] [Fintype β] (pA : α → ℝ) (pE : β → ℝ)
  (s : α → β → ℝ) (hA : ∀ a, 0 < pA a) (hE : ∀ e, 0 < pE e)
  (hT : 0 < ∑ a, ∑ e, stratum pA pE s a e) (hind : TableIndep (stratum pA pE s)) :
  ∃ g : β → ℝ, ∃ h : α → ℝ, ∀ a e, s a e = g e * h a

Converse of the multiplicative survival model. If A ⫫ E with positive margins and A and E are independent in the selected stratum, which has positive mass, then the selection probability is multiplicative: P(S = 1 | A = a, E = e) = g(e) h(a) for some g and h. So with marginally independent causes, independence within a stratum of their common effect holds exactly under a multiplicative model for that stratum.

CausalInference.Bias.deaths_indep_ifftheorem

theorem deaths_indep_iff (pA pE g h : Bool → ℝ) (hA : ∀ a, 0 < pA a) (hE : ∀ e, 0 < pE e) :
  TableIndep (stratum pA pE fun a e ↦ 1 - g e * h a) ↔
    (g true - g false) * (h true - h false) = 0

With binary A and E that are independent with positive margins, and a multiplicative survival model P(Y = 0 | E = e, A = a) = g(e) h(a), the two causes are independent among the deaths Y = 1 if and only if (g 1 - g 0) (h 1 - h 0) = 0, that is, if and only if one of them has no effect on survival. What If (Technical Point 8.2) states that 1 - g(e) h(a) is not multiplicative and hence A and E are dependent given Y = 1; this theorem is the precise form: dependence among the deaths holds exactly when both causes affect survival.

CausalInference.Bias.berndefinition

def bern (p : ℝ) (b : Bool) : ℝ

The law of a binary variable with success probability p: P(B = 1) = p, P(B = 0) = 1 - p.

CausalInference.Bias.causeSpecificSurvivaldefinition

def causeSpecificSurvival (qA : α → ℝ) (qE : β → ℝ) (qO : ℝ) (a : α) (e : β) : ℝ

Survival probability in the cause-specific model of What If section 8.6 (Figure 8.13). Death Y is Y_A ∨ Y_E ∨ Y_O, where the cause-specific deaths are conditionally independent given (A, E), P(Y_A = 1 | A = a, E = e) = qA a depends on a only, P(Y_E = 1 | ...) = qE e depends on e only, and P(Y_O = 1) = qO depends on neither. The value is P(Y = 0 | A = a, E = e), the sum of the product law over the cause-specific outcomes that give Y = 0.

CausalInference.Bias.causeSpecific_survivaltheorem

theorem causeSpecific_survival (qA : α → ℝ) (qE : β → ℝ) (qO : ℝ) (a : α) (e : β) :
  causeSpecificSurvival qA qE qO a e = (1 - qE e) * ((1 - qO) * (1 - qA a))

The derivation in What If, Technical Point 8.2: in the cause-specific model, P(Y = 0 | E = e, A = a) = P(Y_E = 0 | e) * (P(Y_O = 0) P(Y_A = 0 | a)), a multiplicative survival model with g(e) = 1 - qE e and h(a) = (1 - qO) (1 - qA a).

CausalInference.Bias.causeSpecific_survivors_indeptheorem

theorem causeSpecific_survivors_indep [Fintype α] [Fintype β] (pA : α → ℝ) (pE : β → ℝ)
  (qA : α → ℝ) (qE : β → ℝ) (qO : ℝ) :
  TableIndep (stratum pA pE (causeSpecificSurvival qA qE qO))

Selection without bias (What If, section 8.6): in the cause-specific model with independent causes A and E, the two remain independent among the survivors Y = 0.

CausalInference.Bias.causeSpecific_deaths_indep_ifftheorem

theorem causeSpecific_deaths_indep_iff (pA pE qA qE : Bool → ℝ) (qO : ℝ)
  (hA : ∀ a, 0 < pA a) (hE : ∀ e, 0 < pE e) (hO : qO ≠ 1) :
  TableIndep (stratum pA pE fun a e ↦ 1 - causeSpecificSurvival qA qE qO a e) ↔
    (qE true - qE false) * (qA true - qA false) = 0

In the cause-specific model with binary A and E, positive margins, and qO ≠ 1, the causes are independent among the deaths Y = 1 if and only if qE or qA is constant, that is, if and only if A or E has no effect on death. When both have an effect, conditioning on death creates an association although conditioning on survival does not.

CausalInference.Bias.halfLawdefinition

def halfLaw (_ : Bool) : ℝ

The fair coin law on Bool.

CausalInference.Bias.colliderSelectiondefinition

def colliderSelection (a y : Bool) : ℝ

Selection on a common effect: an individual with treatment a and outcome y is selected if and only if a = 1 or y = 1.

CausalInference.Bias.colliderExample_marginal_indeptheorem

theorem colliderExample_marginal_indep : TableIndep (stratum halfLaw halfLaw fun _ _ ↦ 1)

In the collider example, treatment and outcome are independent fair coins before selection.

CausalInference.Bias.colliderExample_selected_masstheorem

theorem colliderExample_selected_mass :
  ∑ a, ∑ y, stratum halfLaw halfLaw colliderSelection a y = 3 / 4

The selected stratum of the collider example has probability 3/4.

CausalInference.Bias.colliderExample_selected_valuestheorem

theorem colliderExample_selected_values :
  stratum halfLaw halfLaw colliderSelection true true / (3 / 4) = 1 / 3 ∧
    (∑ y, stratum halfLaw halfLaw colliderSelection true y) / (3 / 4) *
        ((∑ a, stratum halfLaw halfLaw colliderSelection a true) / (3 / 4)) = 4 / 9

The normalized numbers of the collider example: among the selected, P(A = 1, Y = 1 | S = 1) = 1/3 while P(A = 1 | S = 1) P(Y = 1 | S = 1) = 2/3 * 2/3 = 4/9.

CausalInference.Bias.colliderExample_selected_not_indeptheorem

theorem colliderExample_selected_not_indep :
  ¬ TableIndep (stratum halfLaw halfLaw colliderSelection)

Selection bias (What If, section 8.1): treatment and outcome, independent before selection, are dependent among the selected. Normalized, P(A = 1, Y = 1 | S = 1) = 1/3 while P(A = 1 | S = 1) P(Y = 1 | S = 1) = 4/9.

CausalInference.Bias.andSurvivaldefinition

def andSurvival (a e : Bool) : ℝ

An "and" survival mechanism: death if and only if both A = 1 and E = 1. The survival probability 1 - [a = 1 ∧ e = 1] is not multiplicative (the two causes act through a common mechanism, as in What If Figure 8.14).

CausalInference.Bias.andMechanism_survivors_masstheorem

theorem andMechanism_survivors_mass :
  ∑ a, ∑ e, stratum halfLaw halfLaw andSurvival a e = 3 / 4

The survivors of the "and" mechanism have probability 3/4.

CausalInference.Bias.andMechanism_survivors_not_indeptheorem

theorem andMechanism_survivors_not_indep :
  ¬ TableIndep (stratum halfLaw halfLaw andSurvival)

Without a multiplicative survival model, selection on survival biases: under the "and" mechanism, independent fair causes A and E are dependent among the survivors.

CausalInference.Sensitivity.BiasFormulas

CausalInference/Sensitivity/BiasFormulas.lean · 459 lines · 21 public theorems · 6 definitions

Bias formulas for unmeasured confounding. Population-level, finite and algebraic sensitivity analysis for a binary treatment A and a binary unmeasured confounder U. The data are summarized by the stratum means m a u = E[Y | A = a, U = u] (or the stratum risks R u = P(Y = 1 | A = a, U = u)) and the prevalences π a = P(U = 1 | A = a). By the law of total expectation the observed mean in arm a is π a * m a true + (1 - π a) * m a false. If U suffices for confounding control, the causal contrast is the U-standardized difference ∑ u, P(U = u) * (m true u - m false u), written with r = P(U = 1).

Sources: Cornfield, Haenszel, Hammond, Lilienfeld, Shimkin and Wynder (1959); VanderWeele and Arah (2011); Ding and VanderWeele (2016); VanderWeele and Ding (2017)

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.observedMeandefinition

def observedMean (m : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (π : Bool → ℝ) (a : Bool) : ℝ

The observed mean E[Y | A = a] = π a * m a true + (1 - π a) * m a false, by the law of total expectation over the binary confounder U, where m a u = E[Y | A = a, U = u] and π a = P(U = 1 | A = a).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.standardizedEffectdefinition

def standardizedEffect (m : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (r : ℝ) : ℝ

The U-standardized treatment effect r * (m true true - m false true) + (1 - r) * (m true false - m false false) with reference prevalence r = P(U = 1). When U suffices for confounding control this is the average causal effect E[Y^1] - E[Y^0].

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.unadjustedBiasdefinition

def unadjustedBias (m : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (π : Bool → ℝ) (r : ℝ) : ℝ

The bias of the unadjusted difference in observed means relative to the standardized effect.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.unadjustedBias_eqtheorem

theorem unadjustedBias_eq (m : Bool → Bool → ℝ) (π : Bool → ℝ) (r : ℝ) :
  unadjustedBias m π r =
    (m true true - m true false) * (π true - r) -
      (m false true - m false false) * (π false - r)

General bias formula (VanderWeele and Arah 2011, binary U): the bias of the unadjusted difference in means equals (m 1 1 - m 1 0) (π 1 - r) - (m 0 1 - m 0 0) (π 0 - r). The identity holds for every reference prevalence r.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.unadjustedBias_eq_of_no_interactiontheorem

theorem unadjustedBias_eq_of_no_interaction {m : Bool → Bool → ℝ} {γ : ℝ}
  (h₁ : m true true - m true false = γ) (h₀ : m false true - m false false = γ)
  (π : Bool → ℝ) (r : ℝ) :
  unadjustedBias m π r = γ * (π true - π false)

Simple bias formula (VanderWeele and Arah 2011): if the effect of U on the outcome is the same value γ in both treatment arms (no interaction), the bias of the unadjusted difference in means is γ * (P(U = 1 | A = 1) - P(U = 1 | A = 0)), whatever the reference prevalence r.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.observedRiskdefinition

def observedRisk (R : Bool → ℝ) (π : Bool → ℝ) (a : Bool) : ℝ

The observed risk P(Y = 1 | A = a) = π a * R true + (1 - π a) * R false under the null of no treatment effect within levels of U: R u = P(Y = 1 | A = a, U = u) does not depend on a.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.cornfield_prevalencetheorem

theorem cornfield_prevalence {R π : Bool → ℝ} (hR₀ : 0 ≤ R false) (hR : R false ≤ R true)
  (hπ₀ : 0 < π false) (hobs₀ : 0 < observedRisk R π false)
  (hRR : 1 < observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false) :
  observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false ≤ π true / π false

Cornfield's condition for the prevalence ratio. Assume no effect of treatment within levels of U, that U is coded as a risk factor (0 ≤ R false ≤ R true), P(U = 1 | A = 0) > 0, and a positive observed risk in the untreated arm. If the observed risk ratio exceeds one, then P(U = 1 | A = 1) / P(U = 1 | A = 0) is at least the observed risk ratio.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.cornfield_riskRatiotheorem

theorem cornfield_riskRatio {R π : Bool → ℝ} (hR₀ : 0 < R false) (hR : R false ≤ R true)
  (hπ₀ : 0 ≤ π false) (hπ₁ : π true ≤ 1) :
  observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false ≤ R true / R false

Cornfield's condition for the confounder-outcome risk ratio. Under the null of no effect within levels of U, with 0 < R false ≤ R true and prevalences 0 ≤ π false, π true ≤ 1, the risk ratio R true / R false of U for the outcome is at least the observed risk ratio.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.observedRisk_recodetheorem

theorem observedRisk_recode (R π : Bool → ℝ) (a : Bool) :
  observedRisk (fun u => R (!u)) (fun a => 1 - π a) a = observedRisk R π a

Recoding the confounder (U ↦ 1 - U) leaves the observed risks unchanged.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.cornfield_prevalence_maxtheorem

theorem cornfield_prevalence_max {R π : Bool → ℝ} (hR₀ : 0 ≤ R false) (hR₁ : 0 ≤ R true)
  (hπ₀ : 0 < π false) (hπ₀' : π false < 1) (hobs₀ : 0 < observedRisk R π false)
  (hRR : 1 < observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false) :
  observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false ≤
    max (π true / π false) ((1 - π true) / (1 - π false))

Coding-free Cornfield condition: under the null of no effect within levels of U, with 0 < P(U = 1 | A = 0) < 1 and observed risk ratio above one, the larger of the prevalence ratios of U = 1 and of U = 0 is at least the observed risk ratio.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.cornfield_prevalence_coding_neededtheorem

theorem cornfield_prevalence_coding_needed :
  ∃ R π : Bool → ℝ, 0 ≤ R true ∧ 0 ≤ R false ∧ 0 < π false ∧ π false < 1 ∧ 0 < π true ∧
    π true < 1 ∧ 0 < observedRisk R π false ∧
    1 < observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false ∧
    π true / π false < observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false

The coding hypothesis R false ≤ R true cannot be dropped from cornfield_prevalence: with R = (1, 0) and prevalences π = (1/2, 1/4) (untreated, treated) the observed risk ratio is 3/2 > 1, yet the prevalence ratio is 1/2.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.boundingFactordefinition

def boundingFactor (a b : ℝ) : ℝ

The joint bounding factor a * b / (a + b - 1) of Ding and VanderWeele (2016) for two risk ratio parameters a and b.

theorem boundingFactor_comm (a b : ℝ) : boundingFactor a b = boundingFactor b a

The bounding factor is symmetric.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.boundingFactor_mono_lefttheorem

theorem boundingFactor_mono_left {a a' b : ℝ} (ha : 1 ≤ a) (hle : a ≤ a') (hb : 1 ≤ b) :
  boundingFactor a b ≤ boundingFactor a' b

For b ≥ 1 the bounding factor is nondecreasing in its first argument on [1, ∞).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.boundingFactor_monotheorem

theorem boundingFactor_mono {a a' b b' : ℝ} (ha : 1 ≤ a) (hle : a ≤ a') (hb : 1 ≤ b)
  (hle' : b ≤ b') : boundingFactor a b ≤ boundingFactor a' b'

The bounding factor is nondecreasing in both arguments on [1, ∞) × [1, ∞).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.jointBoundingFactor_nulltheorem

theorem jointBoundingFactor_null {R π : Bool → ℝ} (hR₀ : 0 < R false) (hR : R false ≤ R true)
  (hπ₀ : 0 < π false) (hπ : π false ≤ π true) (hπ₁ : π true ≤ 1) :
  observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false ≤
    boundingFactor (R true / R false) (π true / π false)

The joint bounding factor of Ding and VanderWeele (2016) for a binary confounder, under the null of no treatment effect within levels of U (true risk ratio one). With U coded as a risk factor (0 < R false ≤ R true) and more prevalent among the treated (0 < π false ≤ π true ≤ 1), write RR_UD = R true / R false and RR_EU = π true / π false. Then the observed risk ratio is at most boundingFactor RR_UD RR_EU = RR_UD * RR_EU / (RR_UD + RR_EU - 1).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.one_le_max_divtheorem

theorem one_le_max_div {x y : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) (hy : 0 < y) : 1 ≤ max (x / y) (y / x)

The larger of x / y and y / x is at least one for x, y > 0.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.one_le_max_prevRatiotheorem

theorem one_le_max_prevRatio {p₀ p₁ : ℝ} (h₀ : 0 < p₀) (h₀' : p₀ < 1) :
  1 ≤ max (p₁ / p₀) ((1 - p₁) / (1 - p₀))

The larger of the prevalence ratios p₁ / p₀ and (1 - p₁) / (1 - p₀) is at least one for 0 < p₀ < 1.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.jointBoundingFactor_null_maxtheorem

theorem jointBoundingFactor_null_max {R π : Bool → ℝ} (hR₀ : 0 < R false) (hR₁ : 0 < R true)
  (hπ₀ : 0 < π false) (hπ₀' : π false < 1) (hπ₁ : 0 ≤ π true) (hπ₁' : π true ≤ 1) :
  observedRisk R π true / observedRisk R π false ≤
    boundingFactor (max (R true / R false) (R false / R true))
      (max (π true / π false) ((1 - π true) / (1 - π false)))

Coding-free joint bounding factor under the null of no effect within levels of U: for positive risks R u and prevalences 0 < P(U = 1 | A = 0) < 1, 0 ≤ P(U = 1 | A = 1) ≤ 1, the observed risk ratio is at most boundingFactor RR_UD RR_EU, where RR_UD = max (R true / R false) (R false / R true) and RR_EU = max (π true / π false) ((1 - π true) / (1 - π false)) are maxima over the two codings of U.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.evalue_le_maxtheorem

theorem evalue_le_max {RR a b : ℝ} (hRR : 1 < RR) (ha : 1 ≤ a) (hb : 1 ≤ b)
  (h : RR ≤ boundingFactor a b) : RR + Real.sqrt (RR * (RR - 1)) ≤ max a b

The E-value inequality. If 1 < RR, 1 ≤ a, 1 ≤ b, and RR ≤ boundingFactor a b, then RR + sqrt (RR * (RR - 1)) ≤ max a b. Read contrapositively: an unmeasured confounder whose two risk ratio parameters both stay below the E-value RR + sqrt (RR * (RR - 1)) cannot explain away an observed risk ratio RR (VanderWeele and Ding 2017).

The mean in arm a standardized to the reference prevalence r = P(U = 1): r * m a true + (1 - r) * m a false.

A convex combination of two positive numbers is positive.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.ratio_le_boundingFactor_of_letheorem

theorem ratio_le_boundingFactor_of_le {m : Bool → Bool → ℝ} {π : Bool → ℝ} {w r K L : ℝ}
  (hm : ∀ a u, 0 < m a u) (hπ₀ : 0 < π false) (hπ₁' : π true ≤ 1)
  (hπ : π false ≤ π true) (hw : 0 ≤ w) (hw' : w ≤ 1) (hr : r = w * π true + (1 - w) * π false)
  (hK : π true ≤ K * π false)
  (hL : ∀ a, m a true ≤ L * m a false ∧ m a false ≤ L * m a true) :
  (observedMean m π true / observedMean m π false) /
    (standardizedMean m r true / standardizedMean m r false) ≤ boundingFactor K L

The aligned case of ratio_le_boundingFactor, where P(U = 1 | A = 0) ≤ P(U = 1 | A = 1).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.ratio_le_boundingFactortheorem

theorem ratio_le_boundingFactor {m : Bool → Bool → ℝ} {π : Bool → ℝ} {w r K L : ℝ}
  (hm : ∀ a u, 0 < m a u) (hπ₀ : 0 < π false) (hπ₀' : π false < 1) (hπ₁ : 0 ≤ π true)
  (hπ₁' : π true ≤ 1) (hw : 0 ≤ w) (hw' : w ≤ 1) (hr : r = w * π true + (1 - w) * π false)
  (hK₁ : π true ≤ K * π false) (hK₀ : 1 - π true ≤ K * (1 - π false))
  (hL : ∀ a, m a true ≤ L * m a false ∧ m a false ≤ L * m a true) :
  (observedMean m π true / observedMean m π false) /
    (standardizedMean m r true / standardizedMean m r false) ≤ boundingFactor K L

The bounding factor of Ding and VanderWeele (2016) away from the null, for a binary confounder U. Let m a u = P(Y = 1 | A = a, U = u) > 0 be arm specific risks (no null hypothesis is assumed), π a = P(U = 1 | A = a) with 0 < π false < 1 and 0 ≤ π true ≤ 1, and let the reference prevalence be the mixture r = w * π true + (1 - w) * π false with 0 ≤ w ≤ 1 (for instance r = P(U = 1) with w = P(A = 1)). If K bounds the prevalence ratios of both levels of U (π true ≤ K * π false, 1 - π true ≤ K * (1 - π false)) and L bounds the risk ratios of U for the outcome within each arm, in both directions, then the observed risk ratio divided by the U-standardized risk ratio is at most boundingFactor K L = K L / (K + L - 1).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.ratio_le_boundingFactor_maxtheorem

theorem ratio_le_boundingFactor_max {m : Bool → Bool → ℝ} {π : Bool → ℝ} {w r : ℝ}
  (hm : ∀ a u, 0 < m a u) (hπ₀ : 0 < π false) (hπ₀' : π false < 1) (hπ₁ : 0 ≤ π true)
  (hπ₁' : π true ≤ 1) (hw : 0 ≤ w) (hw' : w ≤ 1) (hr : r = w * π true + (1 - w) * π false) :
  (observedMean m π true / observedMean m π false) /
    (standardizedMean m r true / standardizedMean m r false) ≤
    boundingFactor (max (π true / π false) ((1 - π true) / (1 - π false)))
      (max (max (m true true / m true false) (m true false / m true true))
        (max (m false true / m false false) (m false false / m false true)))

ratio_le_boundingFactor with the parameters of Ding and VanderWeele (2016) written as maxima: K = max (π true / π false) ((1 - π true) / (1 - π false)) and L the largest within arm risk ratio of U for the outcome, over both arms and both codings of U.

CausalInference.Sensitivity.Rosenbaum

CausalInference/Sensitivity/Rosenbaum.lean · 753 lines · 60 public theorems · 19 definitions

Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis for matched pairs. A finite, combinatorial treatment of Rosenbaum's model for hidden bias in matched pair studies and of the sensitivity bounds for the sign test.

Sources: Rosenbaum (1987); Rosenbaum (2002)

Public declarations (79)

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.bernWeightdefinition

def bernWeight {n : ℕ} (q : Fin n → ℝ) (x : Fin n → Bool) : ℝ

The product weight ∏ i, (if x i then q i else 1 - q i) of the outcome x : Fin n → Bool: the probability of x when the coordinates are independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities q i.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.countdefinition

def count {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → Bool) : ℕ

The number of coordinates i with x i = true.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.tailProbdefinition

def tailProb {n : ℕ} (q : Fin n → ℝ) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The upper tail probability P(count ≥ k) of the number of successes among n independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities q i, as a finite sum with product weights.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.tailProb_succtheorem

theorem tailProb_succ {n : ℕ} (q : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) (k : ℕ) :
  tailProb q k =
    q 0 * tailProb (Fin.tail q) (k - 1) + (1 - q 0) * tailProb (Fin.tail q) k

Conditioning on the first coordinate: the tail is an affine function of q 0.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.bernWeight_nonnegtheorem

theorem bernWeight_nonneg {n : ℕ} {q : Fin n → ℝ} (hq : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i ∧ q i ≤ 1)
  (x : Fin n → Bool) : 0 ≤ bernWeight q x

Product weights with success probabilities in [0, 1] are nonnegative.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.tailProb_antitonetheorem

theorem tailProb_antitone {n : ℕ} {q : Fin n → ℝ} (hq : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i ∧ q i ≤ 1) {k k' : ℕ}
  (hk : k ≤ k') : tailProb q k' ≤ tailProb q k

The tail probability is nonincreasing in the threshold.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.tailProb_monotheorem

theorem tailProb_mono {n : ℕ} {q q' : Fin n → ℝ} (hq : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i ∧ q i ≤ 1)
  (hq' : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q' i ∧ q' i ≤ 1) (hle : ∀ i, q i ≤ q' i) (k : ℕ) :
  tailProb q k ≤ tailProb q' k

Monotonicity of the upper tail of a sum of independent Bernoulli variables in the success probabilities: if q i ≤ q' i for all i, with all values in [0, 1], then P(count ≥ k) under q is at most the same probability under q', for every k.

def countProb {n : ℕ} (q : Fin n → ℝ) (j : ℕ) : ℝ

The probability P(count = j) that exactly j of the n independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities q i equal true.

theorem countProb_succ_zero {n : ℕ} (q : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) :
  countProb q 0 = (1 - q 0) * countProb (Fin.tail q) 0

Conditioning on the first coordinate for the event of no successes.

  countProb q (j + 1) =
    q 0 * countProb (Fin.tail q) j + (1 - q 0) * countProb (Fin.tail q) (j + 1)

Conditioning on the first coordinate for the event of j + 1 successes.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.countProb_consttheorem

theorem countProb_const (n : ℕ) (r : ℝ) (j : ℕ) :
  countProb (fun _ : Fin n => r) j = (n.choose j : ℝ) * r ^ j * (1 - r) ^ (n - j)

With all success probabilities equal to r, the count is Binomial(n, r): P(count = j) = (n choose j) r ^ j (1 - r) ^ (n - j).

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModeldefinition

def InSensitivityModel (Γ p : ℝ) : Prop

Rosenbaum's sensitivity model with parameter Γ ≥ 1 for the probability p that the first unit of a pair is the treated one: 1 ≤ Γ and 1 / (1 + Γ) ≤ p ≤ Γ / (1 + Γ). The bound 1 ≤ Γ is part of the predicate, so that the predicate never holds for a parameter outside the model (for Γ < 1 the interval would be empty or, for Γ ≤ -1, would not consist of probabilities).

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModel.one_letheorem

theorem InSensitivityModel.one_le {Γ p : ℝ} (h : InSensitivityModel Γ p) : 1 ≤ Γ

A sensitivity parameter allowed by the model is at least one.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModel.lower_letheorem

theorem InSensitivityModel.lower_le {Γ p : ℝ} (h : InSensitivityModel Γ p) :
  1 / (1 + Γ) ≤ p

The lower end of the model interval.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModel.le_uppertheorem

theorem InSensitivityModel.le_upper {Γ p : ℝ} (h : InSensitivityModel Γ p) :
  p ≤ Γ / (1 + Γ)

The upper end of the model interval.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.pairProbdefinition

def pairProb (π₁ π₂ : ℝ) : ℝ

The closed form π₁ (1 - π₂) / (π₁ (1 - π₂) + π₂ (1 - π₁)). By pairProb_eq_cond it is the conditional probability that the first of two independently treated units (with treatment probabilities π₁ and π₂) is treated, given that exactly one of them is treated.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.bernWeight_pairtheorem

theorem bernWeight_pair (π₁ π₂ : ℝ) (z : Fin 2 → Bool) :
  bernWeight ![π₁, π₂] z =
    (if z 0 then π₁ else 1 - π₁) * (if z 1 then π₂ else 1 - π₂)

The product weight of an assignment of two units treated independently with probabilities π₁ and π₂.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.exactlyOneProbdefinition

def exactlyOneProb (π₁ π₂ : ℝ) : ℝ

The probability P(Z₁ + Z₂ = 1) that exactly one of two units, treated independently with probabilities π₁ and π₂, is treated.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.firstOnlyProbdefinition

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.exactlyOneProb_eqtheorem

theorem exactlyOneProb_eq (π₁ π₂ : ℝ) :
  exactlyOneProb π₁ π₂ = π₁ * (1 - π₂) + π₂ * (1 - π₁)

The probability that exactly one unit is treated, computed from the four product weights.
