CausalInference.Rosenbaum.exactlyOneProb_postheorem

theorem exactlyOneProb_pos {π₁ π₂ : ℝ} (h₁ : 0 < π₁) (h₁' : π₁ < 1) (h₂ : 0 < π₂)
  (h₂' : π₂ < 1) : 0 < exactlyOneProb π₁ π₂

For treatment probabilities in (0, 1) the event that exactly one unit is treated has positive probability, so conditioning on it is not degenerate.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.pairProb_eq_condtheorem

theorem pairProb_eq_cond (π₁ π₂ : ℝ) :
  firstOnlyProb π₁ π₂ / exactlyOneProb π₁ π₂ = pairProb π₁ π₂

pairProb is a conditional probability: for two units treated independently with probabilities π₁ and π₂, P(Z₁ = 1 | Z₁ + Z₂ = 1) = pairProb π₁ π₂, where both probabilities are computed from the product weights bernWeight ![π₁, π₂]. The conditioning event has positive probability when π₁, π₂ ∈ (0, 1) (exactlyOneProb_pos).

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.inSensitivityModel_pairProb_ifftheorem

theorem inSensitivityModel_pairProb_iff {Γ π₁ π₂ : ℝ} (hΓ : 0 < Γ) (h₁ : 0 < π₁)
  (h₁' : π₁ < 1) (h₂ : 0 < π₂) (h₂' : π₂ < 1) :
  InSensitivityModel Γ (pairProb π₁ π₂) ↔
    odds π₁ ≤ Γ * odds π₂ ∧ odds π₂ ≤ Γ * odds π₁

Odds-ratio form of Rosenbaum's model: for treatment probabilities π₁, π₂ ∈ (0, 1) and Γ > 0, the conditional probability pairProb π₁ π₂ satisfies the sensitivity model with parameter Γ (in particular Γ ≥ 1) if and only if odds π₁ ≤ Γ * odds π₂ and odds π₂ ≤ Γ * odds π₁, that is, the treatment odds of the two units differ by at most a factor Γ.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.inSensitivityModel_one_ifftheorem

theorem inSensitivityModel_one_iff {p : ℝ} : InSensitivityModel 1 p ↔ p = 1 / 2

With Γ = 1 the model forces p = 1 / 2: the randomized paired experiment.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModel.monotheorem

theorem InSensitivityModel.mono {Γ Γ' p : ℝ} (hle : Γ ≤ Γ')
  (h : InSensitivityModel Γ p) : InSensitivityModel Γ' p

The sensitivity model grows with Γ: every probability allowed at Γ is allowed at every Γ' ≥ Γ.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModel.nonnegtheorem

theorem InSensitivityModel.nonneg {Γ p : ℝ} (h : InSensitivityModel Γ p) : 0 ≤ p

A probability allowed by the model is nonnegative.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModel.le_onetheorem

theorem InSensitivityModel.le_one {Γ p : ℝ} (h : InSensitivityModel Γ p) : p ≤ 1

A probability allowed by the model is at most one.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.InSensitivityModel.one_subtheorem

theorem InSensitivityModel.one_sub {Γ p : ℝ} (h : InSensitivityModel Γ p) :
  InSensitivityModel Γ (1 - p)

The model is symmetric under exchanging the two units of a pair.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signStatdefinition

def signStat {S : ℕ} (f : Fin S → Bool) (z : Fin S → Bool) : ℕ

The sign statistic under the sharp null hypothesis with binary discordant pairs. The fixed pattern f s = true records that the first unit of pair s has the larger outcome (outcomes are fixed under the sharp null, and in a discordant pair exactly one unit has the larger outcome). The statistic counts the pairs in which the treated unit has the larger outcome, that is, the s with z s = f s.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signTestTaildefinition

def signTestTail {S : ℕ} (p : Fin S → ℝ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The tail probability P(T ≥ k) of the sign statistic T when the first unit of pair s is treated with probability p s, independently across pairs.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.successProbdefinition

def successProb {S : ℕ} (p : Fin S → ℝ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (s : Fin S) : ℝ

The probability that the treated unit of pair s has the larger outcome: p s if the first unit has the larger outcome and 1 - p s otherwise.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.matchEquivdefinition

def matchEquiv {S : ℕ} (f : Fin S → Bool) : (Fin S → Bool) ≃ (Fin S → Bool)

The involution z ↦ (s ↦ (z s == f s)) of Fin S → Bool, which sends an assignment to the indicator of the pairs in which the treated unit has the larger outcome.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signTestTail_eq_tailProbtheorem

theorem signTestTail_eq_tailProb {S : ℕ} (p : Fin S → ℝ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  signTestTail p f k = tailProb (successProb p f) k

The sign statistic is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities successProb p f s.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.successProb_memtheorem

theorem successProb_mem {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} {p : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hp : ∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) (f : Fin S → Bool) (s : Fin S) :
  InSensitivityModel Γ (successProb p f s)

Under the sensitivity model the success probabilities of the sign statistic lie in [1 / (1 + Γ), Γ / (1 + Γ)].

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.upper_mem_unittheorem

theorem upper_mem_unit {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 0 ≤ Γ) : 0 ≤ Γ / (1 + Γ) ∧ Γ / (1 + Γ) ≤ 1

Γ / (1 + Γ) is a probability for Γ ≥ 0.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.lower_mem_unittheorem

theorem lower_mem_unit {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 0 ≤ Γ) : 0 ≤ 1 / (1 + Γ) ∧ 1 / (1 + Γ) ≤ 1

1 / (1 + Γ) is a probability for Γ ≥ 0.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signTestTail_le_binomialTailtheorem

theorem signTestTail_le_binomialTail {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) {p : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hp : ∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  signTestTail p f k ≤ binomialTail S (Γ / (1 + Γ)) k

Rosenbaum's upper bound for the sign test: under the sensitivity model with parameter Γ ≥ 1, P(T ≥ k) is at most the upper tail of Binomial(S, Γ / (1 + Γ)), for every k.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.binomialTail_le_signTestTailtheorem

theorem binomialTail_le_signTestTail {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) {p : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hp : ∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  binomialTail S (1 / (1 + Γ)) k ≤ signTestTail p f k

Rosenbaum's lower bound for the sign test: under the sensitivity model with parameter Γ ≥ 1, P(T ≥ k) is at least the upper tail of Binomial(S, 1 / (1 + Γ)), for every k.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signTestTail_upper_attainedtheorem

theorem signTestTail_upper_attained {S : ℕ} (Γ : ℝ) (k : ℕ) :
  signTestTail (fun _ : Fin S => Γ / (1 + Γ)) (fun _ => true) k =
    binomialTail S (Γ / (1 + Γ)) k

The upper bound is attained by the assignment probabilities p s = Γ / (1 + Γ) when the first unit of every pair has the larger outcome; these lie in the model when Γ ≥ 1 (inSensitivityModel_upper). See signTestTail_upperAssign for every outcome pattern.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signTestTail_eq_binomialTail_halftheorem

theorem signTestTail_eq_binomialTail_half {S : ℕ} {p : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hp : ∀ s, InSensitivityModel 1 (p s)) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  signTestTail p f k = binomialTail S (1 / 2) k

With Γ = 1 the sign statistic has exactly the Binomial(S, 1 / 2) tail, as in a randomized paired experiment.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.binomialTail_upper_monotheorem

theorem binomialTail_upper_mono {S : ℕ} {Γ Γ' : ℝ} (hΓ : 0 ≤ Γ) (hle : Γ ≤ Γ') (k : ℕ) :
  binomialTail S (Γ / (1 + Γ)) k ≤ binomialTail S (Γ' / (1 + Γ')) k

The upper bound on the sign test p-value is nondecreasing in Γ.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.binomialTail_lower_antitheorem

theorem binomialTail_lower_anti {S : ℕ} {Γ Γ' : ℝ} (hΓ : 0 ≤ Γ) (hle : Γ ≤ Γ') (k : ℕ) :
  binomialTail S (1 / (1 + Γ')) k ≤ binomialTail S (1 / (1 + Γ)) k

The lower bound on the sign test p-value is nonincreasing in Γ.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.inSensitivityModel_uppertheorem

theorem inSensitivityModel_upper {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) : InSensitivityModel Γ (Γ / (1 + Γ))

For Γ ≥ 1, the value Γ / (1 + Γ) is allowed by the sensitivity model.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.inSensitivityModel_lowertheorem

theorem inSensitivityModel_lower {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) : InSensitivityModel Γ (1 / (1 + Γ))

For Γ ≥ 1, the value 1 / (1 + Γ) is allowed by the sensitivity model.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.alignedAssigndefinition

def alignedAssign {S : ℕ} (f : Fin S → Bool) (r : ℝ) (s : Fin S) : ℝ

The assignment probabilities that make the success probability of every pair equal to r: the first unit of pair s is treated with probability r if it has the larger outcome and with probability 1 - r otherwise.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.successProb_alignedAssigntheorem

theorem successProb_alignedAssign {S : ℕ} (f : Fin S → Bool) (r : ℝ) :
  successProb (alignedAssign f r) f = fun _ => r

Under alignedAssign f r every success probability equals r.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.alignedAssign_upper_memtheorem

theorem alignedAssign_upper_mem {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (s : Fin S) :
  InSensitivityModel Γ (alignedAssign f (Γ / (1 + Γ)) s)

For Γ ≥ 1, alignedAssign f (Γ / (1 + Γ)) satisfies the sensitivity model.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.alignedAssign_lower_memtheorem

theorem alignedAssign_lower_mem {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (s : Fin S) :
  InSensitivityModel Γ (alignedAssign f (1 / (1 + Γ)) s)

For Γ ≥ 1, alignedAssign f (1 / (1 + Γ)) satisfies the sensitivity model.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signTestTail_upperAssigntheorem

theorem signTestTail_upperAssign {S : ℕ} (Γ : ℝ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  signTestTail (alignedAssign f (Γ / (1 + Γ))) f k = binomialTail S (Γ / (1 + Γ)) k

For every outcome pattern f, the assignment alignedAssign f (Γ / (1 + Γ)) attains the upper bound: its sign test tail is the Binomial(S, Γ / (1 + Γ)) tail.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signTestTail_lowerAssigntheorem

theorem signTestTail_lowerAssign {S : ℕ} (Γ : ℝ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  signTestTail (alignedAssign f (1 / (1 + Γ))) f k = binomialTail S (1 / (1 + Γ)) k

For every outcome pattern f, the assignment alignedAssign f (1 / (1 + Γ)) attains the lower bound: its sign test tail is the Binomial(S, 1 / (1 + Γ)) tail.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.isGreatest_signTestTailtheorem

theorem isGreatest_signTestTail {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  IsGreatest {t | ∃ p : Fin S → ℝ, (∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) ∧ t = signTestTail p f k}
    (binomialTail S (Γ / (1 + Γ)) k)

Sharp upper bound: for Γ ≥ 1 and every outcome pattern f, the largest value of the sign test tail P(T ≥ k) over all assignment probabilities in the sensitivity model is the Binomial(S, Γ / (1 + Γ)) tail.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.isLeast_signTestTailtheorem

theorem isLeast_signTestTail {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  IsLeast {t | ∃ p : Fin S → ℝ, (∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) ∧ t = signTestTail p f k}
    (binomialTail S (1 / (1 + Γ)) k)

Sharp lower bound: for Γ ≥ 1 and every outcome pattern f, the smallest value of the sign test tail P(T ≥ k) over all assignment probabilities in the sensitivity model is the Binomial(S, 1 / (1 + Γ)) tail.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.weightedScoredefinition

def weightedScore {n : ℕ} (d : Fin n → ℝ) (x : Fin n → Bool) : ℝ

The weighted count ∑ i, d i * 1{x i} of the coordinates with x i = true.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.weightedTaildefinition

def weightedTail {n : ℕ} (q d : Fin n → ℝ) (c : ℝ) : ℝ

The upper tail probability P(∑ i, d i * 1{x i} ≥ c) for independent Bernoulli coordinates with success probabilities q i, as a finite sum with product weights.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.weightedScore_constheorem

theorem weightedScore_cons {n : ℕ} (d : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) (b : Bool) (t : Fin n → Bool) :
  weightedScore d (Fin.cons b t) = (if b then d 0 else 0) + weightedScore (Fin.tail d) t

Splitting off the first coordinate of the weighted count.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.bernWeight_constheorem

theorem bernWeight_cons {n : ℕ} (q : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) (b : Bool) (t : Fin n → Bool) :
  bernWeight q (Fin.cons b t) = (if b then q 0 else 1 - q 0) * bernWeight (Fin.tail q) t

Splitting off the first coordinate of the product weight.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.weightedTail_succtheorem

theorem weightedTail_succ {n : ℕ} (q d : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) (c : ℝ) :
  weightedTail q d c = q 0 * weightedTail (Fin.tail q) (Fin.tail d) (c - d 0) +
    (1 - q 0) * weightedTail (Fin.tail q) (Fin.tail d) c

Conditioning on the first coordinate in the weighted tail.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.weightedTail_antitonetheorem

theorem weightedTail_antitone {n : ℕ} {q : Fin n → ℝ} (hq : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i ∧ q i ≤ 1)
  (d : Fin n → ℝ) {c c' : ℝ} (hc : c ≤ c') : weightedTail q d c' ≤ weightedTail q d c

The weighted tail is nonincreasing in the threshold.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.weightedTail_monotheorem

theorem weightedTail_mono {n : ℕ} {q q' d : Fin n → ℝ} (hq : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i ∧ q i ≤ 1)
  (hq' : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q' i ∧ q' i ≤ 1) (hle : ∀ i, q i ≤ q' i) (hd : ∀ i, 0 ≤ d i) (c : ℝ) :
  weightedTail q d c ≤ weightedTail q' d c

Weighted monotonicity: for nonnegative scores d i and success probabilities q i ≤ q' i in [0, 1], P(∑ i, d i * 1{x i} ≥ c) under q is at most the same probability under q', for every threshold c.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signScoredefinition

def signScore {S : ℕ} (d : Fin S → ℝ) (f z : Fin S → Bool) : ℝ

The sign-score statistic ∑ s, d s * 1{z s = f s}: the total score of the pairs in which the treated unit has the larger outcome.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signScoreTaildefinition

def signScoreTail {S : ℕ} (p d : Fin S → ℝ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (c : ℝ) : ℝ

The tail probability P(T ≥ c) of the sign-score statistic T when the first unit of pair s is treated with probability p s, independently across pairs.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signScoreTail_eq_weightedTailtheorem

theorem signScoreTail_eq_weightedTail {S : ℕ} (p d : Fin S → ℝ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (c : ℝ) :
  signScoreTail p d f c = weightedTail (successProb p f) d c

The sign-score statistic is a weighted sum of independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities successProb p f s.

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.signScoreTail_letheorem

theorem signScoreTail_le {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) {p d : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hp : ∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) (hd : ∀ s, 0 ≤ d s) (f : Fin S → Bool) (c : ℝ) :
  signScoreTail p d f c ≤ weightedTail (fun _ => Γ / (1 + Γ)) d c

Rosenbaum's upper bound for sign-score statistics: under the sensitivity model with parameter Γ ≥ 1 and nonnegative scores, P(T ≥ c) is at most the tail of ∑ s, d s * B s with B s independent Bernoulli variables of mean Γ / (1 + Γ).

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.le_signScoreTailtheorem

theorem le_signScoreTail {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) {p d : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hp : ∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) (hd : ∀ s, 0 ≤ d s) (f : Fin S → Bool) (c : ℝ) :
  weightedTail (fun _ => 1 / (1 + Γ)) d c ≤ signScoreTail p d f c

Rosenbaum's lower bound for sign-score statistics: under the sensitivity model with parameter Γ ≥ 1 and nonnegative scores, P(T ≥ c) is at least the tail of ∑ s, d s * B s with B s independent Bernoulli variables of mean 1 / (1 + Γ).

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.isGreatest_signScoreTailtheorem

theorem isGreatest_signScoreTail {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) {d : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hd : ∀ s, 0 ≤ d s) (f : Fin S → Bool) (c : ℝ) :
  IsGreatest
    {t | ∃ p : Fin S → ℝ, (∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) ∧ t = signScoreTail p d f c}
    (weightedTail (fun _ => Γ / (1 + Γ)) d c)

Sharpness for sign-score statistics: for Γ ≥ 1, nonnegative scores, and every outcome pattern f, the largest value of P(T ≥ c) over the sensitivity model is the upper bound of signScoreTail_le, attained by alignedAssign f (Γ / (1 + Γ)).

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.isLeast_signScoreTailtheorem

theorem isLeast_signScoreTail {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) {d : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hd : ∀ s, 0 ≤ d s) (f : Fin S → Bool) (c : ℝ) :
  IsLeast
    {t | ∃ p : Fin S → ℝ, (∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) ∧ t = signScoreTail p d f c}
    (weightedTail (fun _ => 1 / (1 + Γ)) d c)

Sharpness of the lower bound for sign-score statistics, attained by alignedAssign f (1 / (1 + Γ)).

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.wilcoxon_signScoreTail_boundstheorem

theorem wilcoxon_signScoreTail_bounds {S : ℕ} {Γ : ℝ} (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) {p : Fin S → ℝ}
  (hp : ∀ s, InSensitivityModel Γ (p s)) (rk : Fin S → ℕ) (f : Fin S → Bool) (c : ℝ) :
  weightedTail (fun _ => 1 / (1 + Γ)) (fun s => (rk s : ℝ)) c ≤
      signScoreTail p (fun s => (rk s : ℝ)) f c ∧
    signScoreTail p (fun s => (rk s : ℝ)) f c ≤
      weightedTail (fun _ => Γ / (1 + Γ)) (fun s => (rk s : ℝ)) c

Rosenbaum's bounds for the Wilcoxon signed rank statistic. Under the sharp null hypothesis the absolute paired differences, hence their ranks rk s, and the pattern f of which unit has the larger outcome are fixed; the statistic is the sum of the ranks of the pairs in which the treated unit has the larger outcome. Under the sensitivity model with Γ ≥ 1, its tail P(T ≥ c) lies between the tails of ∑ s, rk s * B s with B s independent Bernoulli variables of mean 1 / (1 + Γ) and of mean Γ / (1 + Γ).

CausalInference.Sensitivity.Probability

CausalInference/Sensitivity/Probability.lean · 278 lines · 11 public theorems · 3 definitions · imports Sensitivity.BiasFormulas, Sensitivity.Rosenbaum

Probability space versions of the sensitivity formulas. The files CausalInference.Sensitivity.Rosenbaum and CausalInference.Sensitivity.BiasFormulas are finite and algebraic. This file ties them to measures.

Sources: VanderWeele and Arah (2011); Hernán and Robins (2020)

Public declarations (14)

CausalInference.Rosenbaum.binomialTail_eq_binomial_realtheorem

theorem binomialTail_eq_binomial_real (n : ℕ) (r : unitInterval) (k : ℕ) :
  binomialTail n (r : ℝ) k = (binomial n r).real (Set.Ici k)

The finite binomial tail is the tail of Mathlib's binomial distribution: for r ∈ [0, 1], binomialTail n r k = Bin(n, r)({j | k ≤ j}).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.setIntegral_eq_measureReal_mul_integral_condtheorem

theorem setIntegral_eq_measureReal_mul_integral_cond {μ : Measure Ω} [IsFiniteMeasure μ]
  {s : Set Ω} (f : Ω → ℝ) : ∫ ω in s, f ω ∂μ = μ.real s * ∫ ω, f ω ∂μ[|s]

For a finite measure, the set integral over s is μ(s) times the conditional mean given s. Both sides vanish when μ s = 0.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.measureReal_mul_integral_cond_eq_sumtheorem

theorem measureReal_mul_integral_cond_eq_sum {μ : Measure Ω} [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {s : Set Ω}
  (hs : MeasurableSet s) {X : Ω → Bool} (hX : Measurable X) {f : Ω → ℝ}
  (hf : Integrable f μ) :
  μ.real s * ∫ ω, f ω ∂μ[|s] = ∑ x, μ.real (s ∩ X ⁻¹' {x}) *
    ∫ ω, f ω ∂μ[|s ∩ X ⁻¹' {x}]

Law of total expectation over a binary covariate: for a finite measure, a measurable event s, a measurable X : Ω → Bool, and an integrable f, μ(s) E[f | s] = ∑ₓ μ(s ∩ {X = x}) E[f | s ∩ {X = x}].

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.cond_real_eqtheorem

theorem cond_real_eq {μ : Measure Ω} {s : Set Ω} (hs : MeasurableSet s) (t : Set Ω) :
  (μ[|s]).real t = μ.real (s ∩ t) / μ.real s

The real conditional probability: P(t | s) = μ(s ∩ t) / μ(s) for measurable s.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.cellMeandefinition

def cellMean (μ : Measure Ω) (A U : Ω → Bool) (Y : Ω → ℝ) (a u : Bool) : ℝ

The cell mean E[Y | A = a, U = u] of the outcome Y for a binary treatment A and a binary confounder U. On a null cell this is the junk value 0.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.condPrevdefinition

def condPrev (μ : Measure Ω) (A U : Ω → Bool) (a : Bool) : ℝ

The prevalence P(U = 1 | A = a) of the confounder in treatment arm a.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.margPrevdefinition

def margPrev (μ : Measure Ω) (U : Ω → Bool) : ℝ

The marginal prevalence P(U = 1) of the confounder.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.measureReal_inter_falsetheorem

theorem measureReal_inter_false {μ : Measure Ω} [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {s : Set Ω} {U : Ω → Bool}
  (hU : Measurable U) :
  μ.real (s ∩ U ⁻¹' {false}) = μ.real s - μ.real (s ∩ U ⁻¹' {true})

The two levels of a binary variable split an event: for a finite measure, μ(s ∩ {U = 0}) = μ(s) - μ(s ∩ {U = 1}).

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.integral_cond_eq_observedMeantheorem

theorem integral_cond_eq_observedMean {μ : Measure Ω} [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {A U : Ω → Bool}
  (hA : Measurable A) (hU : Measurable U) {Y : Ω → ℝ} (hY : Integrable Y μ) (a : Bool)
  (ha : μ (A ⁻¹' {a}) ≠ 0) :
  ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ[|A ⁻¹' {a}] = observedMean (cellMean μ A U Y) (condPrev μ A U) a

Law of total expectation for the observed mean: for a finite measure, measurable binary A and U, an integrable outcome Y, and an arm a of positive measure, E[Y | A = a] = observedMean (cellMean μ A U Y) (condPrev μ A U) a, that is, P(U = 1 | A = a) E[Y | A = a, U = 1] + P(U = 0 | A = a) E[Y | A = a, U = 0].

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.integral_cond_eq_observedRisktheorem

theorem integral_cond_eq_observedRisk {μ : Measure Ω} [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {A U : Ω → Bool}
  (hA : Measurable A) (hU : Measurable U) {Y : Ω → ℝ} (hY : Integrable Y μ) {R : Bool → ℝ}
  (hnull : ∀ a u, cellMean μ A U Y a u = R u) (a : Bool) (ha : μ (A ⁻¹' {a}) ≠ 0) :
  ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ[|A ⁻¹' {a}] = observedRisk R (condPrev μ A U) a

Under the null of no treatment effect within levels of U, stated on the cell means (E[Y | A = a, U = u] = R u for both arms), the observed mean in arm a is observedRisk R (condPrev μ A U) a. With Y the indicator of an event, these are risks.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.integral_eq_standardizedtheorem

theorem integral_eq_standardized {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {A U : Ω → Bool}
  (hA : Measurable A) (hU : Measurable U) {Y : Ω → ℝ} {Ypo : Bool → Ω → ℝ}
  (hYpo : ∀ a, Integrable (Ypo a) μ) (hcons : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, Y ω = Ypo (A ω) ω)
  (hexch : ∀ a u, μ (A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0 →
    ∫ ω, Ypo a ω ∂μ[|A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}] = ∫ ω, Ypo a ω ∂μ[|U ⁻¹' {u}])
  (hpos : ∀ a u, μ (U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0 → μ (A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0) (a : Bool) :
  ∫ ω, Ypo a ω ∂μ = standardizedMean (cellMean μ A U Y) (margPrev μ U) a

Standardization identifies the mean potential outcome. Let μ be a probability measure, A U : Ω → Bool measurable, Y the observed outcome and Ypo a the potential outcome under treatment a, integrable. Assume consistency (Y = Ypo A almost surely), conditional mean exchangeability given U in every cell of positive measure (E[Y^a | A = a, U = u] = E[Y^a | U = u]), and positivity in every stratum of positive measure (P(U = u) > 0 implies P(A = a, U = u) > 0). Then E[Y^a] is the standardized mean standardizedMean (cellMean μ A U Y) (margPrev μ U) a.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.standardizedEffect_eq_atetheorem

theorem standardizedEffect_eq_ate {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {A U : Ω → Bool}
  (hA : Measurable A) (hU : Measurable U) {Y : Ω → ℝ} {Ypo : Bool → Ω → ℝ}
  (hYpo : ∀ a, Integrable (Ypo a) μ) (hcons : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, Y ω = Ypo (A ω) ω)
  (hexch : ∀ a u, μ (A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0 →
    ∫ ω, Ypo a ω ∂μ[|A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}] = ∫ ω, Ypo a ω ∂μ[|U ⁻¹' {u}])
  (hpos : ∀ a u, μ (U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0 → μ (A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0) :
  standardizedEffect (cellMean μ A U Y) (margPrev μ U) =
    ∫ ω, Ypo true ω ∂μ - ∫ ω, Ypo false ω ∂μ

Under the assumptions of integral_eq_standardized, the standardized effect of the cell means is the average treatment effect E[Y^1] - E[Y^0].

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.measure_arm_ne_zerotheorem

theorem measure_arm_ne_zero {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {A U : Ω → Bool}
  (hpos : ∀ a u, μ (U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0 → μ (A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0) (a : Bool) :
  μ (A ⁻¹' {a}) ≠ 0

Positivity in the strata of positive measure gives both arms positive measure.

CausalInference.BiasFormulas.crude_sub_ate_eqtheorem

theorem crude_sub_ate_eq {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {A U : Ω → Bool}
  (hA : Measurable A) (hU : Measurable U) {Y : Ω → ℝ} {Ypo : Bool → Ω → ℝ}
  (hY : Integrable Y μ) (hYpo : ∀ a, Integrable (Ypo a) μ)
  (hcons : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, Y ω = Ypo (A ω) ω)
  (hexch : ∀ a u, μ (A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0 →
    ∫ ω, Ypo a ω ∂μ[|A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}] = ∫ ω, Ypo a ω ∂μ[|U ⁻¹' {u}])
  (hpos : ∀ a u, μ (U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0 → μ (A ⁻¹' {a} ∩ U ⁻¹' {u}) ≠ 0) :
  (∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ[|A ⁻¹' {true}] - ∫ ω, Y ω ∂μ[|A ⁻¹' {false}]) -
      (∫ ω, Ypo true ω ∂μ - ∫ ω, Ypo false ω ∂μ) =
    (cellMean μ A U Y true true - cellMean μ A U Y true false) *
        (condPrev μ A U true - margPrev μ U) -
      (cellMean μ A U Y false true - cellMean μ A U Y false false) *
        (condPrev μ A U false - margPrev μ U)

The bias of the crude contrast for the average treatment effect. Under consistency, conditional mean exchangeability given U, and positivity in the strata of positive measure (the assumptions of integral_eq_standardized), the crude contrast E[Y | A = 1] - E[Y | A = 0] minus the average treatment effect E[Y^1] - E[Y^0] equals the general bias formula of VanderWeele and Arah, (m 1 1 - m 1 0) (π 1 - r) - (m 0 1 - m 0 0) (π 0 - r) with cell means m a u = E[Y | A = a, U = u], prevalences π a = P(U = 1 | A = a), and r = P(U = 1).

Longitudinal treatments

Histories, treatment regimes and the g-formula over a finite horizon.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Basic

CausalInference/Longitudinal/Basic.lean · 330 lines · 20 public theorems · 18 definitions · imports Basic.FiniteDistribution

Longitudinal causal inference: finite setting, histories and regimes. The basic objects of longitudinal causal inference in the sense of Robins (1986), in a finite setting: a finite sample space Ω carrying a nonnegative mass function, finitely many time points, treatments and covariates with values in finite types. Every conditional probability and conditional mean is conditioning on an event; such a quantity is a ratio, and every theorem that uses one has an explicit positivity hypothesis making the denominator positive wherever the ratio matters. Nothing here is a general measurable-space statement.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Robins (1986)

CausalInference.Longitudinal.MeanIndepOndefinition

def MeanIndepOn [DecidableEq Ω] (m : Ω → ℝ) (s t : Finset Ω) (f : Ω → ℝ) : Prop

Within the event s, the variable f is mean independent of the event t, stated without division: E[1_{s ∩ t} f] P(s) = E[1_s f] P(s ∩ t). If P(s ∩ t) > 0 this is the equality of conditional means E[f | s ∩ t] = E[f | s] (meanIndepOn_iff_condMean_eq); if P(s ∩ t) = 0 both sides vanish and the condition is empty.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.condMean_eq_sum_condProb_multheorem

theorem condMean_eq_sum_condProb_mul [Fintype Ω] [DecidableEq Ω] (hm : ∀ ω, 0 ≤ m ω)
  {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (s : Finset Ω) (X : Ω → α) (f : Ω → ℝ) :
  condMean m s f = ∑ x, condProb m s (ev X x) * condMean m (s ∩ ev X x) f

The law of total expectation for a finite-valued variable X given an event s: E[f | s] = Σ_x P(X = x | s) E[f | s, X = x]. Terms whose conditioning event s ∩ {X = x} has zero mass carry the weight P(X = x | s) = 0, a zero numerator. The identity is meaningful when P(s) > 0; if P(s) = 0 both sides are the conventional value 0, and every use of this lemma in the library is under the hypothesis P(s) > 0.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.histdefinition

def hist {K : ℕ} (A : Fin K → Ω → 𝒜) (L : Fin K → Ω → 𝓛) (a : Fin K → 𝒜) (l : Fin K → 𝓛)
  (t : ℕ) : Finset Ω

The history event at time t (a natural number, at most the number K of time points) for the treatment path a and the covariate path l: for every time point s < t, the covariate L s equals l s and the treatment A s equals a s. At t = 0 it is the sure event, at t = K it fixes the whole observed history.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.histLdefinition

def histL {K : ℕ} (A : Fin K → Ω → 𝒜) (L : Fin K → Ω → 𝓛) (a : Fin K → 𝒜) (l : Fin K → 𝓛)
  (t : Fin K) : Finset Ω

The history event at the time point t including the covariate measured at t: L̄_t = l̄_t, Ā_{t-1} = ā_{t-1}. This is the conditioning event of sequential exchangeability at time t.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.hist_zerotheorem

  (l : Fin K → 𝓛) : hist A L a l 0 = univ

CausalInference.Longitudinal.hist_cons_succtheorem

theorem hist_cons_succ {K : ℕ} (A : Fin (K + 1) → Ω → 𝒜) (L : Fin (K + 1) → Ω → 𝓛)
  (a : Fin (K + 1) → 𝒜) (l0 : 𝓛) (l : Fin K → 𝓛) (t : ℕ) :
  hist A L a (Fin.cons l0 l) (t + 1) =
    (ev (L 0) l0 ∩ ev (A 0) (a 0)) ∩ hist (Fin.tail A) (Fin.tail L) (Fin.tail a) l t

The history event of a path starting with l0, after t + 1 time points, is the first time point event L 0 = l0, A 0 = a 0 intersected with the history event of the shifted model after t time points.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Modelstructure

structure Model (Ω : Type*) [Fintype Ω] (K : ℕ) (𝒜 𝓛 : Type*)

A longitudinal model with K time points on the finite sample space Ω. At each time point t : Fin K the covariate L t (values in 𝓛) is measured and then the treatment A t (values in 𝒜) is assigned; the outcome Y is measured after the last time point. For every static regime, that is a treatment sequence a : Fin K → 𝒜, the model carries the potential outcome Ypo a and the potential covariates Lpo a t. Consistency and the dependence of Lpo a t on earlier treatments only are not built in; they are the explicit hypotheses Model.Consistent and Model.Nonanticipating.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.Nonanticipatingdefinition

def Nonanticipating : Prop

The potential covariate at time t depends only on the treatments strictly before t.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.OutcomeConsistentdefinition

def OutcomeConsistent (a : Fin K → 𝒜) : Prop

Outcome consistency for the static regime a: a sample point whose observed treatments follow a at every time point has observed outcome equal to the potential outcome Ypo a.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.CovariateConsistentdefinition

def CovariateConsistent : Prop

Covariate consistency: a sample point whose observed treatments before t follow a has observed covariate at t equal to the potential covariate Lpo a t.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.Consistentdefinition

def Consistent : Prop

Consistency of outcomes for every static regime and of covariates.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.SeqExchangeabledefinition

def SeqExchangeable (a : Fin K → 𝒜) : Prop

Sequential exchangeability for the static regime a, in the mean independence form: for every time point t and every covariate path l, within the history event L̄_t = l̄_t, Ā_{t-1} = ā_{t-1} the potential outcome Ypo a is mean independent of the event A t = a t (in the division free form of MeanIndepOn). This is weaker than full conditional independence Y(ā) ⫫ A_t | L̄_t, Ā_{t-1} = ā_{t-1}.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.SeqPositivedefinition

def SeqPositive (a : Fin K → 𝒜) : Prop

Sequential positivity for the static regime a: every history event L̄_t = l̄_t, Ā_{t-1} = ā_{t-1} of positive probability keeps positive probability after adding A t = a t.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.DynamicRegimedefinition

def DynamicRegime (K : ℕ) (𝒜 𝓛 : Type*) : Type _

A dynamic treatment regime with K time points: at time t it assigns a treatment as a function of the covariate history L_0, …, L_t and of the treatment history A_0, …, A_{t-1}.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.DynamicRegime.ofStaticdefinition

def DynamicRegime.ofStatic {K : ℕ} {𝒜 𝓛 : Type*} (a : Fin K → 𝒜) : DynamicRegime K 𝒜 𝓛

The static regime a seen as a dynamic regime that ignores the history.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Counterexamples

CausalInference/Longitudinal/Counterexamples.lean · 196 lines · 11 public theorems · 12 definitions · imports Longitudinal.Weighting

Treatment-confounder feedback: the g-formula is right, regression adjustment is wrong. A concrete finite model with two time points in which the time-varying covariate L1 is affected by the first treatment A0 and affects both the second treatment A1 and (through an unmeasured common cause U) the outcome. Sequential exchangeability and sequential positivity hold, so the g-formula and inverse probability weighting recover the true mean of every potential outcome; but the naive contrast that adjusts for L1 by stratification and the unadjusted contrast both give a nonzero effect, while the true effect is zero.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Robins (1986)

  p.expect (Ypo true true) - p.expect (Ypo false false) = 0 ∧
    gFormula2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => true) (fun _ _ => true) Y -
      gFormula2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => false) (fun _ _ => false) Y = 0 ∧
    naiveAdjusted ≠ 0 ∧ unadjusted ≠ 0

Regression adjustment fails under treatment-confounder feedback. In this model the true effect E[Y(1, 1)] - E[Y(0, 0)] is 0 and the g-formula contrast is 0, while the naive contrast adjusting for L1 and the unadjusted contrast are both nonzero.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.GFormula

CausalInference/Longitudinal/GFormula.lean · 207 lines · 8 public theorems · 2 definitions · imports Longitudinal.Basic

The finite-horizon g-formula for static regimes. The g-formula of Robins (1986) for any finite number K of time points and a static regime, in the finite setting of CausalInference.Longitudinal.Basic, proved by induction on K.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Robins (1986)

Public declarations (10)

CausalInference.Longitudinal.gFormuladefinition

def gFormula {K : ℕ} (m : Ω → ℝ) (A : Fin K → Ω → 𝒜) (L : Fin K → Ω → 𝓛)
  (a : Fin K → 𝒜) (Y : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ

The sum-product form of the g-formula for the static regime a under the mass function m: the sum over all covariate paths l of E[Y | L̄_K = l̄, Ā_K = ā] times the product over the time points t of P(L_t = l_t | L̄_{t-1} = l̄_{t-1}, Ā_{t-1} = ā_{t-1}).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.iceGFormuladefinition

def iceGFormula : (K : ℕ) → (Ω → ℝ) → (Fin K → Ω → 𝒜) → (Fin K → Ω → 𝓛) →
  (Fin K → 𝒜) → (Ω → ℝ) → ℝ

The recursive (iterated conditional expectation) form of the g-formula for the static regime a under the mass function m. With no time points it is E[Y]. With K + 1 time points it is Σ_l P(L_0 = l) · G_l, where G_l is the recursive form for the remaining K time points under m restricted to the event L_0 = l, A_0 = a_0.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.gFormula_eq_iceGFormulatheorem

  (L : Fin K → Ω → 𝓛) (a : Fin K → 𝒜) (Y : Ω → ℝ),
  gFormula m A L a Y = iceGFormula K m A L a Y

The sum-product and the recursive forms of the g-formula are equal, for every mass function and with no hypotheses: the two expressions consist of the same ratios.

  MeanIndepOn (restrict m s) t u f ↔ MeanIndepOn m (s ∩ t) u f

CausalInference.Longitudinal.histL_cons_succtheorem

theorem histL_cons_succ {K : ℕ} (A : Fin (K + 1) → Ω → 𝒜) (L : Fin (K + 1) → Ω → 𝓛)
  (a : Fin (K + 1) → 𝒜) (l0 : 𝓛) (l : Fin K → 𝓛) (t : Fin K) :
  histL A L a (Fin.cons l0 l) t.succ =
    (ev (L 0) l0 ∩ ev (A 0) (a 0)) ∩ histL (Fin.tail A) (Fin.tail L) (Fin.tail a) l t

The history event at time t + 1 including the covariate, for a path starting with l0, is the first time point event intersected with the corresponding event of the shifted model.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.condMean_eq_iceGFormulatheorem

theorem condMean_eq_iceGFormula : ∀ (K : ℕ) {m : Ω → ℝ} (_hm : ∀ ω, 0 ≤ m ω)
  (_hm0 : 0 < wmass m univ) (A : Fin K → Ω → 𝒜) (L : Fin K → Ω → 𝓛) (a : Fin K → 𝒜) (Z : Ω → ℝ)
  (_hex : ∀ (l : Fin K → 𝓛) (t : Fin K), MeanIndepOn m (histL A L a l t) (ev (A t) (a t)) Z)
  (_hpos : ∀ (l : Fin K → 𝓛) (t : Fin K), 0 < wmass m (histL A L a l t) →
    0 < wmass m (histL A L a l t ∩ ev (A t) (a t))),
  condMean m univ Z = iceGFormula K m A L a Z

The recursive g-formula identifies the mean of the target (core form). For a nonnegative mass function m of positive total mass, a static regime a and a target variable Z, if Z is mean independent of A t = a t within every history event L̄_t = l̄_t, Ā_{t-1} = ā_{t-1} (sequential exchangeability) and each such event of positive mass keeps positive mass after adding A t = a t (sequential positivity), then E[Z] = iceGFormula K m A L a Z.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.gFormula_congrtheorem

theorem gFormula_congr {K : ℕ} (m : Ω → ℝ) (A : Fin K → Ω → 𝒜) (L : Fin K → Ω → 𝓛)
  (a : Fin K → 𝒜) {Y Z : Ω → ℝ} (h : ∀ l, ∀ ω ∈ hist A L a l K, Y ω = Z ω) :
  gFormula m A L a Y = gFormula m A L a Z

If two functions agree on every full history event, their g-formulas agree.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.expect_eq_condMeantheorem

theorem expect_eq_condMean (f : Ω → ℝ) : M.p.expect f = condMean M.p univ f

The mean under the model distribution is the conditional mean given the sure event.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.expect_Ypo_eq_iceGFormulatheorem

theorem expect_Ypo_eq_iceGFormula (a : Fin K → 𝒜) (hex : M.SeqExchangeable a)
  (hpos : M.SeqPositive a) :
  M.p.expect (M.Ypo a) = iceGFormula K M.p M.A M.L a (M.Ypo a)

The finite-horizon g-formula, recursive form. Under sequential exchangeability and sequential positivity for the static regime a, the mean of the potential outcome Y(ā) equals the recursive g-formula applied to Y(ā); with outcome consistency the recursive formula may be applied to the observed outcome (expect_Ypo_eq_gFormula).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Model.expect_Ypo_eq_gFormulatheorem

theorem expect_Ypo_eq_gFormula (a : Fin K → 𝒜) (hcons : M.OutcomeConsistent a)
  (hex : M.SeqExchangeable a) (hpos : M.SeqPositive a) :
  M.p.expect (M.Ypo a) = gFormula M.p M.A M.L a M.Y ∧
    gFormula M.p M.A M.L a M.Y = iceGFormula K M.p M.A M.L a M.Y

The finite-horizon g-formula. In a longitudinal model with K time points, assume outcome consistency, sequential exchangeability (mean independence form) and sequential positivity for the static regime a. Then E[Y(ā)] = Σ_{l̄} E[Y | L̄_K = l̄, Ā_K = ā] · Π_{t < K} P(L_t = l_t | L̄_{t-1} = l̄_{t-1}, Ā_{t-1} = ā_{t-1}), and this equals the recursive form iceGFormula K p A L a Y.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.TwoTime

CausalInference/Longitudinal/TwoTime.lean · 198 lines · 4 public theorems · 6 definitions · imports Longitudinal.Basic

The g-formula at two time points. The g-formula of Robins (1986) for two time points, in the finite setting of CausalInference.Longitudinal.Basic: a finite sample space with a nonnegative mass function, the time ordering L0, A0, L1, A1, Y, with covariates in a finite type 𝓛.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Robins (1986)

Public declarations (10)

CausalInference.Longitudinal.gFormula2definition

def gFormula2 (m : Ω → ℝ) (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (A0 : Ω → 𝒜) (L1 : Ω → 𝓛) (A1 : Ω → 𝒜)
  (d0 : 𝓛 → 𝒜) (d1 : 𝓛 → 𝓛 → 𝒜) (Y : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ

The two time point g-formula functional under the mass function m, with treatment value d0 l0 at time 0 and d1 l0 l1 at time 1: Σ_{l0, l1} E[Y | L0 = l0, A0 = d0 l0, L1 = l1, A1 = d1 l0 l1] · P(L1 = l1 | L0 = l0, A0 = d0 l0) · P(L0 = l0).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.SeqExchangeable2definition

def SeqExchangeable2 (m : Ω → ℝ) (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (A0 : Ω → 𝒜) (L1 : Ω → 𝓛) (A1 : Ω → 𝒜)
  (d0 : 𝓛 → 𝒜) (d1 : 𝓛 → 𝓛 → 𝒜) (Z : Ω → ℝ) : Prop

Sequential exchangeability at two time points for the target Z, in the mean independence form of MeanIndepOn: given L0 = l0, Z is mean independent of A0 = d0 l0; given L0 = l0, A0 = d0 l0, L1 = l1, Z is mean independent of A1 = d1 l0 l1.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.SeqPositive2definition

def SeqPositive2 (m : Ω → ℝ) (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (A0 : Ω → 𝒜) (L1 : Ω → 𝓛) (A1 : Ω → 𝒜)
  (d0 : 𝓛 → 𝒜) (d1 : 𝓛 → 𝓛 → 𝒜) : Prop

Sequential positivity at two time points: P(L0 = l0) > 0 implies P(L0 = l0, A0 = d0 l0) > 0, and P(L0 = l0, A0 = d0 l0, L1 = l1) > 0 implies P(L0 = l0, A0 = d0 l0, L1 = l1, A1 = d1 l0 l1) > 0.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.gFormula2_eqtheorem

theorem gFormula2_eq {m : Ω → ℝ} (hm : ∀ ω, 0 ≤ m ω) {L0 : Ω → 𝓛} {A0 : Ω → 𝒜}
  {L1 : Ω → 𝓛} {A1 : Ω → 𝒜} {d0 : 𝓛 → 𝒜} {d1 : 𝓛 → 𝓛 → 𝒜} {Y Z : Ω → ℝ}
  (hcons : ∀ ω, A0 ω = d0 (L0 ω) → A1 ω = d1 (L0 ω) (L1 ω) → Y ω = Z ω)
  (hex : SeqExchangeable2 m L0 A0 L1 A1 d0 d1 Z) (hpos : SeqPositive2 m L0 A0 L1 A1 d0 d1) :
  wsum m univ Z = gFormula2 m L0 A0 L1 A1 d0 d1 Y

The two time point g-formula (core form). Let the treatment values be d0 l0 at time 0 and d1 l0 l1 at time 1. Assume consistency (every sample point following these values has observed outcome Y equal to the target Z), sequential exchangeability for Z and sequential positivity. Then the weighted sum of Z over the whole space (the mean E[Z] when m is a probability mass function) equals the g-formula functional.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.gFormula2_statictheorem

theorem gFormula2_static (p : FiniteDist Ω) {L0 : Ω → 𝓛} {A0 : Ω → 𝒜} {L1 : Ω → 𝓛}
  {A1 : Ω → 𝒜} {Y : Ω → ℝ} {Ypo : 𝒜 → 𝒜 → Ω → ℝ} {a0 a1 : 𝒜}
  (hcons : ∀ ω, A0 ω = a0 → A1 ω = a1 → Y ω = Ypo a0 a1 ω)
  (hex : SeqExchangeable2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => a0) (fun _ _ => a1) (Ypo a0 a1))
  (hpos : SeqPositive2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => a0) (fun _ _ => a1)) :
  p.expect (Ypo a0 a1) =
    ∑ l0, ∑ l1, condMean p (ev L0 l0 ∩ ev A0 a0 ∩ ev L1 l1 ∩ ev A1 a1) Y *
      condProb p (ev L0 l0 ∩ ev A0 a0) (ev L1 l1) * p.prob (ev L0 l0)

The two time point g-formula for a static regime. Let p be a finite probability distribution, Ypo a0 a1 the potential outcome under the static regime (a0, a1), and assume consistency A0 = a0, A1 = a1 ⇒ Y = Ypo a0 a1, sequential exchangeability for Ypo a0 a1 and sequential positivity. Then E[Y(a0, a1)] = Σ_{l0, l1} E[Y | L0 = l0, A0 = a0, L1 = l1, A1 = a1] · P(L1 = l1 | L0 = l0, A0 = a0) · P(L0 = l0).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.DynamicRegime.firstdefinition

def DynamicRegime.first (g : DynamicRegime 2 𝒜 𝓛) (l0 : 𝓛) : 𝒜

The decision rule at time 0 of a dynamic regime with two time points, as a function of the first covariate.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.DynamicRegime.seconddefinition

def DynamicRegime.second (g : DynamicRegime 2 𝒜 𝓛) (l0 l1 : 𝓛) (a0 : 𝒜) : 𝒜

The decision rule at time 1 of a dynamic regime with two time points, as a function of the two covariates and the first treatment.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.dynamicOutcome2definition

def dynamicOutcome2 (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (L1po : 𝒜 → Ω → 𝓛) (Ypo : 𝒜 → 𝒜 → Ω → ℝ)
  (g : DynamicRegime 2 𝒜 𝓛) (ω : Ω) : ℝ

The potential outcome under the dynamic regime g with two time points. The first treatment is a0 = g(L0), the potential covariate at time 1 under a0 is L1po a0, the second treatment is a1 = g(L0, L1po a0, a0), and the outcome is the static potential outcome Ypo a0 a1. The baseline covariate L0 precedes all treatment and has no potential version; L1po a0 depends only on the earlier treatment a0 by construction.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.dynamicOutcome2_consistenttheorem

theorem dynamicOutcome2_consistent {L0 L1 : Ω → 𝓛} {A0 A1 : Ω → 𝒜} {Y : Ω → ℝ}
  {L1po : 𝒜 → Ω → 𝓛} {Ypo : 𝒜 → 𝒜 → Ω → ℝ} (g : DynamicRegime 2 𝒜 𝓛)
  (hY : ∀ ω a0 a1, A0 ω = a0 → A1 ω = a1 → Y ω = Ypo a0 a1 ω)
  (hL : ∀ ω a0, A0 ω = a0 → L1 ω = L1po a0 ω) (ω : Ω)
  (h0 : A0 ω = g.first (L0 ω)) (h1 : A1 ω = g.second (L0 ω) (L1 ω) (g.first (L0 ω))) :
  Y ω = dynamicOutcome2 L0 L1po Ypo g ω

Consistency for a dynamic regime follows from outcome and covariate consistency: a sample point whose observed treatments follow g has observed outcome equal to Y^g.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.gFormula2_dynamictheorem

theorem gFormula2_dynamic (p : FiniteDist Ω) {L0 L1 : Ω → 𝓛} {A0 A1 : Ω → 𝒜} {Y : Ω → ℝ}
  {L1po : 𝒜 → Ω → 𝓛} {Ypo : 𝒜 → 𝒜 → Ω → ℝ} (g : DynamicRegime 2 𝒜 𝓛)
  (hY : ∀ ω a0 a1, A0 ω = a0 → A1 ω = a1 → Y ω = Ypo a0 a1 ω)
  (hL : ∀ ω a0, A0 ω = a0 → L1 ω = L1po a0 ω)
  (hex : SeqExchangeable2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 g.first (fun l0 l1 => g.second l0 l1 (g.first l0))
    (dynamicOutcome2 L0 L1po Ypo g))
  (hpos : SeqPositive2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 g.first (fun l0 l1 => g.second l0 l1 (g.first l0))) :
  p.expect (dynamicOutcome2 L0 L1po Ypo g) =
    gFormula2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 g.first (fun l0 l1 => g.second l0 l1 (g.first l0)) Y

The two time point g-formula for a dynamic regime. Assume outcome consistency for every static regime, covariate consistency at time 1, sequential exchangeability for Y^g with the treatment values prescribed by g, and sequential positivity for those values. Then E[Y^g] = Σ_{l0, l1} E[Y | L0 = l0, A0 = g(l0), L1 = l1, A1 = g(l0, l1, g(l0))] · P(L1 = l1 | L0 = l0, A0 = g(l0)) · P(L0 = l0).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.Weighting

CausalInference/Longitudinal/Weighting.lean · 181 lines · 5 public theorems · 4 definitions · imports Longitudinal.TwoTime

Inverse probability of treatment weighting at two time points. The inverse probability of treatment weighting identity of Robins, Hernán and Brumback (2000) for a static regime at two time points, in the finite setting of CausalInference.Longitudinal.Basic, and the fact that stabilized weights have mean one.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Robins, Hernán and Brumback (2000)

Public declarations (9)

CausalInference.Longitudinal.prop0definition

def prop0 (m : Ω → ℝ) (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (A0 : Ω → 𝒜) (ω : Ω) : ℝ

The probability of the observed first treatment given the first covariate, P(A0 = A0(ω) | L0 = L0(ω)).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.prop1definition

def prop1 (m : Ω → ℝ) (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (A0 : Ω → 𝒜) (L1 : Ω → 𝓛) (A1 : Ω → 𝒜)
  (ω : Ω) : ℝ

The probability of the observed second treatment given the past, P(A1 = A1(ω) | L0 = L0(ω), A0 = A0(ω), L1 = L1(ω)).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.ipw2definition

def ipw2 (m : Ω → ℝ) (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (A0 : Ω → 𝒜) (L1 : Ω → 𝓛) (A1 : Ω → 𝒜)
  (a0 a1 : 𝒜) (Y : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ

The inverse probability of treatment weighted mean for the static regime (a0, a1): E[1{A0 = a0, A1 = a1} · Y / (P(A0 | L0) · P(A1 | L0, A0, L1))].

CausalInference.Longitudinal.wsum_ite_andtheorem

theorem wsum_ite_and {m : Ω → ℝ} (A0 A1 : Ω → 𝒜) (a0 a1 : 𝒜) (g : Ω → ℝ) :
  wsum m univ (fun ω => (if A0 ω = a0 ∧ A1 ω = a1 then 1 else 0) * g ω) =
    wsum m (ev A0 a0 ∩ ev A1 a1) g

A weighted sum of an indicator times a function is the weighted sum over the event.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.ipw2_statictheorem

theorem ipw2_static [Finite 𝓛] (p : FiniteDist Ω) {L0 : Ω → 𝓛} {A0 : Ω → 𝒜} {L1 : Ω → 𝓛}
  {A1 : Ω → 𝒜} {Y : Ω → ℝ} {Ypo : 𝒜 → 𝒜 → Ω → ℝ} {a0 a1 : 𝒜}
  (hcons : ∀ ω, A0 ω = a0 → A1 ω = a1 → Y ω = Ypo a0 a1 ω)
  (hex : SeqExchangeable2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => a0) (fun _ _ => a1) (Ypo a0 a1))
  (hpos : SeqPositive2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => a0) (fun _ _ => a1)) :
  p.expect (Ypo a0 a1) = ipw2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 a0 a1 Y

The inverse probability of treatment weighting identity at two time points. Under consistency, sequential exchangeability for Y(a0, a1) and sequential positivity for the static regime (a0, a1), E[Y(a0, a1)] = E[1{A0 = a0, A1 = a1} · Y / (P(A0 = a0 | L0) · P(A1 = a1 | L0, A0, L1))].

CausalInference.Longitudinal.meanIndepOn_consttheorem

theorem meanIndepOn_const (m : Ω → ℝ) (s t : Finset Ω) (c : ℝ) :
  MeanIndepOn m s t (fun _ => c)

A constant is mean independent of every event.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.ipw2_onetheorem

theorem ipw2_one [Finite 𝓛] (p : FiniteDist Ω) {L0 : Ω → 𝓛} {A0 : Ω → 𝒜} {L1 : Ω → 𝓛} {A1 : Ω → 𝒜}
  {a0 a1 : 𝒜} (hpos : SeqPositive2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => a0) (fun _ _ => a1)) :
  ipw2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 a0 a1 (fun _ => 1) = 1

Unstabilized weights have mean one on the regime: under sequential positivity for (a0, a1), E[1{A0 = a0, A1 = a1} / (P(A0 = a0 | L0) · P(A1 = a1 | L0, A0, L1))] = 1.

CausalInference.Longitudinal.stabilizedWeight2definition

def stabilizedWeight2 (m : Ω → ℝ) (L0 : Ω → 𝓛) (A0 : Ω → 𝒜) (L1 : Ω → 𝓛)
  (A1 : Ω → 𝒜) (ω : Ω) : ℝ

The stabilized weight at two time points: P(A0 = A0(ω)) · P(A1 = A1(ω) | A0 = A0(ω)) / (prop0(ω) · prop1(ω)).

CausalInference.Longitudinal.expect_stabilizedWeight2theorem

theorem expect_stabilizedWeight2 [Finite 𝒜] [Finite 𝓛] (p : FiniteDist Ω) {L0 : Ω → 𝓛} {A0 : Ω → 𝒜}
  {L1 : Ω → 𝓛} {A1 : Ω → 𝒜}
  (hpos : ∀ a0 a1, 0 < p.prob (ev A0 a0 ∩ ev A1 a1) →
    SeqPositive2 p L0 A0 L1 A1 (fun _ => a0) (fun _ _ => a1)) :
  p.expect (stabilizedWeight2 p L0 A0 L1 A1) = 1

Stabilized weights have mean one. If sequential positivity holds for every static regime (a0, a1) that occurs with positive probability, then E[SW] = 1 for the stabilized weight SW = P(A0) P(A1 | A0) / (P(A0 | L0) P(A1 | L0, A0, L1)).

Effect measures

Risk difference, risk ratio and odds ratio, collapsibility, the sure-thing principle and Simpson's reversal, with checked probability examples.

CausalInference.Measures.Collapsibility

CausalInference/Measures/Collapsibility.lean · 419 lines · 24 public theorems · 12 definitions · imports Measures.EffectMeasures

Collapsibility and effect-measure modification. A binary treatment A, a binary outcome Y, and a stratifying variable V with finitely many levels. The data are the stratum risks p₁ v = Pr[Y = 1 | A = 1, V = v] and p₀ v = Pr[Y = 1 | A = 0, V = v] and the stratum distributions π₁ v = Pr[V = v | A = 1], π₀ v = Pr[V = v | A = 0]. By the law of total probability the marginal risk in arm a is the standardized risk ∑ v, π_a v * p_a v. When V is independent of A (no confounding by V, as in a marginally randomized experiment) π₁ = π₀.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Hernán and Robins (2020)

Public declarations (36)

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.IsWeightsdefinition

def IsWeights (w : V → ℝ) : Prop

Nonnegative weights summing to one: a probability vector on the strata.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.IsCollapsibledefinition

def IsCollapsible (g : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ) (π₁ π₀ p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ) : Prop

Collapsibility (Hernán and Robins, Fine Point 4.3). The effect measure g, applied to the marginal risks ∑ π₁ p₁ and ∑ π₀ p₀, is a weighted average, with some nonnegative weights summing to one, of the stratum measures g (p₁ v) (p₀ v).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.IsCollapsibleOverdefinition

def IsCollapsibleOver (g : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ) (π π₁ π₀ p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ) : Prop

**Collapsibility over Z** (Pearl 2009, Definition 6.5.1). The expectation of the stratum measures under the marginal distribution π of the stratifier equals the measure applied to the marginal risks: E_z g[P(x, y | z)] = g[P(x, y)].

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.IsCollapsibleOver.isCollapsibletheorem

theorem IsCollapsibleOver.isCollapsible {g : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ} {π π₁ π₀ p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ}
  (h : IsCollapsibleOver g π π₁ π₀ p₁ p₀) (hπ : IsWeights π) :
  IsCollapsible g π₁ π₀ p₁ p₀

Pearl's collapsibility implies collapsibility in the weighted-average sense.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.lt_standardizedRisktheorem

theorem lt_standardizedRisk {π r : V → ℝ} {m : ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π) (hr : ∀ v, m < r v) :
  m < standardizedRisk π r

A weighted average of values all strictly above m is strictly above m.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.standardizedRisk_lttheorem

theorem standardizedRisk_lt {π r : V → ℝ} {M : ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π) (hr : ∀ v, r v < M) :
  standardizedRisk π r < M

A weighted average of values all strictly below M is strictly below M.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskDiff_isCollapsibleOver_of_indeptheorem

theorem riskDiff_isCollapsibleOver_of_indep (π p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ) :
  IsCollapsibleOver riskDiff π π π p₁ p₀

The risk difference is collapsible under (U1). If the stratifier has the same distribution π in both arms, the marginal risk difference is the π-average of the stratum risk differences (Pearl, Section 6.5.1).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskDiff_isCollapsibleOver_of_consttheorem

theorem riskDiff_isCollapsibleOver_of_const {π π₁ π₀ p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} {c₁ c₀ : ℝ}
  (hπ : ∑ v, π v = 1) (hπ₁ : ∑ v, π₁ v = 1) (hπ₀ : ∑ v, π₀ v = 1)
  (h₁ : ∀ v, p₁ v = c₁) (h₀ : ∀ v, p₀ v = c₀) :
  IsCollapsibleOver riskDiff π π₁ π₀ p₁ p₀

The risk difference is collapsible under (U2). If the stratum risks do not depend on the stratum (V is unassociated with Y given A), the marginal risk difference equals the average of the stratum risk differences, whatever the stratum distributions in the two arms (Pearl, Section 6.5.1).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskDiff_mem_Icctheorem

theorem riskDiff_mem_Icc {π p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} {m M : ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π)
  (h : ∀ v, riskDiff (p₁ v) (p₀ v) ∈ Set.Icc m M) :
  riskDiff (standardizedRisk π p₁) (standardizedRisk π p₀) ∈ Set.Icc m M

With V independent of A, the risk difference is collapsible, and the marginal risk difference lies between the smallest and the largest stratum risk difference.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.rrWeightdefinition

def rrWeight (π p₀ : V → ℝ) (v : V) : ℝ

The weights of the risk ratio (Hernán and Robins, Technical Point 4.3): w v = Pr[Y = 1 | A = 0, V = v] Pr[V = v] / Pr[Y = 1 | A = 0], the share of stratum v among the outcome events of the untreated arm.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.isWeights_rrWeighttheorem

theorem isWeights_rrWeight {π p₀ : V → ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π) (h₀ : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v) :
  IsWeights (rrWeight π p₀)

The risk ratio weights are weights when the baseline risks are positive.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskRatio_eq_sum_rrWeighttheorem

theorem riskRatio_eq_sum_rrWeight {π p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π) (h₀ : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v) :
  riskRatio (standardizedRisk π p₁) (standardizedRisk π p₀) =
    ∑ v, rrWeight π p₀ v * riskRatio (p₁ v) (p₀ v)

Marginal versus conditional risk ratio (Hernán and Robins, Technical Point 4.3). With V independent of A (stratum distribution π in both arms) and positive baseline risks, the marginal risk ratio is the rrWeight-weighted average of the stratum risk ratios.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskRatio_isCollapsibletheorem

theorem riskRatio_isCollapsible {π p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π) (h₀ : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v) :
  IsCollapsible riskRatio π π p₁ p₀

The risk ratio is collapsible (Hernán and Robins, Fine Point 4.3), when V is independent of A and the baseline risks are positive.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskRatio_mem_Icctheorem

theorem riskRatio_mem_Icc {π p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} {m M : ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π)
  (h₀ : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v) (h : ∀ v, riskRatio (p₁ v) (p₀ v) ∈ Set.Icc m M) :
  riskRatio (standardizedRisk π p₁) (standardizedRisk π p₀) ∈ Set.Icc m M

The marginal risk ratio lies between the smallest and the largest stratum risk ratio (Hernán and Robins, Fine Point 4.3).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.marginal_riskRatio_lt_one_ifftheorem

theorem marginal_riskRatio_lt_one_iff {π p₁ p₀ : Bool → ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π)
  (hπt : 0 < π true) (h₀ : ∀ l, 0 < p₀ l)
  (hRR₁ : riskRatio (p₁ true) (p₀ true) = 1 / 2)
  (hRR₀ : riskRatio (p₁ false) (p₀ false) = 2) :
  riskRatio (standardizedRisk π p₁) (standardizedRisk π p₀) < 1 ↔
    2 * π false / π true < p₀ true / p₀ false

Technical Point 4.3 criterion. Two strata L = true and L = false with Pr[L = l] = π l > 0, positive baseline risks, conditional risk ratio 1/2 in stratum true and 2 in stratum false. Then the marginal risk ratio is below 1 if and only if p₀ true / p₀ false > 2 π false / π true.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsRatio_isCollapsible_of_sharpNulltheorem

theorem oddsRatio_isCollapsible_of_sharpNull {π p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} (hπ : IsWeights π)
  (hnull : ∀ v, p₁ v = p₀ v) (h0 : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v) (h1 : ∀ v, p₀ v < 1) :
  IsCollapsibleOver oddsRatio π π π p₁ p₀ ∧
    oddsRatio (standardizedRisk π p₁) (standardizedRisk π p₀) = 1

The odds ratio is collapsible under the sharp null (Hernán and Robins, Fine Point 4.3). If treatment has no effect in any stratum and the baseline risks are in (0, 1), the odds ratio is collapsible: every stratum odds ratio and the marginal odds ratio equal 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.table44definition

def table44 : Bool → Bool → Bool → ℕ

The counts of Hernán and Robins, Table 4.4, indexed by V, A, Y.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.risk44definition

def risk44 (a v : Bool) : ℝ

The stratum risk Pr[Y = 1 | A = a, V = v] in Table 4.4.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.condV44definition

def condV44 (a v : Bool) : ℝ

The stratum distribution Pr[V = v | A = a] in Table 4.4.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.margV44definition

The marginal distribution Pr[V = v] in Table 4.4.

The marginal risk Pr[Y = 1 | A = a] in Table 4.4, computed from the counts.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.table44_indeptheorem

theorem table44_indep (a v : Bool) : condV44 a v = margV44 v

In Table 4.4 the stratifier is independent of treatment: Pr[V = v | A = a] = Pr[V = v] (both equal 1/2). There is no confounding by V.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.margRisk44_eqtheorem

theorem margRisk44_eq (a : Bool) :
  margRisk44 a = standardizedRisk (condV44 a) (risk44 a)

In Table 4.4 the marginal risk is the standardized risk (law of total probability).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.isWeights_condV44theorem

theorem isWeights_condV44 (a : Bool) : IsWeights (condV44 a)

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.table44_stratum_oddsRatiotheorem

theorem table44_stratum_oddsRatio (v : Bool) : oddsRatio (risk44 true v) (risk44 false v) = 6

Table 4.4: both stratum odds ratios are 6.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.table44_stratum_riskRatiotheorem

theorem table44_stratum_riskRatio :
  riskRatio (risk44 true false) (risk44 false false) = 2 ∧
    riskRatio (risk44 true true) (risk44 false true) = 3

Table 4.4: the stratum risk ratios are 2 for men and 3 for women.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.table44_marginal_oddsRatiotheorem

theorem table44_marginal_oddsRatio : oddsRatio (margRisk44 true) (margRisk44 false) = 49 / 9

Table 4.4: the marginal odds ratio is 49/9.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.table44_marginal_riskRatiotheorem

theorem table44_marginal_riskRatio : riskRatio (margRisk44 true) (margRisk44 false) = 7 / 3

Table 4.4: the marginal risk ratio is 7/3, between the stratum values 2 and 3.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsRatio_not_collapsible_table44theorem

theorem oddsRatio_not_collapsible_table44 :
  ¬ IsCollapsible oddsRatio (condV44 true) (condV44 false) (risk44 true) (risk44 false) ∧
    ¬ IsCollapsibleOver oddsRatio margV44 (condV44 true) (condV44 false)
      (risk44 true) (risk44 false)

The odds ratio is not collapsible (Hernán and Robins, Fine Point 4.3 and Table 4.4; Pearl, Section 6.5). In Table 4.4 the stratifier V is independent of treatment (table44_indep), both stratum odds ratios equal 6, yet the marginal odds ratio 49/9 is not a weighted average of the stratum odds ratios. Hence neither collapsibility notion holds.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.AdditiveModificationdefinition

def AdditiveModification (p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ) : Prop

Additive effect modification by V: the stratum risk difference varies across strata.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.MultiplicativeModificationdefinition

def MultiplicativeModification (p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ) : Prop

Multiplicative effect modification by V: the stratum risk ratio varies across strata.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.QualitativeModificationdefinition

def QualitativeModification (p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ) : Prop

Qualitative effect modification by V: the effect is harmful in some stratum and beneficial in another.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.qualitative_imp_additive_and_multiplicativetheorem

theorem qualitative_imp_additive_and_multiplicative {p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} (h₀ : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v)
  (hq : QualitativeModification p₁ p₀) :
  AdditiveModification p₁ p₀ ∧ MultiplicativeModification p₁ p₀

Qualitative modification shows on both scales (Hernán and Robins, Section 4.1). With positive baseline risks, qualitative effect modification is both additive and multiplicative effect modification.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.null_or_const_of_no_modificationtheorem

theorem null_or_const_of_no_modification {p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} (h₀ : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v)
  (hA : ¬ AdditiveModification p₁ p₀) (hM : ¬ MultiplicativeModification p₁ p₀) :
  (∀ v, p₁ v = p₀ v) ∨ ∀ v w, p₀ v = p₀ w

No modification on either scale. With positive baseline risks, if neither the risk difference nor the risk ratio varies across strata, then either the effect is null in every stratum or the baseline risk is the same in every stratum.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.modification_of_baseline_variestheorem

theorem modification_of_baseline_varies {p₁ p₀ : V → ℝ} (h₀ : ∀ v, 0 < p₀ v)
  (hvar : ∃ v w, p₀ v ≠ p₀ w) (heff : ∃ v, p₁ v ≠ p₀ v) :
  AdditiveModification p₁ p₀ ∨ MultiplicativeModification p₁ p₀

Effect modification is guaranteed on some scale (Hernán and Robins, Section 4.3). If the baseline risk Pr[Y^{a=0} = 1 | V = v] > 0 varies with v and the effect is nonnull in at least one stratum, there is additive or multiplicative effect modification by V.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.scaleDependence_exampletheorem

theorem scaleDependence_example :
  let p₀ : Bool → ℝ := fun v => if v then 8 / 10 else 1 / 10
  let p₁ : Bool → ℝ := fun v => if v then 9 / 10 else 2 / 10
  ¬ AdditiveModification p₁ p₀ ∧ MultiplicativeModification p₁ p₀

Scale dependence (Hernán and Robins, Section 4.1). Baseline risks 0.8 and 0.1, treated risks 0.9 and 0.2: the risk difference is 0.1 in both strata, the risk ratios are 9/8 and 2. There is multiplicative but no additive effect modification.

CausalInference.Measures.EffectMeasures

CausalInference/Measures/EffectMeasures.lean · 195 lines · 16 public theorems · 5 definitions

Effect measures for a binary outcome. For a binary outcome, an effect of a binary treatment is summarized by two risks: p₁, the risk of the outcome under treatment, and p₀, the risk under no treatment. These may be causal risks Pr[Y^{a=1} = 1], Pr[Y^{a=0} = 1] or associational risks Pr[Y = 1 | A = a]; the algebra is the same. This file defines the three standard effect measures and proves their elementary relations.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020)

Public declarations (21)

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskDiffdefinition

def riskDiff (p₁ p₀ : ℝ) : ℝ

The risk difference p₁ - p₀: the effect on the additive scale.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskRatiodefinition

def riskRatio (p₁ p₀ : ℝ) : ℝ

The risk ratio p₁ / p₀: the effect on the multiplicative scale. It is meaningful only when p₀ > 0, which every result below assumes.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsdefinition

def odds (p : ℝ) : ℝ

The odds p / (1 - p) of an event of probability p. It is meaningful only when p < 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsRatiodefinition

def oddsRatio (p₁ p₀ : ℝ) : ℝ

The odds ratio odds p₁ / odds p₀. It is meaningful when 0 < p₀ < 1 and p₁ < 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskDiff_eq_zero_ifftheorem

theorem riskDiff_eq_zero_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} : riskDiff p₁ p₀ = 0 ↔ p₁ = p₀

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskRatio_eq_one_ifftheorem

theorem riskRatio_eq_one_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₀ : 0 < p₀) : riskRatio p₁ p₀ = 1 ↔ p₁ = p₀

The risk ratio is 1 exactly when the risks are equal (given a positive baseline risk).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.odds_postheorem

theorem odds_pos {p : ℝ} (h0 : 0 < p) (h1 : p < 1) : 0 < odds p

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.odds_lt_odds_ifftheorem

theorem odds_lt_odds_iff {p q : ℝ} (hp1 : p < 1) (hq1 : q < 1) :
  odds p < odds q ↔ p < q

The odds are strictly increasing on (-∞, 1), in particular on [0, 1).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.odds_injOntheorem

theorem odds_injOn {p q : ℝ} (hp1 : p < 1) (hq1 : q < 1) (h : odds p = odds q) : p = q

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsRatio_eq_one_ifftheorem

theorem oddsRatio_eq_one_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₁1 : p₁ < 1) (h₀0 : 0 < p₀)
  (h₀1 : p₀ < 1) : oddsRatio p₁ p₀ = 1 ↔ p₁ = p₀

The odds ratio is 1 exactly when the risks are equal (given 0 < p₀ < 1 and p₁ < 1).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.null_ifftheorem

theorem null_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₁1 : p₁ < 1) (h₀0 : 0 < p₀) (h₀1 : p₀ < 1) :
  (riskDiff p₁ p₀ = 0 ↔ riskRatio p₁ p₀ = 1) ∧
    (riskRatio p₁ p₀ = 1 ↔ oddsRatio p₁ p₀ = 1)

The null values coincide. If 0 < p₀ < 1 and p₁ < 1, the risk difference is 0 iff the risk ratio is 1 iff the odds ratio is 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.one_lt_riskRatio_ifftheorem

theorem one_lt_riskRatio_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₀ : 0 < p₀) :
  1 < riskRatio p₁ p₀ ↔ 0 < riskDiff p₁ p₀

A positive risk difference is a risk ratio above 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskRatio_lt_one_ifftheorem

theorem riskRatio_lt_one_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₀ : 0 < p₀) :
  riskRatio p₁ p₀ < 1 ↔ riskDiff p₁ p₀ < 0

A negative risk difference is a risk ratio below 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.one_lt_oddsRatio_ifftheorem

theorem one_lt_oddsRatio_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₁1 : p₁ < 1) (h₀0 : 0 < p₀)
  (h₀1 : p₀ < 1) : 1 < oddsRatio p₁ p₀ ↔ 0 < riskDiff p₁ p₀

A positive risk difference is an odds ratio above 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsRatio_lt_one_ifftheorem

theorem oddsRatio_lt_one_iff {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₁1 : p₁ < 1) (h₀0 : 0 < p₀)
  (h₀1 : p₀ < 1) : oddsRatio p₁ p₀ < 1 ↔ riskDiff p₁ p₀ < 0

A negative risk difference is an odds ratio below 1.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsRatio_eq_riskRatio_multheorem

theorem oddsRatio_eq_riskRatio_mul {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₁1 : p₁ < 1) (h₀0 : 0 < p₀) (h₀1 : p₀ < 1) :
  oddsRatio p₁ p₀ = riskRatio p₁ p₀ * ((1 - p₀) / (1 - p₁))

The odds ratio factors as the risk ratio times (1 - p₀) / (1 - p₁).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.riskRatio_lt_oddsRatiotheorem

theorem riskRatio_lt_oddsRatio {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₀0 : 0 < p₀) (h : p₀ < p₁) (h₁1 : p₁ < 1) :
  1 < riskRatio p₁ p₀ ∧ riskRatio p₁ p₀ < oddsRatio p₁ p₀

The odds ratio exaggerates a harmful effect. If 0 < p₀ < p₁ < 1, then 1 < RR < OR: the odds ratio is further from the null than the risk ratio.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.oddsRatio_lt_riskRatiotheorem

theorem oddsRatio_lt_riskRatio {p₁ p₀ : ℝ} (h₁0 : 0 < p₁) (h : p₁ < p₀) (h₀1 : p₀ < 1) :
  oddsRatio p₁ p₀ < riskRatio p₁ p₀ ∧ riskRatio p₁ p₀ < 1

The odds ratio exaggerates a protective effect. If 0 < p₁ < p₀ < 1, then OR < RR < 1: the odds ratio is further from the null than the risk ratio.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.standardizedRiskdefinition

def standardizedRisk {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (π r : V → ℝ) : ℝ

The standardized (marginal) risk ∑ v, π v * r v: the average of the stratum risks r v weighted by the stratum probabilities π v. By the law of total probability this is the marginal risk when π is the distribution of the stratifying variable in the relevant arm.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.standardizedRisk_mem_Icctheorem

theorem standardizedRisk_mem_Icc {V : Type*} [Fintype V] {π r : V → ℝ} {m M : ℝ}
  (hπ : ∀ v, 0 ≤ π v) (hsum : ∑ v, π v = 1) (hr : ∀ v, r v ∈ Set.Icc m M) :
  standardizedRisk π r ∈ Set.Icc m M

A weighted average with nonnegative weights summing to one lies between any lower and upper bound of the averaged values.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.standardizedRisk_mem_unitIntervaltheorem

theorem standardizedRisk_mem_unitInterval {V : Type*} [Fintype V] {π r : V → ℝ}
  (hπ : ∀ v, 0 ≤ π v) (hsum : ∑ v, π v = 1) (hr : ∀ v, r v ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) :
  standardizedRisk π r ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1

A standardized risk of risks is a risk.

CausalInference.Measures.Examples

CausalInference/Measures/Examples.lean · 183 lines · 4 public theorems · 10 definitions

Elementary probability examples. Checked finite computations from the opening chapters of the causal inference primer and from Pearl's discussion of confounding. Each example is a real-valued mass function on a small finite type; probabilities are finite sums and conditional probabilities are ratios whose denominators are shown to be positive in the same statement.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Pearl, Glymour and Jewell (2016)

Public declarations (14)

CausalInference.Paradoxes.IsDistdefinition

def IsDist (m : Ω → ℝ) : Prop

m is a probability mass function on the finite type Ω.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.probOfdefinition

def probOf (m : Ω → ℝ) (P : Ω → Prop) [DecidablePred P] : ℝ

The probability ∑_{ω ∈ P} m ω of the event P.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.condProbdefinition

def condProb (m : Ω → ℝ) (P Q : Ω → Prop) [DecidablePred P] [DecidablePred Q] :
  ℝ

The conditional probability P(P | Q) = P(P ∧ Q) / P(Q). Every use below states that P(Q) > 0.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.expectdefinition

def expect (m : Ω → ℝ) (f : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ

The expectation ∑ ω, m ω * f ω.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.covdefinition

def cov (m : Ω → ℝ) (X Y : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ

The covariance E[X Y] - E[X] E[Y].

CausalInference.Paradoxes.unif3definition

def unif3 : Fin 3 → ℝ

The uniform distribution on three points.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.X3definition

def X3 : Fin 3 → ℝ

X takes the values -1, 0, 1.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.Y3definition

def Y3 (i : Fin 3) : ℝ

Y = X².

CausalInference.Paradoxes.zeroCov_not_indeptheorem

theorem zeroCov_not_indep :
  IsDist unif3 ∧ cov unif3 X3 Y3 = 0 ∧
    probOf unif3 (fun i => X3 i = 0 ∧ Y3 i = 0) ≠
      probOf unif3 (fun i => X3 i = 0) * probOf unif3 (fun i => Y3 i = 0)

Zero covariance does not imply independence. For X uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X², the covariance is 0, but P(X = 0, Y = 0) = 1/3 ≠ 1/9 = P(X = 0) P(Y = 0).

CausalInference.Paradoxes.twoCoinsdefinition

def twoCoins : Bool × Bool → ℝ

Two independent fair coins (true for heads): each outcome has probability 1/4.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.coinBell_collidertheorem

theorem coinBell_collider :
  IsDist twoCoins ∧
    (∀ x y : Bool, probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = x ∧ ω.2 = y) =
      probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = x) * probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.2 = y)) ∧
    0 < probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 || ω.2) = true) ∧
    condProb twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = true) (fun ω => (ω.1 || ω.2) = true) = 2 / 3 ∧
    0 < probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.2 = true ∧ (ω.1 || ω.2) = true) ∧
    condProb twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = true)
      (fun ω => ω.2 = true ∧ (ω.1 || ω.2) = true) = 1 / 2

Coin and bell (Pearl, Glymour and Jewell 2016, Section 2.3). With coins X, Y and the bell Z = X ∨ Y: the coins are independent; P(X = H | Z = 1) = 2/3; and P(X = H | Y = H, Z = 1) = 1/2. Conditioning on the collider Z makes the coins dependent.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.twoCoin_confoundingtheorem

theorem twoCoin_confounding :
  (∀ z x : Bool, probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = z ∧ (ω.1 == ω.2) = x) =
      probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = z) * probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 == ω.2) = x)) ∧
    (∀ z x : Bool, probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.2 = z ∧ (ω.1 == ω.2) = x) =
      probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.2 = z) * probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 == ω.2) = x)) ∧
    (∀ z y : Bool, probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = z ∧ (ω.1 != ω.2) = y) =
      probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.1 = z) * probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 != ω.2) = y)) ∧
    (∀ z y : Bool, probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.2 = z ∧ (ω.1 != ω.2) = y) =
      probOf twoCoins (fun ω => ω.2 = z) * probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 != ω.2) = y)) ∧
    probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 == ω.2) = true ∧ (ω.1 != ω.2) = true) ≠
      probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 == ω.2) = true) *
        probOf twoCoins (fun ω => (ω.1 != ω.2) = true)

Two coins confound jointly (Pearl 2009, Section 6.3.1). Two fair coins Z₁, Z₂; X occurs when they agree and Y when they differ. Each coin is independent of X and of Y (the product rule holds for every pair of values), yet X and Y are dependent: P(X, Y) = 0 ≠ 1/4 = P(X) P(Y).

CausalInference.Paradoxes.montyHallDistdefinition

def montyHallDist : Fin 3 × Fin 3 → ℝ

The Monty Hall model when the contestant has chosen door 0 (door A). An outcome is a pair (door hiding the car, door Monty opens). The car is uniform over the three doors; Monty never opens the chosen door or the car door, and chooses uniformly between doors 1 and 2 when the car is behind door 0.

CausalInference.Paradoxes.montyHalltheorem

theorem montyHall :
  IsDist montyHallDist ∧
    probOf montyHallDist (fun ω => ω.2 = 0 ∨ ω.2 = ω.1) = 0 ∧
    0 < probOf montyHallDist (fun ω => ω.2 = 2) ∧
    condProb montyHallDist (fun ω => ω.1 = 1) (fun ω => ω.2 = 2) = 2 / 3 ∧
    condProb montyHallDist (fun ω => ω.1 = 0) (fun ω => ω.2 = 2) = 1 / 3

Monty Hall (Pearl, Glymour and Jewell 2016, Section 1.3 and Study question 1.3.5). The model is a distribution in which Monty never opens the chosen door or the car door. Given that Monty opened door 2 (door C), the car is behind door 1 (door B) with probability 2/3 and behind the chosen door 0 with probability 1/3: switching doubles the chance of winning.

CausalInference.Measures.Simpson

CausalInference/Measures/Simpson.lean · 175 lines · 9 public theorems · 7 definitions · imports Measures.Collapsibility

The sure-thing principle and Simpson's reversal. A population is partitioned into finitely many strata v (subpopulations F, ¬F in Pearl's notation). Under each action a (treatment C or control ¬C) the strata have probabilities q a v and the event E has stratum probabilities e a v; the overall probability of E under action a is the standardized risk ∑ v, q a v * e a v.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Pearl, Glymour and Jewell (2016)

Public declarations (16)

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.standardizedRisk_subtheorem

theorem standardizedRisk_sub (q e₁ e₀ : V → ℝ) :
  standardizedRisk q e₁ - standardizedRisk q e₀ = standardizedRisk q (fun v => e₁ v - e₀ v)

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.sure_thing_principletheorem

theorem sure_thing_principle {q₁ q₀ e₁ e₀ : V → ℝ} (hq : IsWeights q₀) (hno : q₁ = q₀)
  (h : ∀ v, e₀ v < e₁ v) : standardizedRisk q₀ e₀ < standardizedRisk q₁ e₁

Sure-thing principle (Pearl 2009, Theorem 6.1.1), algebraic form. Let q₁, q₀ be the distributions of the strata under the action and under its absence, and e₁ v, e₀ v the stratum probabilities of E. If the action does not change the distribution of the strata (q₁ = q₀, a probability vector), and increases the probability of E in every stratum, then it increases the probability of E in the population.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.sure_thing_principle_letheorem

theorem sure_thing_principle_le {q₁ q₀ e₁ e₀ : V → ℝ} (hq : IsWeights q₀) (hno : q₁ = q₀)
  (h : ∀ v, e₀ v ≤ e₁ v) : standardizedRisk q₀ e₀ ≤ standardizedRisk q₁ e₁

Sure-thing principle, non-strict version: a weak increase in every stratum gives a weak increase in the population, when the action does not change the distribution of the strata.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.ne_of_reversaltheorem

theorem ne_of_reversal {q₁ q₀ e₁ e₀ : V → ℝ} (hq : IsWeights q₀) (h : ∀ v, e₀ v < e₁ v)
  (hrev : standardizedRisk q₁ e₁ ≤ standardizedRisk q₀ e₀) : q₁ ≠ q₀

Simpson's reversal requires dependence between treatment and stratum. If the action increases the probability of E in every stratum but not in the population, then the distribution of the strata differs between the two arms.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.simpson_table11theorem

theorem simpson_table11 :
  (∀ v, risk11 false v < risk11 true v) ∧ margRisk11 true < margRisk11 false ∧
    margRisk11 true = 273 / 350 ∧ margRisk11 false = 289 / 350

Simpson's reversal in Table 1.1: the drug has the higher recovery rate among men and among women, and the lower recovery rate in the combined data (273/350 < 289/350).

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.table11_dependenttheorem

theorem table11_dependent : condSex11 true ≠ condSex11 false

In Table 1.1 treatment and sex are dependent: the sex distribution differs between the arms (87/350 men among the treated, 270/350 among the untreated), as ne_of_reversal demands.

CausalInference.EffectMeasure.simpson_figure61theorem

theorem simpson_figure61 :
  (∀ f, rate61 true f < rate61 false f) ∧
    standardizedRisk (sex61 true) (rate61 true) = 1 / 2 ∧
    standardizedRisk (sex61 false) (rate61 false) = 2 / 5 ∧
    sex61 false ≠ sex61 true

Simpson's reversal, Figure 6.1 (Pearl 2009, (6.1) to (6.3)): the treatment has the lower recovery rate among males and among females but the higher one combined (0.5 > 0.4); the sex distribution differs between the arms.

Probabilities of causation

Probabilities of necessity and sufficiency in a finite response-type model: identification and sharp bounds.

CausalInference.Attribution.Bounds

CausalInference/Attribution/Bounds.lean · 512 lines · 29 public theorems · 9 definitions · imports PartialIdentification.IdentifiedSet, Attribution.Identification

Bounds on the probabilities of causation. Partial identification of PN, PS, PNS in the finite response-type model of CausalInference.Attribution.Definitions, with no assumption beyond consistency.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Pearl, Glymour and Jewell (2016); Tian and Pearl (2000)

Public declarations (38)

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.ofCellsdefinition

def ofCells (t : Bool → Bool → Bool → ℝ) (hnn : ∀ x y0 y1, 0 ≤ t x y0 y1)
  (hsum : t true false false + t true false true + t true true false + t true true true +
    t false false false + t false false true + t false true false + t false true true = 1) :
  ResponseModel

Build a response-type model from an explicit table of eight cell weights, given their nonnegativity and the fact that they sum to one.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.ofCells_wtheorem

theorem ofCells_w (t : Bool → Bool → Bool → ℝ) (hnn) (hsum) :
  (ofCells t hnn hsum).w = t

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.nonneg_cellstheorem

theorem nonneg_cells (m : ResponseModel) :
  0 ≤ m.w true false false ∧ 0 ≤ m.w true false true ∧ 0 ≤ m.w true true false ∧
    0 ≤ m.w true true true ∧ 0 ≤ m.w false false false ∧ 0 ≤ m.w false false true ∧
    0 ≤ m.w false true false ∧ 0 ≤ m.w false true true

The cell weights of a model, as a list of nonnegativity facts for linarith.
