def expObs (m : ResponseModel) : ℝ × ℝ

The experimental observation: the pair (P(y_x), P(y_x')).

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pns_mem_Icc_exptheorem

theorem pns_mem_Icc_exp (m : ResponseModel) :
  m.PNS ∈ Set.Icc (max 0 (m.pY1 - m.pY0)) (min m.pY1 (1 - m.pY0))

Pearl (2009), bounds (9.9) with P(y_x), P(y_x') in place of the conditional probabilities (the remark after the proof of Theorem 9.2.10), from the Fréchet bounds (9.10): max 0 (P(y_x) - P(y_x')) ≤ PNS ≤ min (P(y_x)) (1 - P(y_x')). Valid for every model.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.expCellsdefinition

def expCells (a b p : ℝ) : Bool → Bool → Bool → ℝ

The cell table of the sharpness witness for the experimental bounds: X is a fair coin independent of the response type, and the response types (Y0, Y1) = (0, 1), (1, 1), (1, 0), (0, 0) have masses p, a - p, b - a + p, 1 - b - p.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.exists_exogenous_of_mem_Icc_exptheorem

theorem exists_exogenous_of_mem_Icc_exp {a b p : ℝ}
  (hp : p ∈ Set.Icc (max 0 (a - b)) (min a (1 - b))) :
  ∃ m : ResponseModel, m.Exogenous ∧ m.pY1 = a ∧ m.pY0 = b ∧ m.PNS = p

Sharpness of the experimental bounds on PNS (Pearl 2009, Theorem 9.2.10, in the form with experimental quantities): for any a, b and any p with max 0 (a - b) ≤ p ≤ min a (1 - b) there is a model with P(y_x) = a, P(y_x') = b, PNS = p, in which moreover X is exogenous.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.identifiedSet_pns_exptheorem

theorem identifiedSet_pns_exp (a b : ℝ) :
  identifiedSet Set.univ expObs PNS (a, b) = Set.Icc (max 0 (a - b)) (min a (1 - b))

The identified set of PNS from experimental data alone is exactly the interval [max 0 (a - b), min a (1 - b)] at the experimental observation (P(y_x), P(y_x')) = (a, b). Both bounds are therefore sharp. (When (a, b) is not attainable, both sides are empty.)

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.CombinedDatastructure

structure CombinedData

The combined observation: the observational joint law of (X, Y) together with the experimental marginals P(y_x) and P(y_x').

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.combObsdefinition

def combObs (m : ResponseModel) : CombinedData

The combined observation of a model.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pns_mem_Icc_combtheorem

theorem pns_mem_Icc_comb (m : ResponseModel) :
  m.PNS ∈ Set.Icc (max (max (max 0 (m.pY1 - m.pY0)) (m.pY - m.pY0)) (m.pY1 - m.pY))
    (min (min (min m.pY1 (1 - m.pY0)) (m.pXY true true + m.pXY false false))
      (m.pY1 - m.pY0 + m.pXY true false + m.pXY false true))

Tian and Pearl bounds on PNS from combined data (Pearl 2009, equation (11.41)): max {0, P(y_x) - P(y_x'), P(y) - P(y_x'), P(y_x) - P(y)} ≤ PNS and PNS ≤ min {P(y_x), P(y'_x'), P(x, y) + P(x', y'), P(y_x) - P(y_x') + P(x, y') + P(x', y)}. Valid for every model.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pn_mem_Icc_combtheorem

theorem pn_mem_Icc_comb (m : ResponseModel) (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true) :
  m.PN ∈ Set.Icc (max 0 ((m.pY - m.pY0) / m.pXY true true))
    (min 1 ((1 - m.pY0 - m.pXY false false) / m.pXY true true))

Tian and Pearl bounds on PN from combined data (Pearl 2009, equation (11.42); Primer equation (4.30)): max {0, (P(y) - P(y_x')) / P(x, y)} ≤ PN ≤ min {1, (P(y'_x') - P(x', y')) / P(x, y)}, assuming P(x, y) > 0. The lower bound is the monotone estimand (9.29), which is thus a lower bound without monotonicity.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.ps_mem_Icc_combtheorem

theorem ps_mem_Icc_comb (m : ResponseModel) (h00 : 0 < m.pXY false false) :
  m.PS ∈ Set.Icc (max 0 ((m.pY1 - m.pY) / m.pXY false false))
    (min 1 ((m.pY1 - m.pXY true true) / m.pXY false false))

Tian and Pearl bounds on PS from combined data (Pearl 2009, equation (11.43)): max {0, (P(y_x) - P(y)) / P(x', y')} ≤ PS ≤ min {1, (P(y_x) - P(x, y)) / P(x', y')}, assuming P(x', y') > 0. The lower bound is the monotone estimand (9.30).

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.armCellsdefinition

def armCells (m : ResponseModel) (α β : ℝ) : Bool → Bool → Bool → ℝ

The cell table obtained from m by moving mass within each treatment arm so that the helped type (Y0, Y1) = (0, 1) has mass α in the arm X = 1 and β in the arm X = 0, keeping the observational law of (X, Y) and the experimental marginals.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.exists_combObs_eqtheorem

theorem exists_combObs_eq (m : ResponseModel) {α β : ℝ}
  (hα0 : 0 ≤ α) (hα1 : m.pY - m.pY0 ≤ α) (hα2 : α ≤ m.pXY true true)
  (hα3 : α ≤ 1 - m.pY0 - m.pXY false false)
  (hβ0 : 0 ≤ β) (hβ1 : m.pY1 - m.pY ≤ β) (hβ2 : β ≤ m.pY1 - m.pXY true true)
  (hβ3 : β ≤ m.pXY false false) :
  ∃ m' : ResponseModel, m'.combObs = m.combObs ∧ m'.w true false true = α ∧
    m'.w false false true = β

Every pair (α, β) of helped masses in the two arms that satisfies the stated linear constraints is realized by a model with the same combined observation as m. The constraints are exactly the nonnegativity of the eight cells of armCells m α β.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.eq_of_combObs_eqtheorem

theorem eq_of_combObs_eq {m m' : ResponseModel} (h : m'.combObs = m.combObs) :
  m'.pXY = m.pXY ∧ m'.pY1 = m.pY1 ∧ m'.pY0 = m.pY0 ∧ m'.pY = m.pY

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pn_lower_eq_err_add_cftheorem

theorem pn_lower_eq_err_add_cf (m : ResponseModel) (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true)
  (hx' : 0 < m.pX false) :
  (m.pY - m.pY0) / m.pXY true true = (m.condY true - m.condY false) / m.condY true +
    (m.condY false - m.pY0) / m.pXY true true

Primer equation (4.31), lower bound: the inner term (P(y) - P(y_x')) / P(x, y) of the lower bound (4.30) on PN equals ERR + CF, with excess risk ratio ERR = (P(y | x) - P(y | x')) / P(y | x) (4.33) and confounding factor CF = (P(y | x') - P(y_x')) / P(x, y) (4.32). Assumes P(x, y) > 0 and P(x') > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pn_upper_eq_err_add_q_add_cftheorem

theorem pn_upper_eq_err_add_q_add_cf (m : ResponseModel) (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true)
  (hx' : 0 < m.pX false) :
  (1 - m.pY0 - m.pXY false false) / m.pXY true true =
    (m.condY true - m.condY false) / m.condY true +
      m.pXY true false / m.pX true / m.condY true +
      (m.condY false - m.pY0) / m.pXY true true

Primer equation (4.31), upper bound: the inner term (P(y'_x') - P(x', y')) / P(x, y) of the upper bound (4.30) on PN equals ERR + q + CF, with q = P(y' | x) / P(y | x) (4.34). Assumes P(x, y) > 0 and P(x') > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.coinBetdefinition

def coinBet : ResponseModel

The coin bet model of Pearl (2009), Example 9.3.1: the bet X and the coin U are independent fair coins and Y = (X ∧ U) ∨ (¬X ∧ ¬U), so (Y0, Y1) = (¬U, U). Each cell with Y0 ≠ Y1 has mass 1/4.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.bookiedefinition

def bookie : ResponseModel

The bookie model of Pearl (2009), Example 9.3.1: the payoff ignores the bet, Y = U with U a fair coin independent of X, so (Y0, Y1) = (U, U). Each cell with Y0 = Y1 has mass 1/4.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.combObs_coinBet_eq_bookietheorem

theorem combObs_coinBet_eq_bookie : coinBet.combObs = bookie.combObs

The coin bet and the bookie agree on the observational law of (X, Y) (every cell 1/4) and on the experimental marginals (P(y_x) = P(y_x') = 1/2).

CausalInference.Attribution.Definitions

CausalInference/Attribution/Definitions.lean · 192 lines · 17 public theorems · 11 definitions

Probabilities of causation for a binary treatment and a binary outcome. A finite response-type model for a binary treatment X and a binary outcome Y. Each unit has a treatment X and a pair of potential outcomes (Y0, Y1), all Boolean. The model is a table of eight nonnegative weights w x y0 y1 summing to one: the joint law of (X, Y0, Y1). The observed outcome is Y = Y1 if X is true and Y = Y0 otherwise, so consistency is built in.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Pearl, Glymour and Jewell (2016)

Public declarations (28)

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModelstructure

structure ResponseModel

A finite response-type model for binary X and Y: a joint law of the treatment X and the potential outcomes (Y0, Y1), given as eight nonnegative weights w x y0 y1 summing to one.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.obsYdefinition

def obsY (x y0 y1 : Bool) : Bool

The observed outcome of a unit with treatment x and potential outcomes (y0, y1): Y = Y1 if x is true and Y = Y0 otherwise (consistency).

The probability of a Boolean event E of (X, Y0, Y1): the total weight of the cells on which E holds.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.PNdefinition

The probability of necessity (Pearl 2009, Definition 9.2.1): PN = P(Y0 = 0 | X = 1, Y = 1). It is meaningful only when P(X = 1, Y = 1) > 0, which every theorem about it assumes.

def PS : ℝ

The probability of sufficiency (Pearl 2009, Definition 9.2.2): PS = P(Y1 = 1 | X = 0, Y = 0). It is meaningful only when P(X = 0, Y = 0) > 0, which every theorem about it assumes.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.PNSdefinition

def PNS : ℝ

The probability of necessity and sufficiency (Pearl 2009, Definition 9.2.3): PNS = P(Y1 = 1, Y0 = 0).

  m.prob (fun x y0 y1 => y1 && !x && !obsY x y0 y1)

Division-free form of Pearl's Lemma 9.2.6: P(Y1 = 1, Y0 = 0) = P(Y0 = 0, X = 1, Y = 1) + P(Y1 = 1, X = 0, Y = 0). It follows from consistency alone.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pns_eq_pXY_mul_pn_addtheorem

theorem pns_eq_pXY_mul_pn_add (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true) (h00 : 0 < m.pXY false false) :
  m.PNS = m.pXY true true * m.PN + m.pXY false false * m.PS

Pearl (2009), Lemma 9.2.6, equation (9.5): PNS = P(x, y) PN + P(x', y') PS, assuming P(X = 1, Y = 1) > 0 and P(X = 0, Y = 0) > 0 so that PN and PS are genuine conditional probabilities.

Worked examples of probabilities of causation. The numerical examples of Pearl (2009), Section 9.3, and of the Primer, Section 4.5.1, checked by computation in the response-type model of CausalInference.Attribution.Definitions.

Sources: Pearl (2009); Pearl, Glymour and Jewell (2016)

In the coin bet model, P(y_x) = P(y_x') = P(y) = 1/2.

In the coin bet model, P(y | x) = P(y | x') = 1/2.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.firingSquaddefinition

def firingSquad : ResponseModel

The firing squad of Pearl (2009), Example 9.3.2. The court order U is a fair coin; rifleman A shoots (X) exactly when ordered; the prisoner dies (Y) if A or B shoots, and B shoots exactly when ordered. So Y1 = 1 and Y0 = U = X: the cell (X, Y0, Y1) = (1, 1, 1) and the cell (0, 0, 1) each have mass 1/2.

theorem firingSquad_pY1 : firingSquad.pY1 = 1

Equation (9.37): P(y_x) = 1.

theorem firingSquad_pY0 : firingSquad.pY0 = 1 / 2

Equation (9.38): P(y_x') = 1/2.

theorem firingSquad_pns : firingSquad.PNS = 1 / 2

Equation (9.39): PNS = 1/2.

theorem firingSquad_pn : firingSquad.PN = 0

PN = 0: rifleman A's shot was not necessary for the death.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.firingSquad_pstheorem

theorem firingSquad_ps : firingSquad.PS = 1

PS = 1: rifleman A's shot would have been sufficient.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.firingSquad_formulastheorem

theorem firingSquad_formulas :
  (firingSquad.pY - firingSquad.pY0) / firingSquad.pXY true true = 0 ∧
    (firingSquad.pY1 - firingSquad.pY) / firingSquad.pXY false false = 1

Equations (9.42), (9.43): the monotone formulas (9.29), (9.30) applied to the data P(x, y) = P(x', y') = 1/2, P(y_x) = 1, P(y_x') = 1/2 give PN = 0 and PS = 1.

Under exogeneity and monotonicity, the data of Table 9.1 (P(y | x) = 30/69160, P(y | x') = 16/59026) give PNS = 33211/204111908 (equation (9.45), exact value).

The response-type law of the radiation witness: monotone, with P(Y0 = 1, Y1 = 1) = 16/59026 and P(Y0 = 0, Y1 = 1) = 30/69160 - 16/59026.

A model realizing the hypotheses of radiation_pns, radiation_pn, radiation_ps: X is a fair coin independent of the response type radiationTypes.

Pearl (2009), Example 9.3.4, and Primer Example 4.5.1: with the data of Table 9.2 (P(x, y) = 2/2000, P(x', y) = 28/2000 observationally, P(y_x') = 14/1000 experimentally), every model has PN = 1. No monotonicity is assumed: the lower bound (11.42) equals one.

A model realizing the full data of Table 9.2: observationally P(x, y) = 1/1000, P(x, y') = 499/1000, P(x', y) = 14/1000, P(x', y') = 486/1000; experimentally P(y_x) = 16/1000, P(y_x') = 14/1000.

  ((16 / 1000 : ℝ) - 14 / 1000) / (16 / 1000) = 0.125

Equation (9.54): the experimental excess risk ratio (P(y_x) - P(y_x')) / P(y_x) = (0.016 - 0.014) / 0.016 = 0.125.

The coin bet model is exogenous (the bet is independent of the coin).

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.coinBet_pns_netheorem

theorem coinBet_pns_ne : coinBet.PNS ≠ coinBet.condY true - coinBet.condY false ∧
  coinBet.PNS ≠ coinBet.pY1 - coinBet.pY0

Without monotonicity, the risk difference formula (9.21) and the monotone formula (9.28) fail even under exogeneity: in the coin bet model PNS = 1/2, while P(y | x) - P(y | x') = P(y_x) - P(y_x') = 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.coinBet_pn_netheorem

theorem coinBet_pn_ne : coinBet.PN ≠ (coinBet.pY - coinBet.pY0) / coinBet.pXY true true

Without monotonicity, the formula (9.29) fails even under exogeneity: in the coin bet model PN = 1, while (P(y) - P(y_x')) / P(x, y) = 0.

theorem firingSquad_pns_ne :
  firingSquad.PNS ≠ firingSquad.condY true - firingSquad.condY false

Without exogeneity, the risk difference formula (9.21) fails even under monotonicity: in the firing squad PNS = 1/2, while P(y | x) - P(y | x') = 1.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.firingSquad_pn_netheorem

Without exogeneity, the relation (9.11) PN = PNS / P(y | x) fails: in the firing squad PN = 0, while PNS / P(y | x) = 1/2.

CausalInference.Attribution.Identification

CausalInference/Attribution/Identification.lean · 208 lines · 19 public theorems · 4 definitions · imports Attribution.Definitions

Identification of the probabilities of causation. Identification of PN, PS, PNS in the finite response-type model of CausalInference.Attribution.Definitions under two assumptions:

Sources: Pearl (2009); Pearl, Glymour and Jewell (2016)

Public declarations (23)

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pRdefinition

def pR (a b : Bool) : ℝ

The law of the response type: P(Y0 = a, Y1 = b).

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.Exogenousdefinition

def Exogenous : Prop

Exogeneity of X relative to Y (Pearl 2009, Definition 9.2.9): the pair of potential outcomes (Y0, Y1) is independent of X, that is, every cell weight factors as P(X = x) P(Y0 = y0, Y1 = y1).

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.Monotonicdefinition

def Monotonic : Prop

Monotonicity of Y relative to X (Pearl 2009, Definition 9.2.13): no unit would have Y = 1 without treatment and Y = 0 with it. In the weight model this is the vanishing of the weights of the response type Y0 = 1, Y1 = 0, for both values of X.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.condYdefinition

def condY (a : Bool) : ℝ

The observational conditional probability P(Y = 1 | X = a) = P(X = a, Y = 1) / P(X = a); meaningful only when P(X = a) > 0, which every theorem about it assumes.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pR_eqtheorem

theorem pR_eq (a b : Bool) : m.pR a b = m.w true a b + m.w false a b

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pXY_le_pXtheorem

theorem pXY_le_pX (a b : Bool) : m.pXY a b ≤ m.pX a

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pns_eq_of_monotonictheorem

theorem pns_eq_of_monotonic (hmono : m.Monotonic) : m.PNS = m.pY1 - m.pY0

Pearl (2009), equation (9.27), and Primer equation (4.42): under monotonicity, PNS = P(y_x) - P(y_x'), with no exogeneity assumption.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pn_eq_of_monotonictheorem

theorem pn_eq_of_monotonic (hmono : m.Monotonic) (_h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true) :
  m.PN = (m.pY - m.pY0) / m.pXY true true

Pearl (2009), Theorem 9.2.15, equation (9.29), and Primer Theorem 4.5.1, equation (4.28): under monotonicity, PN = (P(y) - P(y_x')) / P(x, y), assuming P(x, y) > 0. The experimental quantity P(y_x') and the observational law of (X, Y) identify PN.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.ps_eq_of_monotonictheorem

theorem ps_eq_of_monotonic (hmono : m.Monotonic) (_h00 : 0 < m.pXY false false) :
  m.PS = (m.pY1 - m.pY) / m.pXY false false

Pearl (2009), Theorem 9.2.15, equation (9.30): under monotonicity, PS = (P(y_x) - P(y)) / P(x', y'), assuming P(x', y') > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pX_add_pXtheorem

theorem pX_add_pX : m.pX true + m.pX false = 1

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pX_true_postheorem

theorem pX_true_pos (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true) : 0 < m.pX true

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pX_false_postheorem

theorem pX_false_pos (h00 : 0 < m.pXY false false) : 0 < m.pX false

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pn_eq_err_add_of_monotonictheorem

theorem pn_eq_err_add_of_monotonic (hmono : m.Monotonic) (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true)
  (hx' : 0 < m.pX false) :
  m.PN = (m.condY true - m.condY false) / m.condY true +
    (m.condY false - m.pY0) / m.pXY true true

Pearl (2009), equation (9.31), and Primer Theorem 4.5.1, equation (4.29): under monotonicity, PN is the excess risk ratio (P(y | x) - P(y | x')) / P(y | x) plus the confounding correction (P(y | x') - P(y_x')) / P(x, y). Assumes P(x, y) > 0 and P(x') > 0 so that every conditional probability is genuine.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pY1_eq_pRtheorem

theorem pY1_eq_pR : m.pY1 = m.pR false true + m.pR true true

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pY0_eq_pRtheorem

theorem pY0_eq_pR : m.pY0 = m.pR true false + m.pR true true

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.one_sub_pY0_eq_pRtheorem

theorem one_sub_pY0_eq_pR : 1 - m.pY0 = m.pR false false + m.pR false true

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.condY_true_of_exogenoustheorem

theorem condY_true_of_exogenous (hexo : m.Exogenous) (hx : 0 < m.pX true) :
  m.condY true = m.pY1

Pearl (2009), equation (9.8): under exogeneity, P(y_x) = P(y | x), assuming P(x) > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.condY_false_of_exogenoustheorem

theorem condY_false_of_exogenous (hexo : m.Exogenous) (hx' : 0 < m.pX false) :
  m.condY false = m.pY0

Pearl (2009), equation (9.8) for the control arm: under exogeneity, P(y_x') = P(y | x'), assuming P(x') > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pn_eq_pns_div_of_exogenoustheorem

theorem pn_eq_pns_div_of_exogenous (hexo : m.Exogenous) (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true) :
  m.PN = m.PNS / m.condY true

Pearl (2009), Theorem 9.2.11, equation (9.11): under exogeneity, PN = PNS / P(y | x), assuming P(x, y) > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.ps_eq_pns_div_of_exogenoustheorem

theorem ps_eq_pns_div_of_exogenous (hexo : m.Exogenous) (h00 : 0 < m.pXY false false) :
  m.PS = m.PNS / (1 - m.condY false)

Pearl (2009), Theorem 9.2.11, equation (9.12): under exogeneity, PS = PNS / P(y' | x') = PNS / (1 - P(y | x')), assuming P(x', y') > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pns_eq_of_exogenous_of_monotonictheorem

theorem pns_eq_of_exogenous_of_monotonic (hexo : m.Exogenous) (hmono : m.Monotonic)
  (hx : 0 < m.pX true) (hx' : 0 < m.pX false) :
  m.PNS = m.condY true - m.condY false

Pearl (2009), Theorem 9.2.14, equation (9.21): under exogeneity and monotonicity, PNS is the risk difference P(y | x) - P(y | x'), assuming P(x) > 0 and P(x') > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.pn_eq_of_exogenous_of_monotonictheorem

theorem pn_eq_of_exogenous_of_monotonic (hexo : m.Exogenous) (hmono : m.Monotonic)
  (h11 : 0 < m.pXY true true) (hx' : 0 < m.pX false) :
  m.PN = (m.condY true - m.condY false) / m.condY true

Pearl (2009), Theorem 9.2.14, equation (9.22): under exogeneity and monotonicity, PN is the excess risk ratio (P(y | x) - P(y | x')) / P(y | x), assuming P(x, y) > 0 and P(x') > 0.

CausalInference.Attribution.ResponseModel.ps_eq_of_exogenous_of_monotonictheorem

theorem ps_eq_of_exogenous_of_monotonic (hexo : m.Exogenous) (hmono : m.Monotonic)
  (h00 : 0 < m.pXY false false) (hx : 0 < m.pX true) :
  m.PS = (m.condY true - m.condY false) / (1 - m.condY false)

Pearl (2009), Theorem 9.2.14, equation (9.23): under exogeneity and monotonicity, PS is the relative difference (P(y | x) - P(y | x')) / (1 - P(y | x')), assuming P(x', y') > 0 and P(x) > 0.

Interaction

Counterfactual response types, additive interaction, sufficient-component causes, excess fractions and empirical tests for synergism.

CausalInference.Interaction.ExcessFraction

CausalInference/Interaction/ExcessFraction.lean · 110 lines · 4 public theorems · 6 definitions · imports Interaction.Synergism

Excess fractions for two treatments. Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If (2020), Fine Point 5.4 (and Fine Point 3.5 for the definition). With deterministic counterfactuals, observed treatments A, E and observed outcome Y = Y^{A,E}, the excess fraction for a (single or joint) intervention is the share of the observed cases that would not occur under that intervention: (Pr[Y = 1] - Pr[Y^{intervention} = 1]) / Pr[Y = 1]. Intervening on A alone leaves E at its observed value, so Y^{a=0} = Y^{0,E}.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020)

Public declarations (10)

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.obsRiskdefinition

def obsRisk : ℝ

The observed risk Pr[Y = 1] with Y = Y^{A,E} (consistency).

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.riskA0definition

def riskA0 : ℝ

The risk Pr[Y^{a=0} = 1] when everybody is set to a = 0 and E keeps its observed value.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.riskE0definition

def riskE0 : ℝ

The risk Pr[Y^{e=0} = 1] when everybody is set to e = 0 and A keeps its observed value.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.excessFractionAdefinition

def excessFractionA : ℝ

The excess fraction for A: (Pr[Y = 1] - Pr[Y^{a=0} = 1]) / Pr[Y = 1].

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.excessFractionEdefinition

def excessFractionE : ℝ

The excess fraction for E: (Pr[Y = 1] - Pr[Y^{e=0} = 1]) / Pr[Y = 1].

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.excessFractionJointdefinition

def excessFractionJoint : ℝ

The excess fraction for the joint intervention a = 0, e = 0: (Pr[Y = 1] - Pr[Y^{0,0} = 1]) / Pr[Y = 1].

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.excessFractionA_le_onetheorem

theorem excessFractionA_le_one (h : 0 < P.obsRisk A E) : P.excessFractionA A E ≤ 1

The excess fraction for A is at most one, provided Pr[Y = 1] > 0 (What If, Fine Point 5.4). It can be negative, when A prevents more cases than it causes.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.excessFractionE_le_onetheorem

theorem excessFractionE_le_one (h : 0 < P.obsRisk A E) : P.excessFractionE A E ≤ 1

The excess fraction for E is at most one, provided Pr[Y = 1] > 0.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.excessFractionJoint_le_onetheorem

theorem excessFractionJoint_le_one (h : 0 < P.obsRisk A E) : P.excessFractionJoint A E ≤ 1

The excess fraction for the joint intervention on A and E is at most one, provided Pr[Y = 1] > 0 (What If, Fine Point 5.4).

CausalInference.Interaction.excessFractions_sum_gt_onetheorem

theorem excessFractions_sum_gt_one :
  let P := pointPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
  0 < P.obsRisk (fun _ => true) (fun _ => true) ∧
    P.excessFractionA (fun _ => true) (fun _ => true) = 1 ∧
    P.excessFractionE (fun _ => true) (fun _ => true) = 1 ∧
    1 < P.excessFractionA (fun _ => true) (fun _ => true) +
      P.excessFractionE (fun _ => true) (fun _ => true) ∧
    P.excessFractionJoint (fun _ => true) (fun _ => true) = 1

Fine Point 5.4 of What If: excess fractions do not add. When everybody has type 8 (1000, the outcome only under joint exposure, as for an individual whose only background factor is U5) and receives A = 1 and E = 1, there are cases (Pr[Y = 1] = 1), the excess fractions of A and of E are both one, so their sum is two, while the joint excess fraction is one.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseTypes

CausalInference/Interaction/ResponseTypes.lean · 341 lines · 20 public theorems · 17 definitions

Counterfactual response types and additive interaction. Deterministic counterfactual response types for two binary treatments A, E and a binary outcome Y (Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If, 2020, Chapter 5, Sections 5.1 and 5.3, Technical Point 5.1).

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Miettinen (1982); Greenland and Poole (1988)

Public declarations (37)

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseTypedefinition

abbrev ResponseType

A deterministic counterfactual response type for two binary treatments: r a e is the outcome Y^{a,e} under the joint intervention setting A = a and E = e.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.ofBitsdefinition

def ofBits (y11 y01 y10 y00 : Bool) : ResponseType

The response type with Y^{11} = y11, Y^{01} = y01, Y^{10} = y10, Y^{00} = y00, in the column order of Table 5.2 of What If.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.eq_ofBitstheorem

theorem eq_ofBits (r : ResponseType) :
  r = ofBits (r true true) (r false true) (r true false) (r false false)

Every response type is determined by its four counterfactual outcomes.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.forall_ifftheorem

theorem forall_iff {P : ResponseType → Prop} :
  (∀ r, P r) ↔ ∀ y11 y01 y10 y00 : Bool, P (ofBits y11 y01 y10 y00)

To prove a property of all 16 response types it suffices to check the 16 bit patterns.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.bookNumberdefinition

def bookNumber (r : ResponseType) : ℕ

The number of a response type in Table 5.2 of What If: reading the outcomes Y^{11} Y^{01} Y^{10} Y^{00} as a binary number n, the type number is 16 - n. Thus type 1 is 1111 (doomed), type 8 is 1000, and type 16 is 0000 (immune).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.bookNumber_memtheorem

theorem bookNumber_mem (r : ResponseType) : bookNumber r ∈ Finset.Icc 1 16

The book numbering is a bijection onto 1, ..., 16: it takes values in that range.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.bookNumber_injectivetheorem

theorem bookNumber_injective : Function.Injective bookNumber

The book numbering is injective.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.indContrastdefinition

def indContrast (r : ResponseType) : ℤ

The individual interaction contrast Y^{11} - Y^{01} - Y^{10} + Y^{00} of a response type, as an integer.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.effectAdefinition

def effectA (r : ResponseType) (e : Bool) : ℤ

The individual causal effect of A at a fixed level e of E, Y^{1,e} - Y^{0,e}.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.effectEdefinition

def effectE (r : ResponseType) (a : Bool) : ℤ

The individual causal effect of E at a fixed level a of A, Y^{a,1} - Y^{a,0}.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.NoIndividualInteractiondefinition

def NoIndividualInteraction (r : ResponseType) : Prop

No individual interaction (What If, Section 5.3): for this type the causal effect of A is the same whatever the value of E, and the causal effect of E is the same whatever the value of A.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.noIndividualInteraction_iff_indContrasttheorem

theorem noIndividualInteraction_iff_indContrast (r : ResponseType) :
  NoIndividualInteraction r ↔ indContrast r = 0

Either half of the definition suffices: the effect of A does not depend on E exactly when the individual contrast vanishes, and likewise for E.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.noIndividualInteraction_iff_bookNumbertheorem

theorem noIndividualInteraction_iff_bookNumber (r : ResponseType) :
  NoIndividualInteraction r ↔ bookNumber r ∈ ({1, 4, 6, 11, 13, 16} : Finset ℕ)

Exactly the types numbered 1, 4, 6, 11, 13, 16 in Table 5.2 of What If have no individual interaction: the doomed 1111, the immune 0000, and the types 1100, 1010, 0101, 0011 in which only one of the two treatments matters.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.numCasesdefinition

def numCases (r : ResponseType) : ℕ

The number of the four joint interventions under which the outcome occurs.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.Class1definition

def Class1 (r : ResponseType) : Prop

Greenland and Poole class 1: the outcome occurs under exactly one of the four joint interventions (types 8, 12, 14, 15 of Table 5.2).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.Class2definition

def Class2 (r : ResponseType) : Prop

Greenland and Poole class 2: the outcome occurs under exactly two joint interventions, and the effect of each treatment is reversed by the other (types 7 and 10 of Table 5.2).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.Class3definition

def Class3 (r : ResponseType) : Prop

Greenland and Poole class 3: the outcome occurs under exactly three of the four joint interventions (types 2, 3, 5, 9 of Table 5.2).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.class_iff_bookNumbertheorem

theorem class_iff_bookNumber (r : ResponseType) :
  (Class1 r ↔ bookNumber r ∈ ({8, 12, 14, 15} : Finset ℕ)) ∧
  (Class2 r ↔ bookNumber r ∈ ({7, 10} : Finset ℕ)) ∧
  (Class3 r ↔ bookNumber r ∈ ({2, 3, 5, 9} : Finset ℕ))

The book numbers of the three classes (What If, Section 5.3).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.not_noIndividualInteraction_iff_classtheorem

theorem not_noIndividualInteraction_iff_class (r : ResponseType) :
  ¬ NoIndividualInteraction r ↔ Class1 r ∨ Class2 r ∨ Class3 r

A type has individual interaction exactly when it lies in one of the three classes of Greenland and Poole (What If, Section 5.3).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.recodeAdefinition

def recodeA (r : ResponseType) : ResponseType

Recoding of A: the labels 0 and 1 of the first treatment are switched.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.recodeEdefinition

def recodeE (r : ResponseType) : ResponseType

Recoding of E: the labels 0 and 1 of the second treatment are switched.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.noIndividualInteraction_recodeAtheorem

theorem noIndividualInteraction_recodeA (r : ResponseType) :
  NoIndividualInteraction (recodeA r) ↔ NoIndividualInteraction r

Absence of individual interaction is invariant under recoding of A.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.noIndividualInteraction_recodeEtheorem

theorem noIndividualInteraction_recodeE (r : ResponseType) :
  NoIndividualInteraction (recodeE r) ↔ NoIndividualInteraction r

Absence of individual interaction is invariant under recoding of E.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.class1_recodetheorem

theorem class1_recode (r : ResponseType) :
  (Class1 (recodeA r) ↔ Class1 r) ∧ (Class1 (recodeE r) ↔ Class1 r)

Class 1 is invariant under recoding of A and of E (Greenland and Poole, 1988).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.class2_recodetheorem

theorem class2_recode (r : ResponseType) :
  (Class2 (recodeA r) ↔ Class2 r) ∧ (Class2 (recodeE r) ↔ Class2 r)

Class 2 is invariant under recoding of A and of E (Greenland and Poole, 1988).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.class3_recodetheorem

theorem class3_recode (r : ResponseType) :
  (Class3 (recodeA r) ↔ Class3 r) ∧ (Class3 (recodeE r) ↔ Class3 r)

Class 3 is invariant under recoding of A and of E (Greenland and Poole, 1988).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.bookNumber_recodeA_ofBitstheorem

theorem bookNumber_recodeA_ofBits :
  bookNumber (ofBits true false true false) = 6 ∧
    bookNumber (recodeA (ofBits true false true false)) = 11

In contrast, the book numbering of Miettinen is not invariant under recoding: recoding A sends type 6 (1010, only A matters) to type 11 (0101).

CausalInference.Interaction.Populationstructure

structure Population (ι : Type*) [Fintype ι]

A finite population of individuals for two binary treatments: nonnegative weights summing to one and a deterministic response type for each individual. With ι = ResponseType and resp = id this is a probability distribution over the 16 response types.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.riskdefinition

def risk (a e : Bool) : ℝ

The counterfactual risk p a e = Pr[Y^{a,e} = 1].

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.interactionContrastdefinition

def interactionContrast : ℝ

The additive interaction contrast IC = p11 - p10 - p01 + p00 (What If, Section 5.1).

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.additive_interaction_ifftheorem

theorem additive_interaction_iff :
  (P.risk true true - P.risk false true ≠ P.risk true false - P.risk false false ↔
      P.interactionContrast ≠ 0) ∧
    (P.risk true true - P.risk true false ≠ P.risk false true - P.risk false false ↔
      P.interactionContrast ≠ 0) ∧
    (P.risk true true - P.risk false false ≠
        (P.risk true false - P.risk false false) + (P.risk false true - P.risk false false) ↔
      P.interactionContrast ≠ 0)

The three equivalent forms of additive interaction (What If, Section 5.1 and Technical Point 5.1): the effect of A differs across levels of E, the effect of E differs across levels of A, and the joint effect is not the sum of the separate effects; each is equivalent to a nonzero interaction contrast.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.additive_interaction_iff'theorem

theorem additive_interaction_iff' :
  (P.risk true true - P.risk false false >
      (P.risk true false - P.risk false false) + (P.risk false true - P.risk false false) ↔
    0 < P.interactionContrast) ∧
  (P.risk true true - P.risk false false <
      (P.risk true false - P.risk false false) + (P.risk false true - P.risk false false) ↔
    P.interactionContrast < 0)

Superadditive interaction (the joint effect exceeds the sum of the separate effects) is a positive interaction contrast; subadditive interaction is a negative one (What If, Technical Point 5.1).

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.interactionContrast_eq_sumtheorem

theorem interactionContrast_eq_sum :
  P.interactionContrast = ∑ i, P.weight i * ((ResponseType.indContrast (P.resp i) : ℤ) : ℝ)

The interaction contrast is the population mean of the individual contrasts.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.interactionContrast_eq_zero_of_noInteractiontheorem

theorem interactionContrast_eq_zero_of_noInteraction
  (h : ∀ i, 0 < P.weight i → ResponseType.NoIndividualInteraction (P.resp i)) :
  P.interactionContrast = 0

If every individual of positive mass has a type without individual interaction (types 1, 4, 6, 11, 13, 16), there is no additive interaction (What If, Section 5.3).

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.exists_interacting_of_interactionContrast_ne_zerotheorem

theorem exists_interacting_of_interactionContrast_ne_zero (h : P.interactionContrast ≠ 0) :
  ∃ i, 0 < P.weight i ∧ ¬ ResponseType.NoIndividualInteraction (P.resp i)

A nonzero additive interaction contrast forces positive mass on some type with individual interaction, that is, on one of the Greenland and Poole classes (types 8, 12, 14, 15; 7, 10; or 2, 3, 5, 9) (What If, Section 5.3).

CausalInference.Interaction.cancellationPopulationdefinition

def cancellationPopulation : Population Bool

The population with mass 1/2 on type 7 (1001) and mass 1/2 on type 10 (0110) of Table 5.2: both types interact, but their deviations from additivity cancel.

CausalInference.Interaction.cancellation_exampletheorem

theorem cancellation_example :
  (∀ i, 0 < cancellationPopulation.weight i ∧
      ¬ ResponseType.NoIndividualInteraction (cancellationPopulation.resp i)) ∧
    cancellationPopulation.interactionContrast = 0

The converse of Population.exists_interacting_of_interactionContrast_ne_zero fails: in cancellationPopulation every individual has a type with individual interaction (types 7 and 10) and positive mass, yet the additive interaction contrast is zero (What If, Section 5.3: "an equal proportion of individuals of types 7 and 10").

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses

CausalInference/Interaction/SufficientCauses.lean · 241 lines · 11 public theorems · 8 definitions · imports Interaction.Synergism

Sufficient-component causes. The sufficient-component-cause model for binary treatments and a binary outcome (Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If (2020), Sections 5.4 and 5.5, Fine Point 5.2, Technical Point 5.3; Rothman 1976; Greenland and Poole 1988; VanderWeele and Robins 2007, 2008).

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); Greenland and Poole (1988); Rothman (1976); VanderWeele and Robins (2007); VanderWeele and Robins (2008)

Public declarations (19)

CausalInference.Interaction.OneSufficientCausesstructure

structure OneSufficientCauses

A background-factor configuration for one binary treatment: u0 completes the sufficient cause that needs no treatment component, u1 the one with component A = 1, and u2 the one with component A = 0.

CausalInference.Interaction.OneSufficientCauses.responsedefinition

def response (U : OneSufficientCauses) : Bool → Bool

The counterfactual outcome Y^a = U0 ∨ (a ∧ U1) ∨ (¬a ∧ U2) (What If, Section 5.4).

CausalInference.Interaction.OneSufficientCauses.response_eq_ifftheorem

theorem response_eq_iff (U : OneSufficientCauses) :
  (U.response = (fun _ => true) ↔ U.u0 = true ∨ (U.u1 = true ∧ U.u2 = true)) ∧
  (U.response = (fun a => !a) ↔ U.u0 = false ∧ U.u1 = false ∧ U.u2 = true) ∧
  (U.response = (fun a => a) ↔ U.u0 = false ∧ U.u1 = true ∧ U.u2 = false) ∧
  (U.response = (fun _ => false) ↔ U.u0 = false ∧ U.u1 = false ∧ U.u2 = false)

The table of What If, Fine Point 5.2, for one treatment (Table 5.1 types: doomed 11, helped Y^0 = 1, Y^1 = 0, hurt Y^0 = 0, Y^1 = 1, immune 00).

CausalInference.Interaction.OneSufficientCauses.response_surjectivetheorem

theorem response_surjective : Function.Surjective response

Every one-treatment response type arises from a configuration of background factors.

CausalInference.Interaction.OneSufficientCauses.not_injectivetheorem

theorem not_injective : ¬ Function.Injective response

A response type may arise from several configurations: U0 = 1 alone and U1 = U2 = 1 both give the doomed type (What If, Fine Point 5.2).

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCausesstructure

structure SufficientCauses

A background-factor configuration for two binary treatments: uk = true means the background factors Uk completing the kth sufficient cause are present. The treatment components are: none for u0; A = 1 for u1; A = 0 for u2; E = 1 for u3; E = 0 for u4; A = 1, E = 1 for u5; A = 1, E = 0 for u6; A = 0, E = 1 for u7; A = 0, E = 0 for u8.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.responsedefinition

def response (U : SufficientCauses) : ResponseType

The response type determined by a configuration: the outcome occurs under (a, e) when some present sufficient cause has all its treatment components satisfied (What If, Section 5.4).

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.ofResponsedefinition

def ofResponse (r : ResponseType) : SufficientCauses

The configuration using only the four sufficient causes with two treatment components, present exactly where the response type has outcome 1.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.response_ofResponsetheorem

theorem response_ofResponse (r : ResponseType) : (ofResponse r).response = r

Every one of the 16 response types arises from some configuration (What If, Section 5.4; Greenland and Poole, 1988).

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.response_surjectivetheorem

theorem response_surjective : Function.Surjective response

The map from configurations to response types is onto.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.not_injectivetheorem

theorem not_injective : ¬ Function.Injective response

The map from configurations to response types is not one to one: U0 = 1 alone and U1 = U2 = 1 both give type 1 (doomed).

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.HasSynergismdefinition

def HasSynergism (U : SufficientCauses) : Prop

Sufficient cause interaction in the form of synergism (What If, Section 5.5): A = 1 and E = 1 are components of a common present sufficient cause.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.hasSynergism_of_isSynergistictheorem

theorem hasSynergism_of_isSynergistic (U : SufficientCauses)
  (h : ResponseType.IsSynergistic U.response) : U.HasSynergism

Section 5.5 of What If (VanderWeele and Robins, 2007): if an individual has Y^{11} = 1 and Y^{01} = Y^{10} = 0 (types 7 and 8), then every sufficient-cause representation of that individual contains a sufficient cause with both A = 1 and E = 1.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.NoNegativeComponentdefinition

def NoNegativeComponent (U : SufficientCauses) : Prop

No present sufficient cause has a component A = 0 or E = 0.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.monoOfResponsedefinition

def monoOfResponse (r : ResponseType) : SufficientCauses

The configuration used for monotone types: U0 = Y^{00}, U1 = Y^{10}, U3 = Y^{01}, U5 = Y^{11}, all other background factors absent.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.isMonotone_ifftheorem

theorem isMonotone_iff (r : ResponseType) :
  ResponseType.IsMonotone r ↔ ∃ U : SufficientCauses, U.NoNegativeComponent ∧ U.response = r

Technical Point 5.3 of What If, in its exact form: a response type has monotone effects of A and E if and only if it is the response of some configuration in which no sufficient cause contains A = 0 or E = 0. So such causes are never needed under monotonicity.

CausalInference.Interaction.SufficientCauses.monotone_with_negative_componenttheorem

theorem monotone_with_negative_component :
  ResponseType.IsMonotone ({ u5 := true, u6 := true } : SufficientCauses).response ∧
    ¬ ({ u5 := true, u6 := true } : SufficientCauses).NoNegativeComponent ∧
    ({ u5 := true } : SufficientCauses).response ≠
      ({ u5 := true, u6 := true } : SufficientCauses).response

Technical Point 5.3 cannot be read as saying that sufficient causes with A = 0 or E = 0 are never present under monotonicity. The configuration with U5 = U6 = 1 has a monotone response (type 6, 1010: only A matters), contains the sufficient cause {A = 1, E = 0}, and removing that cause changes the response.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.exists_synergism_of_risk_sub_postheorem

theorem exists_synergism_of_risk_sub_pos (cfg : ι → SufficientCauses)
  (hcfg : ∀ i, (cfg i).response = P.resp i)
  (h : 0 < P.risk true true - P.risk false true - P.risk true false) :
  ∃ i, 0 < P.weight i ∧ (cfg i).HasSynergism

The first test of Fine Point 5.1 detects sufficient cause interaction (What If, Section 5.5): if p11 - p01 - p10 > 0, then in every sufficient-cause representation cfg of the population some individual of positive mass has a present sufficient cause containing both A = 1 and E = 1.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.exists_synergism_of_interactionContrast_postheorem

theorem exists_synergism_of_interactionContrast_pos (cfg : ι → SufficientCauses)
  (hcfg : ∀ i, (cfg i).response = P.resp i)
  (hm : ∀ i, 0 < P.weight i → ResponseType.IsMonotone (P.resp i))
  (h : 0 < P.interactionContrast) :
  ∃ i, 0 < P.weight i ∧ (cfg i).HasSynergism

The second test of Fine Point 5.1 detects sufficient cause interaction: if every individual of positive mass is monotone and IC > 0, then in every sufficient-cause representation some individual of positive mass has a present sufficient cause containing both A = 1 and E = 1.

CausalInference.Interaction.Synergism

CausalInference/Interaction/Synergism.lean · 215 lines · 11 public theorems · 5 definitions · imports Interaction.ResponseTypes

Empirical tests for synergism. Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If (2020), Fine Point 5.1 and Technical Point 5.2, after VanderWeele and Robins (2007, 2008) and Greenland, Lash and Rothman (2008).

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020); VanderWeele and Robins (2007); VanderWeele and Robins (2008); Greenland, Lash and Rothman (2008)

Public declarations (16)

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.IsSynergisticdefinition

def IsSynergistic (r : ResponseType) : Prop

Synergism of a response type in the sense of What If, Fine Point 5.1: the outcome occurs under joint exposure A = 1, E = 1 but under neither single exposure. These are types 7 and 8 of Table 5.2.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.IsType8definition

def IsType8 (r : ResponseType) : Prop

Type 8 of Table 5.2: the outcome occurs only under joint exposure (the form of interaction called compositional epistasis in genetics).

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.IsMonotonedefinition

def IsMonotone (r : ResponseType) : Prop

Monotonicity of the effects of both treatments (What If, Technical Point 5.2): the counterfactual outcome is nondecreasing in a at each e, and in e at each a.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.isSynergistic_iff_bookNumbertheorem

theorem isSynergistic_iff_bookNumber (r : ResponseType) :
  IsSynergistic r ↔ bookNumber r ∈ ({7, 8} : Finset ℕ)

The synergistic types are exactly types 7 and 8 of Table 5.2.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.IsType8.isSynergistictheorem

theorem IsType8.isSynergistic {r : ResponseType} (h : IsType8 r) : IsSynergistic r

Type 8 is synergistic.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.isType8_of_isMonotone_of_isSynergistictheorem

theorem isType8_of_isMonotone_of_isSynergistic (r : ResponseType) (hm : IsMonotone r)
  (hs : IsSynergistic r) : IsType8 r

Monotonicity rules out type 7 (What If, Fine Point 5.1): a monotone synergistic type is type 8.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.toNat_le_of_not_isSynergistictheorem

theorem toNat_le_of_not_isSynergistic (r : ResponseType) (h : ¬ IsSynergistic r) :
  (r true true).toNat ≤ (r false true).toNat + (r true false).toNat

Pointwise core of the first test: for a type that is not synergistic, Y^{11} ≤ Y^{01} + Y^{10}.

CausalInference.Interaction.ResponseType.indContrast_nonpos_of_isMonotonetheorem

theorem indContrast_nonpos_of_isMonotone (r : ResponseType) (hm : IsMonotone r)
  (h : ¬ IsType8 r) : indContrast r ≤ 0

Pointwise core of the second test: a monotone type other than type 8 has a nonpositive individual interaction contrast.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.exists_synergistic_of_risk_sub_postheorem

theorem exists_synergistic_of_risk_sub_pos
  (h : 0 < P.risk true true - P.risk false true - P.risk true false) :
  ∃ i, 0 < P.weight i ∧ ResponseType.IsSynergistic (P.resp i)

The first empirical test for synergism (What If, Fine Point 5.1; VanderWeele and Robins): if Pr[Y^{11} = 1] - Pr[Y^{01} = 1] - Pr[Y^{10} = 1] > 0, then some individual of positive mass has Y^{11} = 1 and Y^{01} = Y^{10} = 0 (type 7 or 8). No monotonicity is assumed.

CausalInference.Interaction.Population.exists_type8_of_interactionContrast_postheorem

theorem exists_type8_of_interactionContrast_pos
  (hm : ∀ i, 0 < P.weight i → ResponseType.IsMonotone (P.resp i))
  (h : 0 < P.interactionContrast) :
  ∃ i, 0 < P.weight i ∧ ResponseType.IsType8 (P.resp i)

The second empirical test for synergism (What If, Fine Point 5.1; Greenland, Lash and Rothman, 2008): if every individual of positive mass has monotone effects of both treatments, then superadditive interaction IC > 0 implies positive mass on type 8.

CausalInference.Interaction.pointPopulationdefinition

def pointPopulation (r : ResponseType) : Population Unit

The population in which every individual has the single response type r.

CausalInference.Interaction.halfPopulationdefinition

def halfPopulation (r s : ResponseType) : Population Bool

The population with mass 1/2 on each of two response types r and s.

CausalInference.Interaction.monotonicity_neededtheorem

theorem monotonicity_needed :
  0 < (pointPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits false false false true)).interactionContrast ∧
    ∀ i, ¬ ResponseType.IsSynergistic
      ((pointPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits false false false true)).resp i)

Monotonicity cannot be dropped from the second test: when everyone has type 15 (0001, the outcome occurs only under no exposure), IC = 1 > 0, yet nobody is synergistic.

CausalInference.Interaction.oneSidedMonotonicity_not_enoughtheorem

theorem oneSidedMonotonicity_not_enough :
  (∀ a, ResponseType.ofBits true true false true a false ≤
      ResponseType.ofBits true true false true a true) ∧
    0 < (pointPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true true false true)).interactionContrast ∧
    ∀ i, ¬ ResponseType.IsSynergistic
      ((pointPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true true false true)).resp i)

Monotonicity in one treatment only is not enough: type 3 (1101) is monotone in E at each level of A, has IC = 1 > 0, and is not synergistic.

CausalInference.Interaction.riskTest_not_necessarytheorem

theorem riskTest_not_necessary :
  (∃ i, 0 < (halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
      (ResponseType.ofBits true true true true)).weight i ∧
      ResponseType.IsSynergistic ((halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true true)).resp i)) ∧
    (∀ i, ResponseType.IsMonotone ((halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true true)).resp i)) ∧
    (halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true true)).risk true true -
      (halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true true)).risk false true -
      (halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true true)).risk true false = 0

The first test is sufficient but not necessary (What If, Fine Point 5.1): with mass 1/2 on type 8 and 1/2 on type 1 (doomed), synergism is present, every individual is monotone, and yet p11 - p01 - p10 = 0.

CausalInference.Interaction.icTest_not_necessarytheorem

theorem icTest_not_necessary :
  (∃ i, 0 < (halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
      (ResponseType.ofBits true true true false)).weight i ∧
      ResponseType.IsType8 ((halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true false)).resp i)) ∧
    (∀ i, ResponseType.IsMonotone ((halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true false)).resp i)) ∧
    (halfPopulation (ResponseType.ofBits true false false false)
        (ResponseType.ofBits true true true false)).interactionContrast = 0

The second test is also not necessary: with mass 1/2 on type 8 and 1/2 on type 2 (1110), every individual is monotone and type 8 has positive mass, yet IC = 0.

Estimation

Estimators, consistency, asymptotic linearity and confidence intervals.

CausalInference.Estimation.AsymptoticLinear

CausalInference/Estimation/AsymptoticLinear.lean · 352 lines · 14 public theorems · 1 definition · imports Estimation.Consistency

Asymptotically linear estimators. An estimator sequence θhat is asymptotically linear at θ with influence function φ when E φ(O) = 0, φ(O) has a finite second moment, and the remainder √n (θhat n - θ) - n^{-1/2} ∑_{i < n} φ(O i) tends to zero in probability.

Sources: van der Vaart (1998); Tsiatis (2006)

Public declarations (15)

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinearstructure

structure IsAsymptoticallyLinear (θhat : ℕ → Ω → ℝ) (θ : ℝ) (φ : 𝒪 → ℝ) (O : ℕ → Ω → 𝒪)
  (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] : Prop

The estimator sequence θhat is asymptotically linear at θ with influence function φ for the sample O under the probability measure μ: φ is measurable, φ (O 0) is square integrable with mean zero, and the remainder √n (θhat n - θ) - n^{-1/2} ∑_{i < n} φ (O i) converges to 0 in probability. The predicate is only formed for a probability measure μ. On an infinite measure a square integrable φ (O 0) need not be integrable, and then the mean zero condition would hold by the convention that the integral of a non-integrable function is 0; on a probability measure the second moment condition implies integrability, so the mean zero condition is genuine. The predicate does not ask θhat n to depend only on the first n observations; the corollaries with suffix _of_isSampleMeasurable add that requirement (IsSampleMeasurable θhat O).

CausalInference.sqrt_mul_inv_selftheorem

lemma sqrt_mul_inv_self (x : ℝ) : √x * x⁻¹ = (√x)⁻¹

√n * n⁻¹ = (√n)⁻¹, including at n = 0.

CausalInference.inv_sqrt_mul_selftheorem

lemma inv_sqrt_mul_self (x : ℝ) (hx : 0 ≤ x) : (√x)⁻¹ * x = √x

(√n)⁻¹ * n = √n, including at n = 0.

CausalInference.sampleMean_isAsymptoticallyLineartheorem

theorem sampleMean_isAsymptoticallyLinear {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
  {O : ℕ → Ω → 𝒪} {f : 𝒪 → ℝ} (hf : Measurable f) (hf2 : MemLp (fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω)) 2 μ) :
  IsAsymptoticallyLinear (sampleMean f O) (μ[fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω)])
    (fun x ↦ f x - μ[fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω)]) O μ

The sample mean is asymptotically linear. If μ is a probability measure, f is measurable and f (O 0) has a finite second moment, then the sample mean of f (O i) is asymptotically linear at E f (O 0) with influence function f - E f (O 0). The remainder is identically zero.

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.integrabletheorem

theorem integrable [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (h : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ) :
  Integrable (fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω)) μ

An asymptotically linear estimator has an integrable influence function at the observation; this is where the probability measure hypothesis of the predicate is used.

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.isConsistenttheorem

theorem isConsistent [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hO : IsIIDSample O μ)
  (h : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ) : IsConsistent θhat θ μ

An asymptotically linear estimator is consistent. The proof writes θhat n - θ = n⁻¹ ∑_{i < n} φ (O i) + n^{-1/2} R n for n ≥ 1, where R n is the remainder; the first term tends to E φ (O 0) = 0 by the law of large numbers and the second is dominated by |R n|.

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.tendstoInDistributiontheorem

theorem tendstoInDistribution [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hO : IsIIDSample O μ)
  (h : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ) (hmeas : ∀ n, AEMeasurable (θhat n) μ)
  {Ω' : Type*} {mΩ' : MeasurableSpace Ω'} {P' : Measure Ω'} [IsProbabilityMeasure P']
  {Y : Ω' → ℝ} (hY : HasLaw Y (gaussianReal 0 (μ[fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω) ^ 2]).toNNReal) P') :
  TendstoInDistribution (fun (n : ℕ) ω ↦ √n * (θhat n ω - θ)) atTop Y (fun _ ↦ μ) P'

Asymptotic normality. Let θhat be asymptotically linear at θ with influence function φ for an i.i.d. sample O under a probability measure μ, with each θhat n almost everywhere measurable. Then √n (θhat n - θ) converges in distribution to any random variable Y whose law is the centered Gaussian N(0, E φ (O 0)²).

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.tendstoInDistribution_of_isSampleMeasurabletheorem

theorem tendstoInDistribution_of_isSampleMeasurable [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
  (hO : IsIIDSample O μ) (h : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ)
  (hθ : IsSampleMeasurable θhat O)
  {Ω' : Type*} {mΩ' : MeasurableSpace Ω'} {P' : Measure Ω'} [IsProbabilityMeasure P']
  {Y : Ω' → ℝ} (hY : HasLaw Y (gaussianReal 0 (μ[fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω) ^ 2]).toNNReal) P') :
  TendstoInDistribution (fun (n : ℕ) ω ↦ √n * (θhat n ω - θ)) atTop Y (fun _ ↦ μ) P'

Asymptotic normality for an estimator built from the sample. The form of IsAsymptoticallyLinear.tendstoInDistribution for an estimator θhat such that each θhat n is a measurable function of the first n observations.

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.ae_eqtheorem

theorem ae_eq [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {ψ : 𝒪 → ℝ} (hO : IsIIDSample O μ)
  (hφ : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ) (hψ : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ ψ O μ) :
  ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, φ (O 0 ω) = ψ (O 0 ω)

Uniqueness of the influence function. If θhat is asymptotically linear at θ with influence functions φ and ψ for an i.i.d. sample under a probability measure, then φ (O 0) = ψ (O 0) almost surely. The difference n^{-1/2} ∑_{i < n} (φ - ψ)(O i) tends to zero in probability, while by the central limit theorem it converges in distribution to N(0, Var((φ - ψ)(O 0))); uniqueness of limits in distribution forces the variance to vanish.

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.of_expansiontheorem

theorem of_expansion [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hφ : Measurable φ)
  (h2 : MemLp (fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω)) 2 μ) (h0 : μ[fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω)] = 0) {r : ℕ → Ω → ℝ}
  (hexp : ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, θhat n ω - θ = sampleMean φ O n ω + r n ω)
  (hr : TendstoInMeasure μ (fun (n : ℕ) ω ↦ √n * r n ω) atTop 0) :
  IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ

Asymptotic linearity from an exact expansion. Let μ be a probability measure and φ a measurable function with φ (O 0) square integrable and of mean zero. If eventually, for almost every ω, θhat n - θ = n⁻¹ ∑_{i < n} φ (O i) + r n with a remainder satisfying √n r n → 0 in probability (that is, r n = o_p(n^{-1/2})), then θhat is asymptotically linear at θ with influence function φ.

  IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat' θ φ O μ

Invariance under negligible perturbations. If θhat is asymptotically linear at θ with influence function φ and √n (θhat' n - θhat n) → 0 in probability (that is, θhat' n - θhat n = o_p(n^{-1/2})), then θhat' is asymptotically linear at θ with the same influence function.

CausalInference.Estimation.ConfidenceInterval

CausalInference/Estimation/ConfidenceInterval.lean · 258 lines · 9 public theorems · 2 definitions · imports Estimation.AsymptoticLinear

Wald confidence intervals. The Wald interval for θ from an estimate θhat, an estimate σhat of the asymptotic standard deviation of √n (θhat - θ) and a critical value z at sample size n is [θhat - z σhat / √n, θhat + z σhat / √n] (waldInterval). The standard error of θhat is σhat / √n; the same interval written with a standard error se is [θhat - z se, θhat + z se] (waldIntervalSE), and waldInterval_eq_waldIntervalSE relates the two.

Sources: van der Vaart (1998)

Public declarations (11)

CausalInference.waldIntervaldefinition

def waldInterval (est sd z : ℝ) (n : ℕ) : Set ℝ

The Wald interval [est - z sd / √n, est + z sd / √n] built from an estimate est, a scale sd, a critical value z and the sample size n. The scale sd is an estimate of the asymptotic standard deviation of √n (θhat n - θ), that is of the standard deviation σ of its normal limit; it is not the standard error of est, which is sd / √n. For an interval built from a standard error use waldIntervalSE; see waldInterval_eq_waldIntervalSE.

CausalInference.waldIntervalSEdefinition

def waldIntervalSE (est se z : ℝ) : Set ℝ

The Wald interval [est - z se, est + z se] built from an estimate est, an estimate se of its standard error and a critical value z.

CausalInference.waldInterval_eq_waldIntervalSEtheorem

theorem waldInterval_eq_waldIntervalSE (est sd z : ℝ) (n : ℕ) :
  waldInterval est sd z n = waldIntervalSE est (sd / √n) z

The Wald interval with asymptotic scale sd at sample size n is the Wald interval with standard error sd / √n.

CausalInference.waldIntervalSE_eq_waldIntervaltheorem

theorem waldIntervalSE_eq_waldInterval (est se z : ℝ) {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
  waldIntervalSE est se z = waldInterval est (√n * se) z n

For n ≥ 1, the Wald interval with standard error se is the Wald interval with asymptotic scale √n se.

CausalInference.mem_waldInterval_ifftheorem

lemma mem_waldInterval_iff {est sd z θ : ℝ} {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
  θ ∈ waldInterval est sd z n ↔ |√n * (est - θ)| - z * sd ≤ 0

For n ≥ 1, θ lies in the Wald interval exactly when |√n (est - θ)| ≤ z sd.

  (hAN : TendstoInDistribution (fun (n : ℕ) ω ↦ √n * (θhat n ω - θ)) atTop Y (fun _ ↦ μ) P')

Asymptotic coverage of the Wald interval. Let μ be a probability measure, θhat and σhat sequences of estimators with σhat n almost everywhere measurable, and suppose that √n (θhat n - θ) converges in distribution to a random variable Y with law N(0, σ²), where σ > 0, and that σhat is consistent for σ. theorem sampleMean_tendsto_waldInterval_coverage {𝒪 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝒪]
  {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {O : ℕ → Ω → 𝒪} (hO : IsIIDSample O μ)
  {f : 𝒪 → ℝ} (hf : Measurable f) (hf2 : MemLp (fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω)) 2 μ)

Wald interval for the sample mean. Let O be an i.i.d. sample under a probability measure μ, f measurable with f (O 0) of finite second moment and positive variance, and let z ≥ 0 satisfy Φ(z) = 1 - α / 2. Then the Wald interval built from the sample mean and the sample standard deviation √(P_n f² - (P_n f)²), [P_n f - z σhat n / √n, P_n f + z σhat n / √n], covers E f (O 0) with probability tending to 1 - α.

CausalInference/Estimation/Consistency.lean · 228 lines · 12 public theorems · 2 definitions · imports Estimation.Estimator

Consistency of estimators. An estimator sequence θhat : ℕ → Ω → ℝ is consistent for θ when θhat n converges to θ in probability, that is MeasureTheory.TendstoInMeasure μ θhat atTop (fun _ ↦ θ).

Sources: van der Vaart (1998)

  (hf' : TendstoInMeasure μ f' l g') :
  TendstoInMeasure μ (fun i ↦ f i + f' i) l (g + g')

Convergence in measure is preserved by sums: if f i → g and f' i → g' in measure, then f i + f' i → g + g' in measure.

CausalInference.IsConsistentdefinition

def IsConsistent (θhat : ℕ → Ω → ℝ) (θ : ℝ) (μ : Measure Ω) : Prop

The estimator sequence θhat is consistent for θ under μ: θhat n converges to θ in probability.

CausalInference.sampleMean_isConsistenttheorem

theorem sampleMean_isConsistent {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {O : ℕ → Ω → 𝒪}
  (hO : IsIIDSample O μ) {f : 𝒪 → ℝ} (hf : Measurable f)
  (hint : Integrable (fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω)) μ) :
  IsConsistent (sampleMean f O) (μ[fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω)]) μ

Weak law of large numbers for the sample mean. If O is an i.i.d. sample under a probability measure μ, f is measurable and f (O 0) is integrable, then the sample mean n⁻¹ ∑_{i < n} f (O i) is consistent for E f (O 0). The proof goes through the strong law of large numbers (ProbabilityTheory.strong_law_ae_real) and the fact that almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability on a finite measure space.

CausalInference.IsConsistent.comptheorem

theorem comp {θhat : ℕ → Ω → ℝ} {θ : ℝ} {g : ℝ → ℝ} (hg : ContinuousAt g θ)
  (h : IsConsistent θhat θ μ) : IsConsistent (fun n ω ↦ g (θhat n ω)) (g θ) μ

Continuous mapping for consistency. If θhat is consistent for θ and g is continuous at θ, then g ∘ θhat is consistent for g θ. No measurability of g is needed.

  (hb : IsConsistent b β μ) : IsConsistent (fun n ω ↦ g (a n ω) (b n ω)) (g α β) μ

Joint continuous mapping for consistency. If a is consistent for α, b is consistent for β, and (x, y) ↦ g x y is continuous at (α, β), then g a b is consistent for g α β.

  IsConsistent (fun n ω ↦ a n ω * b n ω) (α * β) μ

Product rule for consistency. If a is consistent for α and b is consistent for β, then a * b is consistent for α * β.

def sampleSD (f : 𝒪 → ℝ) (O : ℕ → Ω → 𝒪) (n : ℕ) (ω : Ω) : ℝ

The plug-in sample standard deviation √(n⁻¹ ∑_{i < n} f (O i)² - (n⁻¹ ∑_{i < n} f (O i))²) of the transformed observations f (O i). At n = 0 it takes the value 0.

  IsSampleMeasurable (sampleSD f O) O

The sample standard deviation of a measurable transformation is a measurable function of the first n observations.

CausalInference.sampleSD_isConsistenttheorem

theorem sampleSD_isConsistent {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {O : ℕ → Ω → 𝒪}
  (hO : IsIIDSample O μ) {f : 𝒪 → ℝ} (hf : Measurable f)
  (hf2 : MemLp (fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω)) 2 μ) :
  IsConsistent (sampleSD f O) (√(Var[fun ω ↦ f (O 0 ω); μ])) μ

Consistency of the sample standard deviation. If O is an i.i.d. sample under a probability measure μ, f is measurable and f (O 0) has a finite second moment, then the sample standard deviation of f (O i) is consistent for the population standard deviation √(Var f (O 0)). The proof combines the laws of large numbers for f and f² with the joint continuous mapping lemma for (a, b) ↦ √(a - b²).

theorem measure_le_abs_inv_sqrt_mul_sum_le {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
  {O : ℕ → Ω → 𝒪} {φ : 𝒪 → ℝ} (hO : IsIIDSample O μ) (hφ : Measurable φ)
  (h2 : MemLp (fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω)) 2 μ) (h0 : μ[fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω)] = 0) (n : ℕ) {M : ℝ}
  (hM : 0 < M) :
  μ {ω | M ≤ |(√n)⁻¹ * ∑ i ∈ range n, φ (O i ω)|} ≤
    ENNReal.ofReal (μ[fun ω ↦ φ (O 0 ω) ^ 2] / M ^ 2)

Chebyshev's bound for the normalized sum. Let O be an i.i.d. sample under a probability measure μ and φ measurable with φ (O 0) square integrable and of mean zero. Then for every n and M > 0, μ {M ≤ |n^{-1/2} ∑_{i < n} φ (O i)|} ≤ E φ (O 0)² / M².

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.sqrt_mul_sub_boundedInProbabilitytheorem

theorem sqrt_mul_sub_boundedInProbability [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hO : IsIIDSample O μ)
  (h : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ) :
  ∀ η : ℝ≥0∞, 0 < η →
    ∃ M : ℝ, 0 < M ∧ ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, μ {ω | M ≤ |√n * (θhat n ω - θ)|} ≤ η

**Asymptotically linear estimators are √n-bounded in probability.** If θhat is asymptotically linear at θ for an i.i.d. sample under a probability measure, then √n (θhat n - θ) is bounded in probability: for every η > 0 there is M > 0 such that eventually μ {M ≤ |√n (θhat n - θ)|} ≤ η.

CausalInference.IsAsymptoticallyLinear.comp_hasDerivAttheorem

theorem comp_hasDerivAt [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hO : IsIIDSample O μ)
  (h : IsAsymptoticallyLinear θhat θ φ O μ) {g : ℝ → ℝ} {g' : ℝ} (hg : HasDerivAt g g' θ) :
  IsAsymptoticallyLinear (fun n ω ↦ g (θhat n ω)) (g θ) (fun x ↦ g' * φ x) O μ

The delta method. Let θhat be asymptotically linear at θ with influence function φ for an i.i.d. sample O under a probability measure μ, and let g : ℝ → ℝ be differentiable at θ with derivative g'. Then g ∘ θhat is asymptotically linear at g θ with influence function g' φ. The proof writes g x - g θ = g' (x - θ) + ρ x (x - θ) with ρ continuous at θ and ρ θ = 0; then ρ (θhat n) → 0 in probability by consistency, and √n (θhat n - θ) is bounded in probability.

CausalInference.Survival.Basic

CausalInference/Survival/Basic.lean · 322 lines · 23 public theorems · 4 definitions

Discrete-time survival: survival, risk, hazard and the product formula. An event time T : Ω → ℕ on a probability space (Ω, μ), with time measured in discrete intervals. We define

Public declarations (27)

CausalInference.Survival.survivaldefinition

def survival (μ : Measure Ω) (T : Ω → ℕ) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The survival at time k: S k = P(T > k).

CausalInference.Survival.riskdefinition

def risk (μ : Measure Ω) (T : Ω → ℕ) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The risk, or cumulative incidence, at time k: 1 - P(T > k), which equals P(T ≤ k) for a probability measure (risk_eq_measureReal_le).

CausalInference.Survival.atRiskdefinition

def atRisk (μ : Measure Ω) (T : Ω → ℕ) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The probability of being at risk at the start of interval k: P(T ≥ k). For k ≥ 1 this is P(T > k - 1) = S (k - 1) (atRisk_succ).

CausalInference.Survival.hazarddefinition

def hazard (μ : Measure Ω) (T : Ω → ℕ) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The discrete-time hazard at time k: h k = P(T = k) / P(T ≥ k), the probability of the event in interval k among those who had not had it before k (P(T = k | T > k - 1)). It is a conditional probability only when 0 < atRisk μ T k; at other times its value is the conventional 0 and no result uses it as a probability.

CausalInference.Survival.atRisk_succtheorem

theorem atRisk_succ (k : ℕ) : atRisk μ T (k + 1) = survival μ T k

CausalInference.Survival.atRisk_zerotheorem

theorem atRisk_zero [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] : atRisk μ T 0 = 1

CausalInference.Survival.survival_antitonetheorem

theorem survival_antitone : Antitone (survival μ T)

Survival is nonincreasing in time.

CausalInference.Survival.atRisk_antitonetheorem

theorem atRisk_antitone : Antitone (atRisk μ T)

The at-risk probability is nonincreasing in time.

CausalInference.Survival.survival_le_atRisktheorem

theorem survival_le_atRisk (k : ℕ) : survival μ T k ≤ atRisk μ T k

CausalInference.Survival.measureReal_eq_le_atRisktheorem

theorem measureReal_eq_le_atRisk (k : ℕ) : μ.real {ω | T ω = k} ≤ atRisk μ T k

CausalInference.Survival.risk_monotonetheorem

theorem risk_monotone : Monotone (risk μ T)

Risk is nondecreasing in time.

CausalInference.Survival.measureReal_eq_hazard_mul_atRisktheorem

theorem measureReal_eq_hazard_mul_atRisk (k : ℕ) :
  μ.real {ω | T ω = k} = hazard μ T k * atRisk μ T k

P(T = k) = h k * P(T ≥ k) for every k. If P(T ≥ k) = 0 then also P(T = k) = 0 since {T = k} ⊆ {T ≥ k}, so both sides vanish for that reason, whatever the conventional value of the hazard.

Every event defined by a property of a measurable T : Ω → ℕ is measurable.

CausalInference.Survival.atRisk_eq_addtheorem

theorem atRisk_eq_add (k : ℕ) :
  atRisk μ T k = μ.real {ω | T ω = k} + survival μ T k

P(T ≥ k) = P(T = k) + P(T > k).

CausalInference.Survival.survival_eq_atRisk_multheorem

theorem survival_eq_atRisk_mul (k : ℕ) :
  survival μ T k = atRisk μ T k * (1 - hazard μ T k)

S k = P(T ≥ k) * (1 - h k), valid for every k (when P(T ≥ k) = 0 both sides are zero, the right side through the factor P(T ≥ k)).

CausalInference.Survival.measureReal_eq_atRisk_subtheorem

theorem measureReal_eq_atRisk_sub (k : ℕ) :
  μ.real {ω | T ω = k} = atRisk μ T k - atRisk μ T (k + 1)

P(T = k) = P(T ≥ k) - P(T ≥ k + 1).

CausalInference.Survival.risk_eq_measureReal_letheorem

theorem risk_eq_measureReal_le (k : ℕ) : risk μ T k = μ.real {ω | T ω ≤ k}

The risk is the probability of an event by time k: 1 - P(T > k) = P(T ≤ k).

CausalInference.Survival.survival_eq_prod_one_sub_hazard'theorem

theorem survival_eq_prod_one_sub_hazard' (k : ℕ) :
  survival μ T k = ∏ m ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), (1 - hazard μ T m)

The product formula, unconditional form: S k = ∏_{m = 0}^{k} (1 - h m) for every k. At a time m with P(T ≥ m) = 0 the factor 1 - h m is a conventional value, not one minus a conditional probability; such factors occur only after survival has reached zero, and then an earlier factor is a genuine zero (exists_hazard_eq_one_of_survival_eq_zero), so the conventional values do not affect the product. When P(T ≥ k) > 0 no such factor occurs: see survival_eq_prod_one_sub_hazard.

CausalInference.Survival.survival_eq_prod_one_sub_hazardtheorem

theorem survival_eq_prod_one_sub_hazard (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < atRisk μ T k) :
  (∀ m ≤ k, 0 < atRisk μ T m) ∧
    survival μ T k = ∏ m ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), (1 - hazard μ T m)

The product formula of Hernán and Robins (Section 17.2): S k = ∏_{m = 0}^{k} (1 - h m) when the at-risk probability P(T ≥ k) is positive. In that case every at-risk probability P(T ≥ m), m ≤ k, is positive (first conjunct), so each factor is one minus a genuine conditional probability P(T = m | T ≥ m).

CausalInference.Survival.exists_hazard_eq_one_of_survival_eq_zerotheorem

theorem exists_hazard_eq_one_of_survival_eq_zero {k : ℕ} (hk : survival μ T k = 0) :
  ∃ m ≤ k, 0 < atRisk μ T m ∧ hazard μ T m = 1

Once survival reaches zero, the product formula has a genuine zero factor: if S k = 0 then there is a time m ≤ k with positive at-risk probability P(T ≥ m) > 0 and hazard P(T = m | T ≥ m) = 1.

CausalInference.Survival.survival_eq_prod_one_sub_hazard_of_survival_eq_zerotheorem

theorem survival_eq_prod_one_sub_hazard_of_survival_eq_zero {k : ℕ}
  (hk : survival μ T k = 0) :
  survival μ T k = ∏ m ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), (1 - hazard μ T m)

The product formula when survival has reached zero: if S k = 0 then the product ∏_{m = 0}^{k} (1 - h m) is zero as well, because it contains the factor 1 - h m = 0 at a time m with positive at-risk probability (exists_hazard_eq_one_of_survival_eq_zero).

CausalInference.Survival.survival_eq_prod_Icctheorem

theorem survival_eq_prod_Icc (h0 : μ.real {ω | T ω = 0} = 0) (k : ℕ)
  (hk : 0 < atRisk μ T k) :
  survival μ T k = ∏ m ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k, (1 - hazard μ T m)

The product formula in the book's indexing: if nobody has the event at time 0 (P(T = 0) = 0, so S 0 = 1) and P(T ≥ k) > 0, then S k = ∏_{m = 1}^{k} (1 - h m), where each factor is one minus the genuine conditional probability h m = P(T = m | T > m - 1).

CausalInference.Survival.risk_eq_sum_hazard_mul_atRisktheorem

theorem risk_eq_sum_hazard_mul_atRisk (k : ℕ) :
  risk μ T k = ∑ m ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), hazard μ T m * atRisk μ T m

Risk as a cumulative sum of hazards: 1 - S k = ∑_{m = 0}^{k} h m * P(T ≥ m). Each term equals P(T = m) (measureReal_eq_hazard_mul_atRisk); a term with P(T ≥ m) = 0 is zero because P(T = m) = 0, not because of a convention.

CausalInference.Survival.risk_eq_sum_Icctheorem

theorem risk_eq_sum_Icc (h0 : μ.real {ω | T ω = 0} = 0) (k : ℕ) :
  risk μ T k = ∑ m ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k, hazard μ T m * survival μ T (m - 1)

Risk as a cumulative sum, the book's indexing: if P(T = 0) = 0 then 1 - S k = ∑_{m = 1}^{k} h m * S (m - 1).

CausalInference.Survival.hazard_one_eq_risk_onetheorem

theorem hazard_one_eq_risk_one (h0 : μ.real {ω | T ω = 0} = 0) :
  hazard μ T 1 = risk μ T 1

When nobody has the event at time 0, the hazard at time 1 equals the risk at time 1: h 1 = P(T ≤ 1), since everybody is at risk at time 1.

CausalInference.Survival.hazard_eq_of_map_eqtheorem

theorem hazard_eq_of_map_eq {Ω' : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω'] {ν : Measure Ω'} {T' : Ω' → ℕ}
  (hT : Measurable T) (hT' : Measurable T') (h : μ.map T = ν.map T') (k : ℕ) :
  hazard μ T k = hazard ν T' k

The law of T determines the hazards: two event times with the same distribution have the same hazard at every time.

CausalInference.Survival.map_eq_of_hazard_eqtheorem

theorem map_eq_of_hazard_eq [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {Ω' : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω']
  {ν : Measure Ω'} [IsProbabilityMeasure ν] {T' : Ω' → ℕ} (hT' : Measurable T')
  (h : ∀ k, 0 < atRisk μ T k → hazard μ T k = hazard ν T' k) : μ.map T = ν.map T'

Hazards determine the law of T: if μ and ν are probability measures and the hazards of T and T' agree at every time at which T has positive at-risk probability, then T and T' have the same distribution. Times with P(T ≥ k) = 0 impose no condition, and the proof never uses the conventional value of a hazard: it propagates P(T ≥ k + 1) = P(T ≥ k) * (1 - h k), which at such times reads 0 = 0.

CausalInference.Survival.Censoring

CausalInference/Survival/Censoring.lean · 325 lines · 19 public theorems · 7 definitions · imports Survival.Basic

Discrete-time survival under censoring: identification by the product-limit functional. An event time T : Ω → ℕ and a censoring time C : Ω → ℕ on a probability space. Only the observed data (min T C, 1{T ≤ C}) are available: the follow-up time and the indicator that the event was observed. An individual is at risk and uncensored at time k when T ≥ k and C ≥ k; an event at time k is observed when T = k ≤ C.

Public declarations (26)

CausalInference.Survival.observeddefinition

def observed (T C : Ω → ℕ) (ω : Ω) : ℕ × Bool

The observed data: the follow-up time min T C and the indicator 1{T ≤ C} that the event was observed (an event at the censoring time counts as observed).

CausalInference.Survival.observedHazarddefinition

def observedHazard (ν : Measure (ℕ × Bool)) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The observed hazard at k of a law ν of the observed data (X, Δ): the probability of an observed event at k among those with follow-up time at least k, ν(X = k, Δ = true) / ν(X ≥ k). It is a conditional probability only when ν(X ≥ k) > 0.

CausalInference.Survival.productLimitdefinition

def productLimit (ν : Measure (ℕ × Bool)) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The product-limit (Kaplan-Meier) functional of a law ν of the observed data: ∏_{m = 0}^{k} (1 - observedHazard ν m).

CausalInference.Survival.measurable_observedtheorem

theorem measurable_observed (hT : Measurable T) (hC : Measurable C) :
  Measurable (observed T C)

CausalInference.Survival.measureReal_and_of_indepFuntheorem

theorem measureReal_and_of_indepFun (hind : IndepFun T C μ) (p q : ℕ → Prop) :
  μ.real {ω | p (T ω) ∧ q (C ω)} = μ.real {ω | p (T ω)} * μ.real {ω | q (C ω)}

Under independence of T and C, events about T and events about C multiply.

CausalInference.Survival.hazard_eq_of_indepFuntheorem

theorem hazard_eq_of_indepFun (hind : IndepFun T C μ) (k : ℕ)
  (hk : 0 < μ.real {ω | k ≤ T ω ∧ k ≤ C ω}) :
  μ.real {ω | T ω = k ∧ k ≤ C ω} / μ.real {ω | k ≤ T ω ∧ k ≤ C ω} = hazard μ T k

Independent censoring preserves the hazard: if T and C are independent and the at-risk, uncensored event {T ≥ k, C ≥ k} has positive probability, then P(T = k | T ≥ k, C ≥ k) = P(T = k | T ≥ k) = h k.

CausalInference.Survival.observedHazard_map_observedtheorem

theorem observedHazard_map_observed (hT : Measurable T) (hC : Measurable C) (k : ℕ) :
  observedHazard (μ.map (observed T C)) k =
    μ.real {ω | T ω = k ∧ k ≤ C ω} / μ.real {ω | k ≤ T ω ∧ k ≤ C ω}

The observed hazard of the law of the observed data is the hazard among those at risk and uncensored: observedHazard (law of (min T C, 1{T ≤ C})) k = P(T = k, C ≥ k) / P(T ≥ k, C ≥ k).

CausalInference.Survival.productLimit_map_observed_eq_survivaltheorem

theorem productLimit_map_observed_eq_survival [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hT : Measurable T)
  (hC : Measurable C) (hind : IndepFun T C μ) (k : ℕ)
  (hk : 0 < μ.real {ω | k ≤ T ω ∧ k ≤ C ω}) :
  productLimit (μ.map (observed T C)) k = survival μ T k

Identification of survival under independent censoring (Hernán and Robins, Section 17.3): if T and C are independent then, at every time k at which the at-risk probability P(min T C ≥ k) is positive, the product-limit functional of the observed-data law equals the survival P(T > k). Every factor of the product is one minus a genuine conditional probability, since P(min T C ≥ m) ≥ P(min T C ≥ k) > 0 for m ≤ k.

CausalInference.Survival.measureReal_survivor_uncensored_of_indepFuntheorem

theorem measureReal_survivor_uncensored_of_indepFun (hind : IndepFun T C μ) (k : ℕ) :
  μ.real {ω | k < T ω ∧ k ≤ C ω} = survival μ T k * μ.real {ω | k ≤ C ω}

Under independent censoring the fraction of individuals who survived through k and were uncensored through k is P(T > k, C ≥ k) = S k * P(C ≥ k). It differs from the survival S k whenever 0 < S k and P(C ≥ k) < 1.

CausalInference.Survival.CensoringExample.lawTdefinition

def lawT : Measure ℕ

The law of the event time in the book's example: P(T = 1) = 0.1, P(T = 2) = 0.09 and P(T = 3) = 0.81, where T = 3 stands for survival beyond the end of follow-up at 2. So P(T > 1) = 0.9 and P(T > 2 | T > 1) = 0.9.

CausalInference.Survival.CensoringExample.lawCdefinition

def lawC : Measure ℕ

The law of the censoring time in the book's example: nobody is censored at time 1 (C ≥ 1), and half of the population is censored after time 1 (C = 1, uncensored at 1 but not at 2) while the other half is followed through time 2 (C = 2).

CausalInference.Survival.CensoringExample.indepModeldefinition

def indepModel : Measure (ℕ × ℕ)

The book's example (Hernán and Robins, Section 17.3) as a joint law of (T, C) on ℕ × ℕ: the product of lawT and lawC, so that censoring is independent of the event time.

def depModel : Measure (ℕ × ℕ)

A model with dependent censoring and the same observed-data law as indepModel: with probabilities in units of 1/200, (T, C) = (1, 1) with weight 20, (2, 1) with weight 90, (2, 2) with weight 9 and (3, 2) with weight 81. Everyone censored after time 1 has the event at time 2.
