CausalInference.Survival.Comparison

CausalInference/Survival/Comparison.lean · 256 lines · 14 public theorems · 5 definitions · imports Survival.Basic

Comparing two arms: hazard ratios versus survival and risk contrasts. Two arms, each with its own law of the event time: (μ₁, T₁) (for instance treated) and (μ₀, T₀) (untreated); the measures may live on different spaces. In applications they are the conditional laws given A = 1 and A = 0, or the laws of two counterfactual event times.

Public declarations (19)

CausalInference.Survival.hazardRatiodefinition

def hazardRatio (μ₁ : Measure Ω₁) (T₁ : Ω₁ → ℕ) (μ₀ : Measure Ω₀) (T₀ : Ω₀ → ℕ)
  (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The hazard ratio at time k of arm 1 versus arm 0: h₁ k / h₀ k. It is meaningful only when both arms have positive at-risk probability at k and h₀ k > 0.

CausalInference.Survival.survival_div_survival_eq_prodtheorem

theorem survival_div_survival_eq_prod (hT₀ : Measurable T₀) (hT₁ : Measurable T₁) (k : ℕ)
  (hk₀ : 0 < atRisk μ₀ T₀ k) (hk₁ : 0 < atRisk μ₁ T₁ k) (hS₀ : 0 < survival μ₀ T₀ k) :
  (∀ m ≤ k, 0 < 1 - hazard μ₀ T₀ m) ∧
    survival μ₁ T₁ k / survival μ₀ T₀ k =
      ∏ m ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), (1 - hazard μ₁ T₁ m) / (1 - hazard μ₀ T₀ m)

The survival ratio is a product of ratios of one minus the hazards: if both arms have positive at-risk probability at k and S₀ k > 0, then S₁ k / S₀ k = ∏_{m = 0}^{k} (1 - h₁ m) / (1 - h₀ m), and every denominator 1 - h₀ m is positive.

CausalInference.Survival.survival_eq_survival_of_hazard_eqtheorem

theorem survival_eq_survival_of_hazard_eq (hT₀ : Measurable T₀) (hT₁ : Measurable T₁) (k : ℕ)
  (h : ∀ m ≤ k, 0 < atRisk μ₀ T₀ m → hazard μ₁ T₁ m = hazard μ₀ T₀ m) :
  survival μ₁ T₁ k = survival μ₀ T₀ k

Equal hazards give equal survival: if h₁ m = h₀ m at every m ≤ k at which arm 0 has positive at-risk probability, then S₁ k = S₀ k. Times at which arm 0 has at-risk probability zero impose no condition.

CausalInference.Survival.risk_eq_risk_of_hazard_eqtheorem

theorem risk_eq_risk_of_hazard_eq (hT₀ : Measurable T₀) (hT₁ : Measurable T₁) (k : ℕ)
  (h : ∀ m ≤ k, 0 < atRisk μ₀ T₀ m → hazard μ₁ T₁ m = hazard μ₀ T₀ m) :
  risk μ₁ T₁ k = risk μ₀ T₀ k

Equal hazards give equal risks: under the hypothesis of survival_eq_survival_of_hazard_eq the risks 1 - S₁ k and 1 - S₀ k agree.

CausalInference.Survival.survival_eq_prod_hazardRatiotheorem

theorem survival_eq_prod_hazardRatio (hT₁ : Measurable T₁)
  (h0₁ : μ₁.real {ω | T₁ ω = 0} = 0) (k : ℕ) (hk₁ : 0 < atRisk μ₁ T₁ k)
  (hne : ∀ m ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k, hazard μ₀ T₀ m ≠ 0) :
  survival μ₁ T₁ k =
    ∏ m ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k, (1 - hazardRatio μ₁ T₁ μ₀ T₀ m * hazard μ₀ T₀ m)

Survival in arm 1 from the hazard ratios and the hazards of arm 0: if nobody in arm 1 has the event at time 0, arm 1 has positive at-risk probability at k, and h₀ m ≠ 0 for 1 ≤ m ≤ k, then S₁ k = ∏_{m = 1}^{k} (1 - HR m * h₀ m) with HR m = h₁ m / h₀ m. So the survival contrast at k depends on the hazard ratios at all times up to k together with the reference hazards, not on any single hazard ratio.

CausalInference.Survival.risk_sub_risktheorem

theorem risk_sub_risk (k : ℕ) :
  risk μ₁ T₁ k - risk μ₀ T₀ k = survival μ₀ T₀ k - survival μ₁ T₁ k

The risk difference is the survival difference with the sign reversed: (1 - S₁ k) - (1 - S₀ k) = S₀ k - S₁ k.

CausalInference.Survival.hazardRatio_one_eq_risk_ratiotheorem

theorem hazardRatio_one_eq_risk_ratio (hT₀ : Measurable T₀) (hT₁ : Measurable T₁)
  (h0₀ : μ₀.real {ω | T₀ ω = 0} = 0) (h0₁ : μ₁.real {ω | T₁ ω = 0} = 0) :
  hazardRatio μ₁ T₁ μ₀ T₀ 1 = risk μ₁ T₁ 1 / risk μ₀ T₀ 1

At time 1 the hazard ratio is the risk ratio (Hernán and Robins, Technical Point 8.1): if nobody has the event at time 0 in either arm, h₁ 1 / h₀ 1 = P(T₁ ≤ 1) / P(T₀ ≤ 1). From time 2 on, the hazard conditions on survival through the previous time, which is where the selection bias described in Technical Point 8.1 and Fine Point 17.2 enters.

CausalInference.Survival.hazard_eq_hazard_of_survival_eqtheorem

theorem hazard_eq_hazard_of_survival_eq [IsFiniteMeasure μ₀] [IsFiniteMeasure μ₁]
  (hT₀ : Measurable T₀) (hT₁ : Measurable T₁) (k : ℕ)
  (h0 : atRisk μ₁ T₁ 0 = atRisk μ₀ T₀ 0)
  (h : ∀ m ≤ k, survival μ₁ T₁ m = survival μ₀ T₀ m) :
  ∀ m ≤ k, hazard μ₁ T₁ m = hazard μ₀ T₀ m

Equal survival curves give equal hazards: if S₁ m = S₀ m for every m ≤ k and the total masses agree (P(T₁ ≥ 0) = P(T₀ ≥ 0)), then h₁ m = h₀ m for every m ≤ k. Both the event probabilities P(T = m) and the at-risk probabilities agree, so at a time with at-risk probability zero the equality is between two conventional values 0.

    s.indicator (fun _ => a) 1 + s.indicator (fun _ => b) 2 + s.indicator (fun _ => c) 3

CausalInference.Survival.ComparisonExample.arm₁definition

def arm₁ : Measure ℕ

CausalInference.Survival.ComparisonExample.arm₀_realtheorem

theorem arm₀_real (s : Set ℕ) : arm₀.real s =
  s.indicator (fun _ => 1 / 5) 1 + s.indicator (fun _ => 1 / 5) 2 +
    s.indicator (fun _ => 3 / 5) 3

CausalInference.Survival.ComparisonExample.arm₁_realtheorem

theorem arm₁_real (s : Set ℕ) : arm₁.real s =
  s.indicator (fun _ => 1 / 10) 1 + s.indicator (fun _ => 3 / 10) 2 +
    s.indicator (fun _ => 3 / 5) 3

CausalInference.Survival.ComparisonExample.arm₂_realtheorem

theorem arm₂_real (s : Set ℕ) : arm₂.real s =
  s.indicator (fun _ => 1 / 10) 1 + s.indicator (fun _ => 27 / 80) 2 +
    s.indicator (fun _ => 9 / 16) 3

CausalInference.Survival.ComparisonExample.hazardRatio_changes_risk_ratio_onetheorem

theorem hazardRatio_changes_risk_ratio_one :
  hazardRatio arm₁ id arm₀ id 1 = 1 / 2 ∧ hazardRatio arm₁ id arm₀ id 2 = 4 / 3 ∧
    survival arm₁ id 2 = survival arm₀ id 2 ∧ risk arm₁ id 2 / risk arm₀ id 2 = 1 ∧
    survival arm₁ id 1 ≠ survival arm₀ id 1 ∧
    0 < atRisk arm₀ id 2 ∧ 0 < atRisk arm₁ id 2 ∧
    0 < hazard arm₀ id 1 ∧ 0 < hazard arm₀ id 2

The period-specific hazard ratio changes over time (1/2 at time 1, 4/3 at time 2) while the survival and the risk at time 2 coincide in the two arms (3/5 and 2/5), so the risk ratio at time 2 is 1; the survivals at time 1 differ (9/10 versus 4/5). Both arms have positive at-risk probability and positive hazards at times 1 and 2.

CausalInference.Survival.ComparisonExample.weighted_hazardRatio_eq_one_survival_netheorem

theorem weighted_hazardRatio_eq_one_survival_ne :
  (∑ k ∈ Finset.Icc 1 2,
      arm₀.real {x | x = k} / arm₀.real {x | x ≤ 2} * hazardRatio arm₂ id arm₀ id k) = 1 ∧
    survival arm₂ id 2 ≠ survival arm₀ id 2

The average of the hazard ratios at times 1 and 2 (here 1/2 and 3/2), weighted by the distribution of the event time in arm 0 among those with the event by time 2 (w k = P(T₀ = k) / P(T₀ ≤ 2), here 1/2 each), equals 1, yet the survivals at time 2 differ (9/16 versus 3/5).

CausalInference.Survival.KaplanMeier

CausalInference/Survival/KaplanMeier.lean · 127 lines · 5 public theorems · 4 definitions

The finite-sample Kaplan-Meier estimator. A data set of n individuals, each recorded as (X i, Δ i) : ℕ × Bool: the follow-up time and whether the event was observed at that time (Δ i = true) or the individual was censored (Δ i = false). With the at-risk count R m = #{i | X i ≥ m} and the event count E m = #{i | X i = m, Δ i = true}, the Kaplan-Meier (product-limit) estimator is

Public declarations (9)

CausalInference.Survival.atRiskCountdefinition

def atRiskCount (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) (m : ℕ) : ℕ

The number at risk at time m: individuals whose follow-up time is at least m.

CausalInference.Survival.eventCountdefinition

def eventCount (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) (m : ℕ) : ℕ

The number of observed events at time m.

CausalInference.Survival.survivorCountdefinition

def survivorCount (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) (k : ℕ) : ℕ

The number of individuals whose follow-up time exceeds k.

CausalInference.Survival.kaplanMeierdefinition

def kaplanMeier (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) (k : ℕ) : ℝ

The Kaplan-Meier estimator at time k: ∏_{m = 0}^{k} (1 - E m / R m). A factor with R m = 0 takes the conventional value 1.

CausalInference.Survival.atRiskCount_succtheorem

theorem atRiskCount_succ (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) (k : ℕ) :
  atRiskCount d (k + 1) = survivorCount d k

CausalInference.Survival.atRiskCount_zerotheorem

theorem atRiskCount_zero (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) : atRiskCount d 0 = n

CausalInference.Survival.atRiskCount_eq_addtheorem

theorem atRiskCount_eq_add (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) (hd : ∀ i, (d i).2 = true) (m : ℕ) :
  atRiskCount d m = eventCount d m + survivorCount d m

Without censoring, those at risk at m either have the event at m or survive past m: R m = E m + #{i | X i > m}.

CausalInference.Survival.atRiskCount_pos_of_letheorem

theorem atRiskCount_pos_of_le (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) {m k : ℕ} (hmk : m ≤ k)
  (hk : 0 < atRiskCount d k) : 0 < atRiskCount d m

The at-risk count is nonincreasing; in particular R k > 0 gives R m > 0 for every m ≤ k, so every factor of KM k then has a positive denominator.

CausalInference.Survival.kaplanMeier_eq_survivorFractiontheorem

theorem kaplanMeier_eq_survivorFraction (d : Fin n → ℕ × Bool) (hd : ∀ i, (d i).2 = true)
  (hn : 0 < n) (k : ℕ) :
  kaplanMeier d k = (survivorCount d k : ℝ) / n

Without censoring the Kaplan-Meier estimator is the empirical survival fraction: if every event is observed (Δ i = true) and n > 0, then KM k = #{i | X i > k} / n for every k. When R k > 0 all denominators are positive (atRiskCount_pos_of_le). When R k = 0 the survivor fraction is 0; the proof shows that the product is 0 because a partial product KM m reaches 0 (at the first m with no survivors past m, where R m > 0), so the conventional factors with R m = 0 do not affect the value.

CausalInference.SCM.Basic

CausalInference/SCM/Basic.lean · 244 lines · 15 public theorems · 8 definitions · imports Graphical.TopologicalOrder, Basic.FiniteDistribution

Finite Markovian structural causal models. A finite Markovian structural causal model on a directed acyclic graph G : Digraph V: each endogenous vertex v takes values in a finite type α v, has its own exogenous noise in a finite type ε v, and is determined by a structural equation x v = f v (x restricted to the parents of v) (u v). The noises are independent, with law noise v each.

The probability of an event under a pushforward is the probability of its preimage.

CausalInference.SCMstructure

structure SCM (G : Digraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (α : V → Type*) (ε : V → Type*)
  [∀ v, Fintype (ε v)]

A finite Markovian structural causal model on the graph G. Each vertex v has a value type α v and a noise type ε v; the structural equation of v computes its value from the values of its parents and its own noise, x v = f v (x restricted to the parents) (u v); the noises are independent with laws noise v; and G is acyclic, so the system is recursive.

CausalInference.SCM.IsSolutiondefinition

def IsSolution (u : ∀ v, ε v) (x : ∀ v, α v) : Prop

The configuration x solves the structural equations at the noise value u: x v = f v (x restricted to the parents of v) (u v) for every vertex v.

CausalInference.SCM.solvedefinition

def solve (u : ∀ v, ε v) : ∀ v, α v

The solution of the structural equations at the noise value u, by well-founded recursion along the edges of the acyclic graph: the value of v is computed from the values of its parents.

CausalInference.SCM.solve_eqtheorem

theorem solve_eq (u : ∀ v, ε v) (v : V) :
  M.solve u v = M.f v ((G.parentsFinset v).restrict (M.solve u)) (u v)

The unfolding equation of the solution.

CausalInference.SCM.isSolution_solvetheorem

theorem isSolution_solve (u : ∀ v, ε v) : M.IsSolution u (M.solve u)

The solution solves the structural equations.

CausalInference.SCM.eq_solve_of_isSolutiontheorem

theorem eq_solve_of_isSolution {u : ∀ v, ε v} {x : ∀ v, α v} (h : M.IsSolution u x) :
  x = M.solve u

A solution of the structural equations is the solution: uniqueness, by well-founded induction along the edges.

CausalInference.SCM.isSolution_ifftheorem

theorem isSolution_iff {u : ∀ v, ε v} {x : ∀ v, α v} : M.IsSolution u x ↔ x = M.solve u

A configuration solves the structural equations at u if and only if it is the solution.

theorem existsUnique_isSolution (u : ∀ v, ε v) : ∃! x, M.IsSolution u x

Existence and uniqueness of the solution of a recursive structural causal model: at every noise value there is exactly one configuration satisfying all structural equations.

CausalInference.SCM.noiseDistdefinition

def noiseDist : FiniteDist (∀ v, ε v)

The product law of the noises: the noises of the vertices are independent.

CausalInference.SCM.distdefinition

def dist : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)

The distribution induced by the model on the configurations: the pushforward of the noise law along the solution map.

theorem dist_apply (x : ∀ v, α v) :

  M.dist.probOf P = M.noiseDist.probOf (fun u => P (M.solve u))

Probabilities of events under the induced distribution are noise probabilities.

  M.dist.margAt S x = M.noiseDist.probOf (fun u => ∀ v ∈ S, M.solve u v = x v)

The marginal mass of the induced distribution on a set S at x is the noise probability that the solution agrees with x on S.

CausalInference.SCM.Counterfactuals

CausalInference/SCM/Counterfactuals.lean · 345 lines · 23 public theorems · 7 definitions · imports SCM.Intervention

Unit-level counterfactuals in finite structural causal models. The potential response Y_x(u) of a vertex Y to the intervention do(X := x) at the noise value u is the value of Y in the solution of the submodel of do(X := x) at u, that is (M.intervene X x).solve u Y (Pearl 2009, Definition 7.1.4). Since the submodel keeps the noise space, the factual and counterfactual worlds share the same u.

Public declarations (30)

CausalInference.FiniteDist.conddefinition

def cond (p : FiniteDist Ω) (P : Ω → Prop) [DecidablePred P]
  (h : 0 < p.probOf P) : FiniteDist Ω

The conditional distribution of p given an event P of positive probability: mass p ω / P(P) on the outcomes of P and 0 elsewhere.

CausalInference.FiniteDist.probOf_condtheorem

theorem probOf_cond (p : FiniteDist Ω) (P : Ω → Prop) [DecidablePred P] (h : 0 < p.probOf P)
  (Q : Ω → Prop) [DecidablePred Q] :
  (p.cond P h).probOf Q = p.probOf (fun ω => P ω ∧ Q ω) / p.probOf P

Probabilities under a conditional distribution: P(Q | P) = P(P ∧ Q) / P(P).

CausalInference.SCM.potentialResponsedefinition

def potentialResponse (X : Finset V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (u : ∀ v, ε v) : ∀ v, α v

The potential response V_x(u) (Pearl 2009, Definition 7.1.4): the configuration that solves the submodel of do(X := x) at the noise value u. Its value at a vertex Y is Y_x(u). The theorems below are stated with the unfolded form (M.intervene X x).solve u.

CausalInference.SCM.potentialResponse_eqtheorem

theorem potentialResponse_eq (X : Finset V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (u : ∀ v, ε v) :
  M.potentialResponse X x u = (M.intervene X x).solve u

CausalInference.SCM.solve_intervene_of_agreetheorem

theorem solve_intervene_of_agree {X : Finset V} {x : ∀ v, α v} {u : ∀ v, ε v}
  (h : ∀ v ∈ X, M.solve u v = x v) : (M.intervene X x).solve u = M.solve u

Consistency (Pearl 2009, Corollary 7.3.2, equation (7.20)): at a noise value u where the vertices of X take the values x without intervention, the intervention do(X := x) changes nothing: V_x(u) = V(u).

CausalInference.SCM.solve_intervene_intervene_of_agreetheorem

theorem solve_intervene_intervene_of_agree {X W : Finset V} {x w : ∀ v, α v} {u : ∀ v, ε v}
  (h : ∀ v ∈ W, (M.intervene X x).solve u v = w v) :
  ((M.intervene X x).intervene W w).solve u = (M.intervene X x).solve u

Composition (Pearl 2009, Property 1, equation (7.19)), for a later intervention: if the vertices of W take the values w under do(X := x), then additionally setting W := w changes nothing: V_{xw}(u) = V_x(u).

CausalInference.SCM.solve_intervene_union_of_agreetheorem

theorem solve_intervene_union_of_agree {X W : Finset V} {x w : ∀ v, α v} {u : ∀ v, ε v}
  (h : ∀ v ∈ W, (M.intervene X x).solve u v = w v) :
  (M.intervene (X ∪ W) fun v => if v ∈ W then w v else x v).solve u =
    (M.intervene X x).solve u

Composition (Pearl 2009, Property 1, equation (7.19)), for the simultaneous intervention on X ∪ W: if W_x(u) = w, then V_{xw}(u) = V_x(u).

CausalInference.SCM.solve_intervene_intervene_of_memtheorem

theorem solve_intervene_intervene_of_mem {X W : Finset V} {x w : ∀ v, α v} (u : ∀ v, ε v)
  {v : V} (hvX : v ∈ X) (hvW : v ∉ W) :
  ((M.intervene X x).intervene W w).solve u v = x v

Effectiveness (Pearl 2009, Property 2): under do(X := x) followed by do(W := w), a vertex of X outside W takes the value x: X_{xw}(u) = x.

CausalInference.SCM.notMem_descendantsOf_singletontheorem

theorem notMem_descendantsOf_singleton {a b : V} (hne : a ≠ b) (h : ¬ G.IsAncestor a b) :
  b ∉ G.descendantsOf {a}

In a graph, a vertex b ≠ a that is not a strict descendant of a is not in the descendant closure of {a}.

CausalInference.SCM.solve_eq_of_reversibilitytheorem

theorem solve_eq_of_reversibility {Y W : V} (hYW : Y ≠ W) (w y : ∀ v, α v) (u : ∀ v, ε v)
  (h1 : (M.intervene {W} w).solve u Y = y Y) (h2 : (M.intervene {Y} y).solve u W = w W) :
  M.solve u Y = y Y

Reversibility for recursive models (Pearl 2009, Property 3, equation (7.21), and the argument on p. 230): for distinct vertices Y and W, if setting W := w gives Y the value y Y, and setting Y := y gives W the value w W, then Y has the value y Y without intervention. Applied to the submodel M.intervene X x (itself a model), this is Y_{xw}(u) = y ∧ W_{xy}(u) = w → Y_x(u) = y.

CausalInference.SCM.counterfactualProbdefinition

def counterfactualProb (E : (∀ v, α v) → Prop) [DecidablePred E]
  (hE : 0 < M.dist.probOf E) (X : Finset V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (Q : (∀ v, α v) → Prop)
  [DecidablePred Q] : ℝ

Abduction, action, prediction (Pearl 2009, Theorem 7.1.7): the probability of the counterfactual event Q under do(X := x), given the factual evidence E of positive probability. Abduction conditions the noise law on the evidence E(V(u)); action passes to the submodel of do(X := x); prediction is the probability of Q under the pushforward of the conditioned noise law along the submodel's solution map.

CausalInference.SCM.counterfactualProb_eqtheorem

theorem counterfactualProb_eq (E : (∀ v, α v) → Prop) [DecidablePred E]
  (hE : 0 < M.dist.probOf E) (X : Finset V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (Q : (∀ v, α v) → Prop)
  [DecidablePred Q] :
  M.counterfactualProb E hE X x Q =
    M.noiseDist.probOf (fun u => E (M.solve u) ∧ Q ((M.intervene X x).solve u)) /
      M.dist.probOf E

The counterfactual probability given evidence, in closed form (Pearl 2009, equation (7.6)): P(Q(V_x) | E) = P_u(E(V(u)) ∧ Q(V_x(u))) / P(E).

CausalInference.FiniteDist.map_pi_eval_pairtheorem

theorem map_pi_eval_pair (p : ∀ i, FiniteDist (κ i)) {i j : ι} (hij : i ≠ j) :
  (pi p).map (fun ω => (ω i, ω j)) = (p i).prod (p j)

Two distinct coordinates of a product law are independent with the given laws: the joint law of (ω i, ω j) is the product of p i and p j.

CausalInference.SCM.effectdefinition

def effect (X : Finset V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (Y : Finset V) (y : ∀ v, α v) : ℝ

The causal effect P(Y = y_Y | do(X := x_X)): the probability, under the distribution induced by the submodel of do(X := x), that the vertices of Y take the values given by y.

  ∃ w : ∀ v, α v, (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z ∧ w i = a

A configuration with prescribed values on the parents of i and at i.

CausalInference.SCM.probOf_and_parents_eqtheorem

theorem probOf_and_parents_eq (i : V) (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset i, α u) (a : α i) :
  M.dist.probOf (fun w => w i = a ∧ (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z) =
    M.kernel i z a * M.dist.probOf (fun w => (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z)

The kernel of i is the conditional law of i given its parents: P(x_i = a, pa_i = z) = kernel i z a * P(pa_i = z).

CausalInference.SCM.probOf_intervene_singleton_parentstheorem

theorem probOf_intervene_singleton_parents (i : V) (x : ∀ v, α v)
  (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset i, α u) :
  (M.intervene {i} x).dist.probOf (fun w => (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z) =
    M.dist.probOf (fun w => (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z)

The parent configuration of i has the same law with or without an intervention on i.

CausalInference.SCM.probOf_intervene_singleton_multheorem

theorem probOf_intervene_singleton_mul (i : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset i, α u)
  (E : (∀ v, α v) → Prop) [DecidablePred E] :
  (M.intervene {i} x).dist.probOf (fun w => E w ∧ (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z) *
      M.kernel i z (x i) =
    M.dist.probOf (fun w => E w ∧ w i = x i ∧ (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z)

The key step of the adjustment formula: within the stratum pa_i = z, the interventional mass of an event times the kernel kernel i z (x i) is the observational probability of the event together with x_i.

CausalInference.SCM.effect_singleton_eq_sumtheorem

theorem effect_singleton_eq_sum (i : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (Y : Finset V) (y : ∀ v, α v)
  (hpos : ∀ z : (∀ u : G.parentsFinset i, α u),
    0 < M.dist.probOf (fun w => (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z) →
    0 < M.dist.probOf (fun w => w i = x i ∧ (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z)) :
  M.effect {i} x Y y = ∑ z : (∀ u : G.parentsFinset i, α u),
    M.dist.probOf (fun w => (∀ v ∈ Y, w v = y v) ∧ w i = x i ∧
        (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z) /
      M.dist.probOf (fun w => w i = x i ∧ (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z) *
      M.dist.probOf (fun w => (G.parentsFinset i).restrict w = z)

Adjustment for direct causes (Pearl 2009, Theorem 3.2.2, equation (3.13)): the effect of do(X_i := x_i) on any set Y is P(y | do(x_i)) = ∑_{pa_i} P(y, x_i, pa_i) / P(x_i, pa_i) * P(pa_i), that is ∑_{pa_i} P(y | x_i, pa_i) P(pa_i), provided every parent configuration of positive probability gives x_i positive probability. Pearl states it for Y disjoint from {X_i} ∪ PA_i; the identity holds for every Y. A parent configuration of probability zero contributes _ / 0 * 0 = 0 on the right and 0 on the left, so the convention x / 0 = 0 carries nothing.

CausalInference.SCM.Modelstructure

structure SCM.Model (G : Digraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (α : V → Type*)

A finite Markovian structural causal model on G bundled with its noise types (in Type), so that models with different noise spaces form one type. Since every finite type is equivalent to some Fin n, the restriction of the noise types to Type loses no generality.

CausalInference.SCM.IdentifiableFromdefinition

def IdentifiableFrom (C : Set (Model G α)) (O : Finset V) {β : Type*} (Q : Model G α → β) :
  Prop

The query Q is identifiable within the class C of models on G from the observed vertices O: two models of C with the same marginal law of the vertices in O give the same value of Q (Pearl 2009, Definitions 3.2.3 and 3.2.4). This is PointIdentified with the observed marginal as the observation.

theorem _root_.CausalInference.FiniteDist.eq_of_marginal_univ_eq {p q : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)}
  (h : p.marginal univ = q.marginal univ) : p = q

Two distributions with the same marginal on all coordinates are equal.

CausalInference.SCM.identifiableFrom_effect_singletontheorem

theorem identifiableFrom_effect_singleton (i : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) (Y : Finset V)
  (y : ∀ v, α v) :
  IdentifiableFrom {m : Model G α | ∀ w, 0 < m.scm.dist w} univ
    (fun m => m.scm.effect {i} x Y y)

Identification when all variables are observed (a special case of Pearl 2009, Theorem 3.2.5 and Corollary 3.2.6): the effect of an intervention on a single vertex is identifiable from the joint law of all vertices, within the class of models with strictly positive distribution, by the adjustment formula for direct causes.

theorem not_identifiableFrom_effect :
  ¬ IdentifiableFrom {m : Model bow (fun _ => Bool) | ∀ w, 0 < m.scm.dist.margAt {1, 2} w}
    {1, 2} (fun m => m.scm.effect {1} treat {2} treat)

The bow pattern is not identifiable (Pearl 2009, Figure 3.7(a)): with U latent and only X and Y observed, the effect P(Y = true | do(X = true)) is not identifiable within the class of models on the bow graph with strictly positive observed law of (X, Y). Models A and B have the same observed law and the effects 1/2 and 3/4.

CausalInference.SCM.Intervention

CausalInference/SCM/Intervention.lean · 357 lines · 27 public theorems · 2 definitions · imports SCM.Markov

Interventions in finite structural causal models. The intervention do(X := x) on a finite Markovian structural causal model replaces the structural equation of every vertex of X by the constant given by x. The resulting model (the submodel M_x) lives on the mutilated graph G.deleteIncoming X and keeps the noise space, so that potential responses at a fixed noise value can be compared across models.

Public declarations (29)

CausalInference.SCM.mem_parentsFinset_deleteIncomingtheorem

theorem mem_parentsFinset_deleteIncoming {X : Finset V} {v : V} (hv : v ∉ X)
  (p : G.parentsFinset v) : p.1 ∈ (G.deleteIncoming ↑X).parentsFinset v

A parent of v ∉ X in G is a parent of v in G.deleteIncoming X.

CausalInference.SCM.intervenedefinition

def intervene (X : Finset V) (x : ∀ v, α v) : SCM (G.deleteIncoming ↑X) α ε

The submodel of the intervention do(X := x): the structural equation of every v ∈ X is replaced by the constant x v; the other equations and all noise laws are unchanged. It is a model on the graph G.deleteIncoming X, in which the vertices of X have no parents.

CausalInference.SCM.replacedefinition

def replace (X : Finset V) (g : ∀ v, (∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) → ε v → α v)
  (q : ∀ v, FiniteDist (ε v)) : SCM G α ε

A general (soft or conditional) intervention on X: the structural function of every v ∈ X is replaced by g v, a function of the same parents and of a noise of the same type, whose law becomes q v; the other mechanisms are unchanged. The model stays on G. The atomic intervention intervene is the special case of constant functions, on the smaller graph G.deleteIncoming X.

CausalInference.SCM.dist_intervenetheorem

  (M.intervene X x).dist y =
    if ∀ v ∈ X, y v = x v then ∏ v ∈ Xᶜ, M.kernels.factor v y else 0

Truncated factorization (Pearl 2009, equations (1.37), (3.10), (3.14); the g-formula; the manipulation theorem of Spirtes et al. 1993). Property 1 of causal Bayesian networks (Pearl 2009, equation (1.38)), in product form: P(x_v, x_pa) = P_{do(pa := x_pa)}(x_v) * P(x_pa). The conditional law of v given its parents is the law of v when its parents are set by intervention.

    (M.intervene (G.parentsFinset v) y).dist.probOf (fun z => z v = y v)

Property 1 of causal Bayesian networks (Pearl 2009, equation (1.38)), in ratio form: when the parent values y_pa have positive probability, P(y_v | y_pa) = P_{do(pa := y_pa)}(y_v).

CausalInference.SCM.probOf_intervene_union_eqtheorem

theorem probOf_intervene_union_eq {v : V} {S : Finset V} (hvS : v ∉ S) (a : α v) :
  (M.intervene (G.parentsFinset v ∪ S) x).dist.probOf (fun y => y v = a) =
    (M.intervene (G.parentsFinset v) x).dist.probOf (fun y => y v = a)

Property 2 of causal Bayesian networks (Pearl 2009, equation (1.39)): once the parents of v are set by intervention, a further intervention on a set S of vertices not containing v does not change the law of v. (If S meets the parents of v, the values of x win there, as in Pearl's statement for S disjoint from the parents.)

CausalInference.SCM.margAt_insert_parents_intervenetheorem

theorem margAt_insert_parents_intervene {v : V} (hv : v ∉ X) (y : ∀ v, α v) :
  (M.intervene X x).dist.margAt (insert v (G.parentsFinset v)) y =
    M.kernel v ((G.parentsFinset v).restrict y) (y v) *
      (M.intervene X x).dist.margAt (G.parentsFinset v) y

Invariance of the conditional law given the parents (condition (iii) of Pearl 2009, Definition 1.3.1), product form with the original kernel: for v ∉ X, P_{do(X := x)}(y_v, y_pa) = kernel v y_pa y_v * P_{do(X := x)}(y_pa).

theorem margAt_insert_parents_intervene_mul_comm {v : V} (hv : v ∉ X) (y : ∀ v, α v) :
  (M.intervene X x).dist.margAt (insert v (G.parentsFinset v)) y *
      M.dist.margAt (G.parentsFinset v) y =
    M.dist.margAt (insert v (G.parentsFinset v)) y *
      (M.intervene X x).dist.margAt (G.parentsFinset v) y

Invariance of the conditional law given the parents (condition (iii) of Pearl 2009, Definition 1.3.1), division-free form of P_{do(X := x)}(y_v | y_pa) = P(y_v | y_pa) for v ∉ X: P_{do(X := x)}(y_v, y_pa) * P(y_pa) = P(y_v, y_pa) * P_{do(X := x)}(y_pa).

theorem dist_replace (X : Finset V) (g : ∀ v, (∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) → ε v → α v)
  (q : ∀ v, FiniteDist (ε v)) (y : ∀ v, α v) :
  (M.replace X g q).dist y =
    (∏ v ∈ X, (q v).map (g v ((G.parentsFinset v).restrict y)) (y v)) *
      ∏ v ∈ Xᶜ, M.kernels.factor v y

Mechanism replacement (Pearl 2009, section 3.2.3), product form: the distribution after replacing the mechanisms of X is the product of the new kernels (q v).map (g v pa) of the vertices of X and of the original kernels of the other vertices.

CausalInference.SCM.Markov

CausalInference/SCM/Markov.lean · 197 lines · 13 public theorems · 4 definitions · imports SCM.Basic, Graphical.LocalMarkov

The causal Markov condition. The distribution induced by a finite Markovian structural causal model factorizes according to its graph, with the kernel of v given by the law of f v z (u v) for each parent configuration z; hence it satisfies the local (parental) Markov property. Conversely, every distribution that factorizes according to an acyclic graph is induced by a structural causal model on that graph.

Public declarations (17)

CausalInference.SCM.kerneldefinition

def kernel (v : V) (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) : FiniteDist (α v)

The kernel of v: the law of the value M.f v z e of v when its parents take the values z and its noise e has law M.noise v.

CausalInference.SCM.kernel_applytheorem

theorem kernel_apply (v : V) (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) (a : α v) :
  M.kernel v z a = (M.noise v).probOf (fun e => M.f v z e = a)

The kernel of v at a is the noise probability that the structural function of v returns a.

CausalInference.SCM.kernelsdefinition

def kernels : G.MarkovKernels α

The kernels of the model as Markov kernels of the graph.

CausalInference.SCM.kernels_kerneltheorem

theorem kernels_kernel (v : V) (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) (a : α v) :
  M.kernels.kernel v z a = M.kernel v z a

CausalInference.SCM.kernels_factortheorem

theorem kernels_factor (v : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  M.kernels.factor v x =
    (M.noise v).probOf (fun e => M.f v ((G.parentsFinset v).restrict x) e = x v)

The factor of v at a configuration x is the noise probability that the structural equation of v holds at x.

CausalInference.SCM.filter_solve_eqtheorem

theorem filter_solve_eq (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  (univ.filter fun u => M.solve u = x) =
    Fintype.piFinset fun v => univ.filter fun e => M.f v ((G.parentsFinset v).restrict x) e =
      x v

The noise values at which the solution is x form a rectangle: at each vertex, the noise values that make the structural equation of that vertex hold at x.

CausalInference.SCM.dist_eq_prodtheorem

theorem dist_eq_prod (x : ∀ v, α v) : M.dist x = ∏ v, M.kernels.factor v x

Factorization of the induced distribution: the mass of a configuration is the product of the kernels of the vertices at that configuration.

CausalInference.SCM.factorizestheorem

theorem factorizes : G.Factorizes M.dist

Causal Markov condition, factorization form: the distribution induced by a Markovian structural causal model factorizes according to its graph.

CausalInference.SCM.localMarkovtheorem

theorem localMarkov : G.LocalMarkov M.dist

Causal Markov condition (Pearl 2009, Theorem 1.4.1): the distribution induced by a Markovian structural causal model satisfies the parental Markov condition relative to its graph. Every vertex is conditionally independent of its nondescendants other than its parents, given its parents.

CausalInference.SCM.margAt_insert_parentstheorem

theorem margAt_insert_parents (v : V) (x : ∀ v, α v) :
  M.dist.margAt (insert v (G.parentsFinset v)) x =
    M.kernel v ((G.parentsFinset v).restrict x) (x v) * M.dist.margAt (G.parentsFinset v) x

The kernel of v is the conditional law of v given its parents under the induced distribution, in product form: P(x_v, x_pa) = kernel v x_pa x_v * P(x_pa).

CausalInference.SCM.margAt_of_ancestraltheorem

theorem margAt_of_ancestral {A : Finset V} (hA : ∀ v ∈ A, ∀ u, G.Adj u v → u ∈ A)
  (x : ∀ v, α v) : M.dist.margAt A x = ∏ v ∈ A, M.kernels.factor v x

On a set A closed under taking parents, the marginal of the induced distribution is the product of the kernels of the vertices of A.

CausalInference.SCM.dist_eq_of_kernel_eqtheorem

theorem dist_eq_of_kernel_eq {ε' : V → Type*} [∀ v, Fintype (ε' v)] {M' : SCM G α ε'}
  (h : ∀ v z a, M.kernel v z a = M'.kernel v z a) : M.dist = M'.dist

Two models on the same graph with the same kernels induce the same distribution.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.rowdefinition

def row (k : G.MarkovKernels α) (v : V) (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) :
  FiniteDist (α v)

The row of the kernel of v at the parent configuration z, as a finite distribution.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.toSCMdefinition

def toSCM (k : G.MarkovKernels α) (hG : G.IsAcyclic) :
  SCM G α (fun v => (∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) → α v)

The structural causal model with response-function noise realizing the kernels k of an acyclic graph. The noise of v is a response function r from parent configurations to values of v; its values r z at the different parent configurations are independent with laws k.kernel v z; and the structural equation of v is x v = r (x restricted to the parents).

Digraph.MarkovKernels.kernel_toSCMtheorem

theorem kernel_toSCM (k : G.MarkovKernels α) (hG : G.IsAcyclic) (v : V)
  (z : ∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) (a : α v) :
  (k.toSCM hG).kernel v z a = k.kernel v z a

The kernels of the response-function model are the given kernels.

Digraph.MarkovKernels.dist_toSCMtheorem

theorem dist_toSCM (k : G.MarkovKernels α) (hG : G.IsAcyclic) :
  (k.toSCM hG).dist = k.jointDist hG

The response-function model induces the product of the kernels.

Digraph.Factorizes.exists_scmtheorem

theorem _root_.Digraph.Factorizes.exists_scm {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {G : Digraph V}
  [DecidableRel G.Adj] {α : V → Type*} [∀ v, Fintype (α v)] [∀ v, DecidableEq (α v)]
  (hG : G.IsAcyclic) {p : FiniteDist (∀ v, α v)} (h : G.Factorizes p) :
  ∃ M : SCM G α (fun v => (∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) → α v), M.dist = p

Every factorizing distribution has a functional model (Pearl 2009, section 1.4.2): a distribution that factorizes according to an acyclic graph G is the distribution induced by a structural causal model on G. The noise types are the response-function types (∀ u : G.parentsFinset v, α u) → α v.
